sens: Raise one's voice to speak, shout, or call
Take the floor, begin to say something
H2200.detail:
1. The word evokes the idea of shouting or calling out loud: it is to raise one's voice in a clear and audible manner. In Daniel 6:20, the king approaches the lion's den and "takes the floor" — that is, he raises his voice to address Daniel, with a sad voice full of emotion.
2. More broadly, "take the floor" means to begin to speak, to express a thought or a question. The emphasis is on the moment when someone breaks the silence or comes out of their mutism to communicate with someone else.
H2200.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew verb זָעַק (zâ'aq), which literally means "to cry out" or "to call out loud." The root evokes the cry that bursts forth, the urgent call that must be heard. In Hebrew, this verb is used when one cries out to God in distress, or when one calls someone with force. The Aramaic retains exactly this vocal force.
H2200.emploi: This word appears only once in the Aramaic Bible, in Daniel 6:20. King Darius, who has just discovered that Daniel has survived the night in the lion's den, approaches the entrance and "takes the floor" in a sad voice to call Daniel. This moment is crucial: it is when the king, shaken and moved, breaks the silence to check if God's servant is alive. The unique use of the word underscores the emotional intensity of the scene.
H2200.portee: This word shows us King Darius at a moment of sincere vulnerability: he cries out to Daniel, not as a powerful sovereign, but as a troubled man seeking an answer. It is a reminder that true power belongs to God and to those who trust Him, and that even the most powerful kings must acknowledge this reality when their own strength fails.

sens: A powerful vocal sound, an exclamation made with force
A loud protest, a tumult that can be heard
The audible expression of great suffering or distress
The desperate call of one seeking help or justice
The rumor, the news that spreads and circulates
A lament, a prolonged complaint about misfortune
H2201.detail:
1. A powerful vocal sound, an exclamation made with force: the word primarily designates the raw cry, the voice raised intensely. Mordecai "cries out bitterly" (Esther 4:1) upon learning of the death decree against the Jews — it is a cry of brutal pain.
2. A loud protest, a tumult that can be heard: the cry becomes a public manifestation of indignation or revolt. "The cries surround the borders of Moab" (Isaiah 15:8) evokes the sound of collective distress resonating beyond the walls.
3. The audible expression of great suffering or distress: the cry conveys agony, a pain that cannot be contained. The cry of the poor in Proverbs 21:13 is the cry of one suffering from injustice.
4. The desperate call of one seeking help or justice: the cry rises to the one who can hear and help. The word in Genesis 18:20 ("the cry against Sodom") refers to the very accusation that rises to God's ears.
5. The rumor, the news that spreads and circulates: the cry becomes a message that travels. "A cry is heard among the nations" (Jeremiah 50:46) — the news of Babylon's fall spreads across the world.
6. A lament, a prolonged complaint about misfortune: less violent than the cry of a moment, it is the groaning that lasts, the expression of mourning. Jeremiah 20:16 distinguishes "the groans in the morning" and "the cries of war at noon" — different sufferings.
H2201.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root (צעק, zaaq) which means "to cry out" or "to call out loud." It is a fundamental word in the Bible to express the voice in distress: the cry opposes silence, it breaks the mutism and demands to be heard. The root is present throughout the Hebrew Bible and designates both human cries and those of animals, but especially the call that rises to God.
H2201.emploi: The word appears 18 times, mainly in the prophets (Jeremiah and Isaiah) and in the wisdom books. It first describes the personal cry of distress (Mordecai, Job), then expands to the collective and political cry (the borders of Moab, the fall of Babylon). In Proverbs, it expresses the call of the poor for justice. In Genesis 18:20, it almost becomes a moral entity: the cry of the victims rises to God as a witness and an accusation. The term can refer to both the instantaneous cry and the prolonged lament, depending on the context. The Bible uses this word to say that suffering does not remain silent: it cries out, it testifies, it demands accountability.
H2201.portee: This word reminds the reader that suffering has a voice and should not be ignored. The cry of the poor, the weak, the oppressed is the signal of an injustice that rises to God. For the believer, it is an invitation to listen to this cry, not to turn a deaf ear (as in Proverbs 21:13), and to understand that God Himself hears the cry of His suffering children. It is also an assurance: our distress, when it cries out to God, does not fall into indifference.

sens: Location situated on the northern boundary of the promised land
H2202.detail: Ziphron is a place that marked the northern boundary of the territory that God promised to Israel. Moses lists the borders of the land in Numbers 34, and Ziphron is mentioned as a landmark on this northern boundary, before reaching Hatsar-Enan.
H2202.origine: The name Ziphron literally means "fragrance" or "pleasant odor," perhaps because this place was characterized by aromatics or fragrant vegetation. However, it is primarily its role as a territorial boundary that has preserved its memory in the biblical text.
H2202.emploi: Ziphron appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 34:9, in Moses' speech listing the borders of the promised land. It is a geographical reference point with no other function in the biblical narrative than to precisely delineate the territory entrusted to Israel.

sens: black, viscous substance used for waterproofing
material intended to burn
H2203.detail: 1. Pitch is a black, thick, and sticky substance, similar to bitumen or tar. It is applied to surfaces to make them waterproof: in Exodus 2:3, Moses is placed in a basket coated with pitch and tar so that it does not take on water from the Nile. 2. Pitch can also refer to a flammable material that burns: in Isaiah 34:9, the land of Edom is compared to burning pitch, to express destruction and divine judgment — an image of absolute desolation.
H2203.origine: The Hebrew word זֶפֶת (zéphet) belongs to the vocabulary of materials and substances. Its exact etymology is debated, but it clearly designates a viscous and black material, probably related to terms denoting natural asphalt or tar known in Mesopotamia and the Near East. The Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament) translates it with Greek terms designating bitumen or pitch.
H2203.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 2:3, it is used in the account of Moses' birth: the baby's mother uses pitch to waterproof the basket that will protect him from the waters of the Nile. In Isaiah 34:9, the prophet uses it in his vision of judgment on Edom, where burning pitch represents total destruction — the concrete sense (waterproofing substance) gives way to an eschatological sense (material of destruction). These two uses show the practical use of the word and its symbolic weight among the prophets.
H2203.portee: For the reader, the pitch in Exodus 2 reminds us that God can use the simplest and most concrete means to save and protect His people. In Isaiah, it becomes a sign that divine judgment transforms even material elements into instruments of punishment — an image that invites us to take seriously the reality of God's judgment.

sens: Hair that grows on a man's chin and cheeks
Lower part of the face, the chin
H2206.detail:
1. The beard refers to the hair that covers the lower part of a man's face. It is a distinctive feature of masculinity in biblical culture. It can be long and full (like Aaron's, mentioned in Psalm 133:2, where the anointing oil "runs down on the beard"), or shaved as a sign of mourning or shame (like the eighty men in Jeremiah 41:5 who had "shaved beards and torn clothes"). The beard could also be grasped as a gesture of friendship or aggression: Joab "took hold of Amasa's beard to kiss him" before killing him (2 Samuel 20:9).
2. The term also refers to the chin itself, the part of the face where the beard grows. Leviticus 13:29 speaks of a sore "on the head or on the beard," thus distinguishing the different parts of the body affected by the disease.
H2206.origine: The Hebrew word זָקָן (zaqan) literally means "beard" or "that which grows on the chin." It is related to the idea of old age and virility: a man with a fine beard was a sign of maturity and dignity. In ancient Near Eastern cultures, shaving the beard was an act of humiliation or mourning.
H2206.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily to denote the beard as a physical trait or as an element of ritual law. The laws in Leviticus (13:29-30, 14:9, 19:27, 21:5) mention the beard in the context of impurities (skin disease) or prohibitions concerning priests. In narrative context, shaving or cutting the beard carries a strong emotional weight: it symbolizes shame, mourning, or humiliation. Isaiah 7:20 prophesies that the Lord will shave the people's beard as a sign of judgment. David, to mock his enemies, "let his saliva run down his beard" (1 Samuel 21:13), showing how this physical trait marked a man's appearance and dignity.
H2206.portee: Understanding the role of the beard in the Bible helps the reader grasp the symbolic significance of gestures that may seem trivial to us today. Shaving the beard was not merely an aesthetic choice, but a meaningful act: a sign of penitence, shame, or transformation. It illustrates how the Bible associates physical appearance with spiritual state or relationship with God. It is also a reminder that the dignity of the body and its presentation reflect inner realities.

sens: the advance in age, the state of one who has become old
the weakening of the body and its strength that accompanies the later years
H2207.detail:
1. Old age refers to the time of life when a person has aged, when they have accumulated years. It is the natural state of one who has reached a great age, when life has been prolonged for a long time. In Genesis 48:10, Israel (Jacob) is so advanced in age that his sight has become dim and he can hardly see — old age has weakened his eyes.
2. The word also evokes gradual weakening: strength diminishes, the body no longer responds as before, the senses dull. This is why Israel needs to be guided, and his sons approach him so that he can bless them despite his physical frailty.
H2207.origine: The Hebrew word זֹקֶן (zoqen) comes from a root that expresses the idea of aging, of becoming old. It is from the same family as the adjective "old" (zaqen) — in Hebrew, the noun and the adjective are very close. The basic image is that of time accumulating on a person and gradually transforming them.
H2207.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (in Genesis 48:10). It precisely describes Israel's state at the moment he blesses the sons of Joseph: he is a very old man whose eyes are heavy, symbolizing the physical decline that accompanies extreme old age. The word emphasizes that despite advanced age and the weakening of the senses, Israel retains his dignity and his role as patriarch who blesses his descendants.
H2207.portee: Old age in the Bible is never presented as mere decay. In Genesis 48, it accompanies wisdom and the power to bless: Israel, although physically weakened, remains the one who transmits the inheritance to future generations. For the Christian, this word reminds us that the years pass, that the body weakens, but that God also gives old age dignity and a function in His plan.

sens: advanced age, the later years of human life
the time when one can no longer bear children or accomplish easily what one once could
the time when one becomes weak and dependent
H2208.detail: 1. Old age is the extreme stage of human life, when one has accumulated years and approaches the end. God tells Abraham that he will become a father "in his old age" (Genesis 21:2): this is a miracle, for at such an advanced age nature no longer allows for having children. 2. It is also the stage where the body weakens and strength declines. Israel "had Joseph "in his old age" (Genesis 37:3), which explains why he loved him so tenderly: this child born late was a miraculous gift. 3. In the narratives, this age creates dependence: one can no longer fight or travel easily. Joseph's younger brother, "child of his father's old age," remains alone with an old father who loves him and cannot leave him (Genesis 44:20): this is the image of mutual fragility.
H2208.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be old" or "to grow old." It is a very concrete notion: it designates what happens to the body over time, when strength fades. The Bible sees old age not as a shame, but as a dignified age when one has walked with God. In ancient texts, having children at this age is always a miracle, a special blessing from the Creator.
H2208.emploi: The word appears only four times in biblical Hebrew, all in Genesis, and in a very particular context: that of late and miraculous births. Sarah and Abraham had Isaac "in his old age" (Genesis 21:2, 21:7) — it is such an extraordinary event that Sarah herself is astonished. Similarly, Jacob had Joseph in his old age (Genesis 37:3), which explains the special affection he has for him. These usages show that old age is seen as a time when only God can act against nature.
H2208.portee: For the Christian, old age in these narratives is never a time of abandonment or misfortune. It instead becomes the moment when God fulfills His promises in a way that exceeds what one might expect. Abraham and Sarah experience that God does not forget them, and that His promise persists even when the body weakens. It is a lesson in trust: the passing years do not suspend divine faithfulness.

sens: The state of being old, the later years of life
The time when the body weakens and strength declines
An era marked by physical wear and fragility
A period when hair turns gray and one becomes more dependent on others
H2209.detail: 1. Old age is the final stage of human life, when years have accumulated. This is what Sarah experiences when she gives birth in her old age (Genesis 24:36): an age when procreation was no longer naturally possible. 2. Old age is accompanied by a decline in physical strength. Asa suffers from his feet in his old age (1 Kings 15:23), and the psalmist fears being abandoned when his strength fades (Psalms 71:9): it is a growing fragility of the body. 3. Old age makes one vulnerable to external influences and temptations. Solomon in his old age sees his wives turn his heart toward other gods (1 Kings 11:4): age does not spare one from waywardness. 4. Old age is visibly manifested by the graying of hair, referred to as "gray hair" (Psalms 71:18), an outward sign of the wear of time.
H2209.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means to be ancient, to grow old. It designates the natural state of one who has reached an advanced age. The image of "gray hair" relies on the visible transformation of hair that turns gray with age. It is a simple and direct term to speak of the universal phenomenon of human aging.
H2209.emploi: The word is used six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly to describe a period of life when a person loses their vigor. It appears in various contexts: the miracle of Sarah's birth in her old age, Asa's infirmities, Solomon's moral waywardness in old age, and especially in Psalm 71 where the psalmist pleads with God not to abandon him at this stage of his life. Isaiah 46:4 enriches the meaning by showing that God accompanies His people even into old age and beyond. The word paints old age as a physical reality (weakness, graying) and moral (vulnerability).
H2209.portee: Old age reminds the believer that life is limited and that each stage requires renewed trust in God. The cry of Psalm 71:9 is a prayer that any elderly person can make: not to be abandoned when strength declines. Isaiah 46:4 offers a precious promise: God will not cease to accompany and support His people, even in old age. It is a source of hope in the face of the wear of time.

sens: To lift someone from the ground or to set them upright
To raise or erect what was bent
To restore or reinstate in dignity
H2210.detail:
1. To lift up literally means to raise someone who has fallen or is lying on the ground, to set them upright. It is the physical action of one who supports an unfortunate person and lifts them from the ground. In Psalms 145:14, the Lord "upholds all who are falling," an image of concrete lifting.

2. The verb also evokes the gesture of lifting up what was bent or bowed — not only to lift a person but to straighten their posture, their appearance. Both passages speak of those who are "bent": to lift up means to free them from that position.

3. To lift up takes on a moral and spiritual meaning: to restore someone to their dignity, to raise them from their humiliation or misery. This goes beyond physical movement. When God lifts up the bent (Psalms 146:8), He not only restores their standing but also their honor and hope.
H2210.origine: The Hebrew verb zaqqaph comes from a root that suggests upward movement, erection. Its Aramaic equivalent zeqaph (used in the Aramaic passages of the Bible) carries the same meaning. The root evokes the image of regained verticality, the transition from bending to straightness — a vivid and very biblical image of divine restoration.
H2210.emploi: The verb zaqqaph appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in Psalms, in hymns of praise to the Lord. In Psalms 145:14, it describes the Lord who "upholds all who fall" and lifts up the bent — an act of mercy towards the weak. In Psalms 146:8, the same gesture is presented as a manifestation of divine goodness: He "lifts up those who are bent," alongside other acts of rescue (opening the eyes of the blind). In both cases, to lift up is an act of God alone, a divine privilege that shows His love for the humble and the suffering.
H2210.portee: This word reminds the believer that God does not despise those who have fallen or are broken. It is a promise of restoration: not by our own strength, but by the action of God Himself. For one who feels bent under the weight of their trials, to lift up brings hope that the Lord will see them, lift them up, and restore dignity and freedom. It is a word of consolation and honor granted to the poor and the humiliated.

sens: A piece of wood, a beam that is erected vertically
A beam erected to serve as a gallows or execution post
H2211.detail: 1. The word designates a piece of wood, a beam. In Ezra 6:11, it refers to a beam that is torn from the house of a transgressor to be erected: "a piece of wood shall be torn from his house, and it shall be erected." 2. This erected beam becomes an instrument of execution, a gallows. The meaning of "to erect" implies that it is raised vertically to become a post or a cross from which to hang the condemned. The act of "erecting" (zakaph) the beam transforms it into an instrument of public punishment and humiliation.
H2211.origine: The Aramaic word זְקַף (zeqaph) comes from the verb zakaph (זָקַף), which literally means "to raise" or "to erect." The root evokes the action of lifting something up, of putting it upright. It is a specifically Aramaic word, used in the Aramaic portion of the book of Ezra (chapters 4 to 7), which recounts the story of the reconstruction of the temple after the exile.
H2211.emploi: This word appears only once in biblical Aramaic, in Ezra 6:11, in the decree of King Darius regarding the temple in Jerusalem. The king orders that anyone who transgresses his edict shall have a piece of wood torn from their house and erected for them to be attached to — a penalty of execution in use in the Persian empire. This legal and political context shows the word used to describe an action of authority and royal punishment.
H2211.portee: This passage reveals how the Bible reports the laws and customs of pagan empires, including their terrible punishments, without endorsing them. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that God governs even the kingdoms of the world and that His word regarding the reconstruction of His temple prevails over human threats. The contrast between the gallows intended for transgressors and the divine protection of the temple invites trust in God.

sens: To purify a metal by separating impurities through heat or refining
To make pure and clear by filtering or distilling
To refine, perfect by eliminating the superfluous
In a figurative sense: to purify morally or spiritually
H2212.detail:
1. To purify a metal by separating impurities through heat or refining: the word evokes the work of the metallurgist who melts gold or silver in fire to eliminate what is not pure. The altar of incense "purified" in 1 Chronicles 28:18 refers to gold purified by this process, of absolute purity intended for divine service. This is the most concrete image of the word.

2. To make pure and clear by filtering or distilling: the word also applies to the separation of undesirable elements from a liquid. In Isaiah 25:6, the "clarified" wines have become clear and noble, freed from their lees. It is to refine the material to make it worthy of presentation.

3. To refine, perfect by eliminating the superfluous: in Job 28:1, gold is drawn from the ground to be "refined," emphasizing not the chemical separation but the gradual improvement. The silver "purified" seven times in Psalms 12:7 becomes a symbol of what has gone through trial and comes out incomparably better.

4. In a figurative sense: to purify morally or spiritually: this is the transition from the physical to the moral. The words of the Lord in Psalms 12:7 are compared to refined silver, not for their chemical composition, but for their absolute integrity. God purifies His people as fire purifies metal.
H2212.origine: The Hebrew verb זָקַק (zaqaq) is formed from a root expressing the idea of separating, sifting. The basic image is that of a sieve or flame that separates the pure from the impure. The word belongs to the vocabulary of refining, like its cognates in Semitic languages. This root reflects the concrete experience of ancient Middle Eastern peoples who mastered the art of purifying precious metals and oils, essential activities for religious and economic life.
H2212.emploi: The verb appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the context of purifying precious metals intended for worship: the gold of the altar of incense, the weight of the gold from Ophir, and the silver used to cover the temple buildings (1 Chronicles 28:18 and 29:4). In Job 28:1, it refers to the process of extracting and refining gold and silver. Psalm 12:7 transfers the image to the words of God, tested and purified. In Isaiah 25:6, old wines are "clarified." The word thus gains a theological significance: what is "purified" is not only made technically pure but made worthy to serve God or to manifest His nature.
H2212.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on spiritual purification: just as fire tests gold and leaves only the essential, God purifies the believer's heart. The comparison of God's words to refined silver (Psalms 12:7) reminds us that the divine Word withstands every trial and emerges incomparably precious and reliable. For the Christian, this is a promise: God purifies us not to destroy us, but to make us fit for His service and communion.

sens: Edge or frame that borders an object
Relief ornament applied to the perimeter of a surface
Crown or circle placed around the head
H2213.detail:
1. A border is an edge that runs all around an object, like the raised edge of a table or chest. In Exodus 25:25, Moses is instructed to make a border of four fingers around the table of gold, then to place a border of gold on it: this is a protective and ornamental band that frames the perimeter.
2. This element is often a molding, that is, a decorative work in relief that runs all around. In Exodus 30:3, the gold border is placed on the altar of incense "all around," forming an ornamental belt that enhances and protects it.
3. The word can also refer to a circle or crown worn on the head, although this usage does not appear in the verses from the Segond 1910 provided here.
H2213.origine: The word זֵר comes from a root that means "to turn" or "to surround": a border is that which turns around something. In the Greek Bible, this word is often rendered by στέφανος (stephanos), which means crown or victory crown. The family of זֵר includes words that express the idea of circle or circular movement.
H2213.emploi: The word אר appears 10 times in Exodus, exclusively to designate the gold ornaments of the sanctuary furniture: the ark of the covenant, the table, the altar of incense. Each time, the border is a band of gold that runs "all around" the object. It is a detail of the execution of the sanctuary: Moses is instructed to make these borders in Exodus 25, and in Exodus 37, Bezalel and his workers faithfully carry them out. The border is never alone: it always accompanies an object covered in pure gold, which underscores the holiness of the worship furniture.
H2213.portee: The border, although a small detail, reveals how God demands perfection in every aspect of the service of the sanctuary, even in the ornamentation of the perimeter. It shows that nothing is negligible in the worship of God: every part of the furniture, even the smallest, receives attention and beauty. For the believer, this reminds us that faithfulness to God is also manifested in the details.

sens: Physical sensation of repulsion and nausea
Visceral rejection in the face of something that can no longer be tolerated
H2214.detail:
1. It is the feeling one experiences when something deeply displeases us, to the point of raising the stomach. In Numbers 11:20, the manna, this bread from heaven that God gave daily to the Israelites, will become so nauseating to them that it will come out of their nostrils — an extreme image of satiety turning into total disgust.
2. This word also expresses moral and emotional rejection: the Israelites, having disgust for the manna, manifest their deep discontent towards God Himself, whom they have rejected. It is a rejection of the soul, not just of the stomach.
H2214.origine: This Hebrew root evokes the idea of something that raises the heart, that repulses. It refers to a bodily reaction to what is intolerable or repulsive. The word belongs to the semantic field of discomfort and deep aversion.
H2214.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the book of Numbers. God warns Moses that the manna, this daily miracle, will become a thing of disgust for the Israelites — not because the miracle would cease, but because their ingratitude and rebellion will prevent them from enjoying it. It is an act of divine judgment: the gift becomes a burden for one who rejects it.
H2214.portee: This passage reminds us that the rejection of God corrupts even the very blessings He gives us. Ingratitude can turn a miracle into a curse. It is a warning against murmuring and discontent: when we forget from whom our provisions and life come, even abundance becomes unbearable.

sens: To become dry, to dry out under the action of heat
To lose its water, its moisture
To disappear, to cease flowing (referring to a spring or a watercourse)
H2215.detail: 1. The verb describes the action of heat that dries and empties a space of water: melted snow or winter streams disappear when the warmth of the sun arrives. In Job 6:17, Job mentions the melting torrents that "dry up" as soon as the heat returns — the water evaporates or seeps away, leaving the bed dry. 2. It is the natural process of drying: what was full and flowing becomes hollow and arid. 3. Figuratively, the verb is suitable to express the exhaustion or gradual disappearance of what sustains life — water, strength, hope.
H2215.origine: The Hebrew root describes the action of drying or burning. The verb appears here in the passive form ("to be burned", "to be dried up"), which emphasizes that it is the heat of the sun acting on the water, not the water itself acting. This passive form highlights the transformative power of desert heat.
H2215.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 6:17. Job uses it to describe the fragility of desert torrents — those abundant watercourses in winter that completely disappear in summer under the burning sun. It is a poetic image of inconsistency: what one relies on can suddenly abandon us, just like a torrent that dries up. Job implicitly applies it to the friendship of his companions, who have disappointed him.
H2215.portee: This image of the torrent that dries up teaches the fragility of everything that is not founded on God. It invites the Christian not to place his trust in what is perishable or changeable — wealth, human friendship, earthly strength — but to seek the inexhaustible source that is the presence of God.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the exile and return
Grandson of King Jehoiachin
Leader of the first caravan of repatriates returning from Babylon
Governor of Judah after the return
He who laid the foundations of the second temple
H2216.detail:
1. Zerubbabel is a figure in the history of Israel who lived during the Babylonian captivity and the subsequent return. He was born in exile and belongs to the royal lineage of the kingdom of Judah.
2. He is the grandson of King Jehoiachin, which gives him particular importance: he carries within him the continuity of the Davidic line even during the deportation.
3. After the fall of Babylon, Zerubbabel becomes the political leader of the first wave of Jews returning to their land, around 538 BC. This is an act of national restoration.
4. He serves as governor of Judah, meaning he administers the territory on behalf of the Persian king who allows it. Haggai 1:1 calls him "governor of Judah."
5. His most famous role is to lead the reconstruction of the Jerusalem temple, destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar. Ezra 3:8 shows Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua organizing the work, along with the priests, Levites, and the people.
H2216.origine: The name Zerubbabel literally means "sown in Babylon" or "sprouted in Babylon." It is a symbolic name that reminds us that he was born in exile, far from the land of his fathers, but that God has not forgotten him. In some texts like Ezra 1:8 and 5:14, he is also called Shealtiel, which shows the variations of names at that time. His Greek name, Zerubbabel, is the one used in Greek translations and that Matthew uses in the genealogy of Jesus.
H2216.emploi: Zerubbabel appears about 20 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, and Zechariah, which recount the return from exile. He is first mentioned in 1 Chronicles 3:19 as the son of Pedaiah. Then, during the return in 538, he is presented as a leader: in Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 7:7, he is among the leaders of the return. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah address him directly between 520 and 515 BC, encouraging him to continue the temple work despite obstacles. Haggai 1:1 and 2:23 show that the Lord looks upon him with favor: "I will take you, Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, My servant." Zechariah 4:6-10 associates him with the vision of the golden lampstand, a sign that the Lord supports this restoration. His role diminishes after the completion of the temple, around 515.
H2216.portee: Zerubbabel embodies the hope of the people of God at a time when everything seems lost. Even in exile, far from the promised land, God preserves the Davidic lineage and brings His people back. For today's believer, Zerubbabel shows that God honors those who serve Him faithfully in difficult circumstances and that no captivity can prevent His plan of salvation. His presence in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1:12 reminds us that Jesus Himself descends from this leader of the return, linking the Messiah to the restoration of Judah.

sens: The leader of the Judeans returned from exile in Babylon
Grandson of King Jehoiachin
Governor of Judah under Persian rule
H2217.detail: Zerubbabel is a key figure in the return from exile: he leads the first group of Judeans returning from Babylon to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 5:2). His name means "sown in Babylon," reflecting his status as an exile born far from his homeland. He is the grandson of King Jehoiachin, captive in Babylon, which gives him royal legitimacy among the exiles. Under Persian authority, he serves as governor of Judah and wields recognized authority, working alongside the high priest Joshua to restore worship in Jerusalem.
H2217.origine: His Aramaic name (זְרֻבָּבֶל) literally means "sown in Babylon": zera = seed, and Babel = Babylon. This poetic name captures the tragedy of exile: born or raised in captivity, he embodies a whole generation of exiles whose vocation is to return and cultivate the promised land again. Zerubbabel also appears under the name Sheshbazzar in some passages of Ezra.
H2217.emploi: Zerubbabel is mentioned as a major actor in the return from exile in the 6th century BC. He is the son of Pedaiah and grandson of King Jehoiachin; he had several children, including Meshullam and Hananiah. In Ezra 5:2, he rises with Joshua the high priest to restart the interrupted construction of the temple. He plays a central role in the religious restoration of Judah, symbolizing the renewal of God's people after devastation.
H2217.portee: Zerubbabel embodies the hope of return and restoration: even in exile, the people of God are not abandoned. His leadership of the return and his role in the reconstruction of the temple show that God honors faithfulness and revives His people. For the believer, Zerubbabel reminds us that dark periods are never the final word in divine history.

sens: A stream east of the Jordan
A river that crosses the territory of Moab and Edom
A torrent that marked an important stage in the journey of the Israelites
H2218.detail:
1. Zered is a torrent located east of the Jordan, in the mountainous region of Moab and Edom. Its name literally means "willow," which evokes the shrubs that grew along its banks and characterized the waterways of the Middle East (Numbers 21:12).
2. This torrent marked an important natural boundary in the geography of the ancient Near East. The Israelites, during their crossing of the desert toward the Promised Land, had to cross it as a decisive step in their journey (Deuteronomy 2:13).
3. The crossing of the torrent of Zered symbolizes a turning point in the history of Israel: between the departure from Kadesh-Barnea and this moment, thirty-eight years had passed, year after year the rebellious generation was disappearing until only the new generation remained, the one that could enter the Promised Land (Deuteronomy 2:14).
H2218.origine: The name Zered comes from a Semitic root that means "willow," these typical plants of the wet areas of the desert. The word originally designates the torrent where these characteristic shrubs grew. It is a geographical name that describes the natural landscape of the place.
H2218.emploi: Zered appears three times in the Bible, exclusively in the book of Numbers and Deuteronomy, during the account of Israel's journey in the desert. In Numbers 21:12, it is a place where the people set up camp. In Deuteronomy 2:13-14, the torrent becomes a crucial landmark: its crossing marks the passage between two generations and recalls the fulfillment of the divine promise made forty years earlier in the desert. This torrent, although geographically secondary, holds major theological significance in the narrative of the march toward Canaan.
H2218.portee: The torrent of Zered reminds the reader that God guides His people through concrete and measurable steps. It also symbolizes God's patient judgment: the crossing of the torrent was only possible when the unbelieving generation had completely disappeared, showing how God honors His judgments while leading the rest of the people toward the fulfillment of His promise.

sens: To scatter, break into pieces or powder
To separate and send in different directions
To reduce to dust or debris
To conceal or annihilate
To disseminate someone or something among other peoples or in other places
H2219.detail:
1. The verb first describes the material action of scattering or reducing to dust: Moses takes the golden calf, reduces it to ashes, and then "sprinkles" this powder on the water (Exodus 32:20). The image is of something solid transforming into fine particles scattered.
2. It also means to separate and send things or people in opposite directions: "A wise king scatters the wicked" (Proverbs 20:26), meaning he puts them to flight in all directions.
3. In a very similar sense, the verb designates the action of winnowing grain: one throws the wheat into the air so that the wind carries away the chaff (Isaiah 30:24). This operation requires a gesture of dispersion.
4. The word also evokes the idea of annihilating or making disappear: to dissipate impurity or guilt (Ezekiel 22:15).
5. Used in the passive voice or with a human complement, it designates the tragic fate of those whom God scatters among the nations: "He who scattered Israel will gather him" (Jeremiah 31:10). This refers to exile, the breaking apart of a people.
H2219.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of extending, projecting, or breaking into pieces. The root is related to the image of throwing or casting. The word can also carry the idea of "flying away" or "scattering far away," particularly by the action of the wind. It is a concrete and visual verb that paints a palpable action.
H2219.emploi: The verb appears 38 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Ezekiel) and the Psalms. Two main usages dominate: the dispersion of peoples or nations as divine punishment (Ezekiel 5:12, Jeremiah 31:10), and the concrete action of winnowing, scattering materials, or reducing to dust (Exodus 32:20, Isaiah 30:24). The verb can be active (someone scatters) or passive (something or someone is scattered). In contexts of judgment, "to disperse" denotes a punishment that tears apart, separates, or exiles: it is the opposite of gathering (Jeremiah 31:10).
H2219.portee: This verb reminds the believer that God controls the destinies of peoples and can scatter them in judgment just as He can gather them in grace. For Israel, the promise "He who scattered Israel will gather him" (Jeremiah 31:10) affirms that no dispersion is final: the Lord holds His exiles in His hand. It is a word of judgment and hope at the same time.

sens: Member of the human or animal body, from the shoulder to the hand
Shoulder of a sacrificial victim
Strength, power, capacity to act
Mighty hand of God intervening to save
Army, troop, military or political power
H2220.detail:
1. The arm is the member of the body that extends from the shoulder to the hand. It is the instrument of our actions and our physical strength. Samson breaks the cords "that were on his arms" (Judges 16:12) to demonstrate his muscular power.
2. In the sacrificed animal, the shoulder (part of the arm) was taken as a holy portion (Numbers 6:19) and given to the priests according to the law.
3. The arm symbolizes strength and power: this is why we speak of having "an arm" like that of God (Job 40:4), or of girding one's loins "with strength" and strengthening one's arms (Proverbs 31:17) to describe courage and vigor.
4. The arm of God is His saving power: "His arm helps him" (Isaiah 59:16) to designate the direct, personal, and victorious intervention of the Lord with His people.
5. By extension, "arm" designates the armed forces or the political and military power: Ezekiel denounces the princes of Israel who "use their strength to shed blood" (Ezekiel 22:6).
H2220.origine: The Hebrew word זְרוֹעַ (zeroua) comes from a root that expresses the idea of brute strength and power. Linguistically close to other words designating what is extended or spread out, it primarily designates the member that extends from the body. In the Old Testament, this term appears more than 80 times, especially in praise texts (Psalms), historical books, and prophecies where God acts with power. The prophets particularly use "arm" to speak of the arm of the Lord revealing His justice and intervention.
H2220.emploi: This word appears about 84 times in the Old Testament. Its usage varies greatly depending on the context: it designates the physical arm in concrete narratives (Samson, sacrifices); it symbolizes personal strength in wisdom literature and psalms (Proverbs, Job); it especially characterizes the active power of God in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel), where "the arm of the Lord" becomes the key image of His salvation and judgment. God "lifts His arm" (Isaiah 51:5), "stretches out His arm" (Isaiah 40:10), or "shows His arm" (Isaiah 52:10) to designate His victorious intervention. The term can finally mean the military or political power of a nation (Ezekiel 22:6, Daniel 11:15).
H2220.portee: Understanding the "arm" of God in the Bible means grasping that the Lord is not distant: He intervenes personally, with strength and tenderness, among His people. This image assures us that His power is not abstract, but active and determined. For the believer today, it invites recognition that all true power comes from God alone, and that His strength is paradoxically manifested in weakness and service (as ultimately revealed in the Gospel).

sens: The grain or seeds that are sown in the ground for them to grow
What germinates and develops
Figuratively: that which produces fruit, growth
H2221.detail:
1. The seed is the grain or the collection of seeds that one entrusts to the earth for it to germinate and produce a harvest. It concretely refers to the living material that is sown: when dead insects fall on a seed intended to be planted, it remains impure according to the law of Leviticus (Leviticus 11:37). It is the material starting point, the act of sowing.
2. The seed also evokes what will germinate and grow — the process of germination that follows sowing. The psalmist sees the earth producing its germ and the garden making its seeds grow (Isaiah 61:11): it is the image of life in action, of growth from what has been planted.
3. Figuratively, the seed represents that which produces abundant fruit or transformation: in Isaiah, the Lord causes salvation and praise to germinate like a garden makes its seeds grow, showing that salvation grows and flourishes in praise, carried by the nations (Isaiah 61:11).
H2221.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to sow" and refers to the action of casting the seed into the ground and what naturally follows. The family of this word encompasses the idea of sowing, planting, harvesting — everything related to making something grow from a seed.
H2221.emploi: The word "seed" appears twice in the provided Bible. In Leviticus 11:37, it refers to the seed or seeds themselves, concretely, in a context of religious purity. In Isaiah 61:11, it expands: the seed becomes the image of natural and powerful growth, that of salvation flourishing like a garden — the meaning remains concrete, but the scope becomes spiritual and prophetic. It is in this second passage that the word truly shines: it paints the confidence in a divine reality that inevitably grows, like a seed that germinates.
H2221.portee: The seed reminds us that salvation and God's promises are not abstract: they germinate, they grow, they develop until visible flourishing. Like a seed that is sown, the Word and salvation have their own dynamic, carried by God, and we are invited to be transformed by what grows within us and around us.

sens: To pour water drop by drop or in fine rain on the ground
To gradually penetrate moisture into the soil
Figuratively: to fill someone with progressive and abundant blessings
H2222B.detail: 1. The word evokes the concrete image of fine rain falling drop by drop on a field, the rain that soaks the earth. In Psalms 72:6, the psalmist describes the righteous king as a beneficial rain that "waters" the countryside: the comparison suggests that his actions, like rain, bring life and fertility. 2. It is not a violent rain, but a gentle and regular shower that gradually penetrates the soil and makes it productive. This progressive saturation of water in the earth is the image of the word. 3. Applied to the king (or to God), "to water" means to fill, bless, to shower someone with goods and grace constantly and fruitfully, like rain nourishes the harvests.
H2222B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of dripping and liquid that seeps in. It is related to the image of fine rain and saturation: water that falls drop by drop and penetrates. The origin is probably onomatopoeic, imitating the soft sound of drops.
H2222B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 72:6. It is part of a royal psalm where the psalmist prays for the king and asks God that he be just and benevolent. The comparison with the watering rain expresses the hope that the king's justice will bring prosperity and well-being to all the people, just as the rain from heaven brings life to the fields. It is a poetic image of the radiance of just power.
H2222B.portee: This word reminds us that God's blessing, like rain on a dry field, acts gradually but surely. It invites the believer to see in small acts of justice and mercy a power of transformation: what seems weak (a fine rain) nourishes and fertilizes life. It is also a prayer that Christian authorities embody this life-giving benevolence towards those they govern.

sens: A swift and vigilant animal, probably a four-legged creature from antiquity
An animal girded or equipped, ready for action
H2223.detail:
1. The word designates an animal with a muscular body and thin flanks, ready to leap or move quickly. The image evokes a being on alert, tense and dynamic. In Proverbs 30:31, this animal is among the creatures that walk with majesty and grace.
2. The word can also emphasize the idea of being "girded" or "equipped," like someone who has donned their armor or who is prepared for action. It is the image of a creature whose loins are tight, ready to leap or to run.
H2223.origine: The Hebrew word zarzir evokes the idea of tightening, of cinching. Its etymology refers to a root expressing tension and vigilance. Although the exact form of this animal eludes us today — it could be a greyhound, a gazelle, or a now-extinct creature — the word captures the essence of a swift, supple, and alert creature, all nerves and muscles.
H2223.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 30:31. In this passage, it is part of a list of four beings that "walk with majesty": the lion, the rooster, the goat — or perhaps this animal — and finally the invincible king. These creatures symbolize nobility, pride, and dignity. The context suggests that the animal embodies one of the major traits of true greatness: vigilance and well-proportioned power.
H2223.portee: This word reminds us that in the created order, the Bible celebrates creatures that embody alert vigilance and contained strength. For the believer, it is an invitation to see in nature a reflection of admirable qualities: energy, constructive tension, the ability to move with grace and decisiveness. This majestic animal speaks to us of royalty, that which God admires in His creatures — strength tempered by agility.

sens: To speak of the sun or a celestial body rising on the horizon
To burst forth suddenly, to manifest visibly
To shine, to illuminate with intensity
To appear or emerge (referring to a person or thing)
To unfold, to become visible or manifest
H2224.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of the sun or a celestial body rising on the horizon at dawn: "The sun rose as he passed Peniel" (Genesis 32:31). This is the most natural image, that of the celestial body emerging from the earth and illuminating the new day.
2. The word is used for a sudden burst of light, a brilliance that suddenly appears: "He shone from Mount Paran" (Deuteronomy 33:2), where the glory of God manifests in a dazzling way. It is the radiance, the luminous appearance.
3. By extension, the verb describes what shines intensely or illuminates: "His rays after the rain bring forth grass from the earth" (2 Samuel 23:4), where the morning light produces a revitalizing effect.
4. The word can also refer to the sudden appearance of a disease or an event that "bursts forth": "leprosy broke out on his forehead" (2 Chronicles 26:19), like something that emerges and becomes visible without warning.
5. Generally, it refers to what rises, emerges, or manifests in clarity — when something passes from the invisible to the visible, or from rest to action.
H2224.origine: The Hebrew verb zarach first paints the image of the sun rising in the sky. The root expresses emergence, illumination. It is linked to the idea of clarity and manifestation: what "rises" becomes visible and radiant. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this word often translates passages where the light of God or His glory manifests, showing how ancient readers already saw in this verb an image of divine revelation.
H2224.emploi: The verb zarach appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily to describe the rising of the sun (Genesis 32:31; Psalms 104:22; Ecclesiastes 1:5) — this is the most common and concrete usage. It also applies to luminous or radiant manifestations of divine power: God who "rises" or "shines" from Seir or Paran (Deuteronomy 33:2), or the messianic light that "will rise" upon those who are in darkness (Isaiah 58:10; 60:1-2). Finally, it describes events that suddenly emerge: the leprosy that "broke out" on Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:19), or the harvest that "appears" in the fields (Judges 9:33). The meaning thus nuances from the physical to the spiritual, from natural observation to divine intervention.
H2224.portee: For the believer, this verb offers a powerful image of God's revelation and presence. When the Bible speaks of the sun rising, it invites recognition of this daily clarity as a sign of divine faithfulness — every morning, the light returns, God manifests. And when it announces that justice or the light of Christ "rises" upon those suffering in darkness, this word promises a certain and visible intervention. It teaches that God never acts in secrecy or half-measures: when He acts, it is seen, it shines, it changes everything. It is a message of hope for those who await the day.

sens: Light that emanates from a luminous source
Brightness that shines and radiates
In a figurative sense, that which spiritually illuminates or inspires
H2225.detail:
1. A ray is the light that escapes from a source, like the sun or a flame, and spreads through space. It is the visible and brilliant clarity that we perceive.
2. The word also designates the radiance that shines, this brilliance that illuminates everything around it. In Isaiah 60:3, the kings of the world walk in the light of the "rays" of restored Jerusalem, an image of divine light that attracts the nations.
3. Spiritually, the ray represents divine revelation, that which emanates from God to enlighten and guide; it is the inspiration and wisdom that come from heaven.
H2225.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to shine" or "to rise" (like the sun at dawn). It is linked to the idea of bursting light, of clarity that emerges. The basic image is that of the glow of the rising sun gradually illuminating the sky.
H2225.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible. It is found in Isaiah 60:3, where the prophet describes the future glory of Jerusalem. The kings of the world will be attracted by the "rays" emanating from the city, a symbol of messianic light. In this context of restoration and divine splendor, the word carries a strong prophetic charge: it is not merely physical light, but the brilliance of God's presence and blessing manifested visibly.
H2225.portee: This word reminds us that God is the source of light and that His presence radiates to attract and bless the nations. For the believer, it invites consideration of how divine light, coming from Christ and His Church, can illuminate the world and transform it. It is also a promise: the glory of God does not remain hidden; it shines and attracts.

sens: Descendant of Esau, duke of the Edomites
Son of Reuel and grandson of Esau
H2226G.detail: 1. Zerah is a figure from biblical antiquity, son of Reuel and grandson of Esau. He belongs to the lineage of Esau, the twin brother of Jacob, and is counted among the dukes or chiefs of the Edomites, the people descending from Esau. Genesis 36:13 and 36:17 mention him as one of the sons of Reuel, alongside his brothers Nahath, Shammah, and Mizzah. 2. Although few details are given about his personal life, his inclusion in the genealogy of the dukes of Edom (Genesis 36:17) shows that he held a position of chief or leader among the peoples of that region, reflecting the importance of his family in the history of Esau's descendants.
H2226G.origine: The name Zerah means "rising" or "to rise" in Hebrew, evoking the image of the sun or a light that rises. This name reflects the significance given to the image of dawn or beginning in biblical culture. The same name has been borne by several other biblical figures, notably a son of Judah, but the provided usages concern only this Zerah son of Reuel.
H2226G.emploi: Zerah appears three times in the Bible, all references found in the genealogies of Esau and his descendants. He is mentioned in Genesis 36:13 among the sons of Reuel and Basemath, Esau's wife, and again in Genesis 36:17 when these same sons are listed as chiefs or dukes of the Edomites. The third mention, in 1 Chronicles 1:37, reproduces this genealogy in the context of the chronological account of Israel. These passages show that Zerah was a recognized historical figure for his role in the leadership structure of the Edomites, although specific details of his actions are not transmitted to us.

sens: an Edomite chief of antiquity, father of Jobab
H2226H.detail: Zerah is the name of an Edomite chief mentioned in the genealogy of the kings of Edom. His son Jobab succeeded him as king after the death of Bela (Genesis 36:33 and 1 Chronicles 1:44). The name means "to rise" or "to rise up," evoking the image of the sun rising. Although few details are given about him, he holds a place in the royal lineage of Esau's descendants, the elder brother of Jacob.
H2226H.origine: The name Zerah comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to rise" or "to shine," like the sun rising on the horizon. This same name has been borne by other important figures in biblical history — notably a son of Judah and Tamar, and an Ethiopian general who attacked Judah during the reign of King Asa. In this specific case, it designates an Edomite king whose lineage has endured.
H2226H.emploi: Zerah is mentioned twice in the biblical texts, always in a genealogical context: in Genesis 36:33 and in 1 Chronicles 1:44, where these two verses report exactly the same fact. He is presented exclusively as the father of Jobab, who became king of Edom after him. These mentions are part of the official list of kings of Edom, which underscores the importance of royal succession in the chronicle of the nations contemporary to Israel.

sens: son of Judah and Tamar, ancestor of the Zerahites
H2226I.detail: Zerah is a character from the Old Testament, the twin son of Perez born from the union of Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38:30). His name means "rising" or "to rise," evoking the image of the sun rising: at his birth, he was the first to come out of his mother's womb, his hand marked with a scarlet thread, before his brother Perez surpassed him. Zerah becomes the founder of an important lineage in Israel: his descendants form the family of the Zerahites, mentioned in the census of the tribes during the wilderness period (Numbers 26:20). One of his most well-known descendants is Achan, who committed a serious infidelity by taking things devoted to the Lord during the conquest of Jericho, which provoked God's anger against all Israel (Joshua 7:1).
H2226I.origine: The name Zerah comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to rise" or "to shine," like a star at dawn. It is a name chosen intentionally for this child, as it reflects the order of his birth: although his hand came out first, it was his brother who surpassed him. The same root gives rise to several other Hebrew words related to light, dawn, and brightness.
H2226I.emploi: Zerah first appears in the account of Genesis 38, where he is born as the son of Judah, without a legally recognized father. He is one of the twelve ancestors of the tribes of Israel, his descendants being attested in the genealogical lists and censuses of Numbers and Chronicles. The main context where his name remains alive in the Bible is that of the scandal of Achan: Achan is designated as a descendant of Zerah (up to the fourth generation), and this genealogical link marks the shame that fell upon the house of Zerah because of this infidelity. Nevertheless, the tribe of the Zerahites continued to hold an honorable place in Israel and Judah.
H2226I.portee: Zerah embodies how God integrates complex human situations and irregular unions into the plan of salvation. His birth is the result of deception (Tamar deceives Judah), and yet God recognizes him as a legitimate ancestor of a tribe of Israel. This story reminds us that God acts according to His grace and not according to human justice, even when beginnings are tainted by sin. The story of Achan, his distant descendant, also shows how personal sin can affect an entire community, but also how confession and judgment can restore the relationship with God.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, living during the time of the Divided Monarchy
Son of the Levite Iddo
Father of the Levite Jeathraï
H2226J.detail: Zerah is a descendant of Levi mentioned twice in the genealogy of the Levites responsible for the temple service. He first appears in 1 Chronicles 6:21 as the son of Iddo and father of Jeathraï, in the direct genealogical line. A few verses later, in 1 Chronicles 6:41, he is presented in another branch of the same genealogy: he is the son of Zerah (partial list), confirming that he descends from Adaiah. The context shows that this Zerah lived during the period when Israel was divided into two kingdoms, and he was part of the Levitical families responsible for worship at the temple in Jerusalem.
H2226J.origine: The name Zerah means "he who rises" or "rising," evoking the image of the sun rising on the horizon. This name appears several times in biblical history for different characters: a son of Reuel and grandson of Esau among the Edomites, a twin brother of Perez among the sons of Judah, and a son of Simeon. Each Zerah is a distinct character in biblical history, linked to different genealogies.
H2226J.emploi: This Zerah is a Levite from the branch of Gershon, mentioned only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. He fits into the genealogical succession: Iddo (father) — Zerah — Jeathraï (son). The context of 1 Chronicles 6 lists the genealogies of the Levites set apart for temple service after the return from exile. Zerah represents a link in this long genealogical chain that ensured the continuity of Levitical worship.

sens: Ethiopian warrior who attacked the kingdom of Judah
Military leader defeated by King Asa
H2226K.detail:
1. Zerah is a military leader from Ethiopia (or Nubia) who marched against the kingdom of Judah with a huge army: a million soldiers and three hundred chariots (2 Chronicles 14:8). His invasion dates from the reign of King Asa and represents a major threat to Judah.
2. Despite the numerical superiority of his forces, Zerah was defeated by King Asa and his army, who trusted in the Lord in this battle. This victory allowed Judah to repel the invader and assert its political independence.
H2226K.origine: The name Zerah means "he who rises" or "he who shines" in Hebrew, an image of sunrise or dawn. Its etymology suggests a leader of prestige and authority. Although the Bible mentions him only once, ancient historians likely associate him with the Egyptian king Usarken I or Usarken II of the 22nd Egyptian dynasty, which would place his reign and invasion in the 10th-9th century BC.
H2226K.emploi: Zerah appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 14:8-9. He is presented as a king or Ethiopian leader who launched an attack on Judah during the time of King Asa. The text emphasizes the impressive power of his army (a million soldiers, three hundred chariots) but highlights the faith of King Asa and the deliverance granted by God, as Asa had sought the Lord before the battle. This episode illustrates how God supports His people when they turn to Him sincerely.
H2226K.portee: This story encourages the reader to trust in God even when circumstances seem overwhelming. Asa, king of Judah, faces a numerically superior army, but he calls on the Lord rather than relying on his military strength. The victory achieved shows that sincere faith in God outweighs numbers and material power, a motivating message for any Christian facing seemingly insurmountable challenges.

sens: Son of Simeon, ancestor of the Zerahites
H2226L.detail: Zerah is one of the twelve sons of Simeon (the second son of Jacob and Leah), living during the time of Egypt and the wilderness. He is first mentioned in Genesis 46:10 among the children of Simeon who go down to Egypt with Jacob. In Numbers 26:13, he appears during the census in the wilderness: the Zerahites, his descendants, form one of the families of the tribe of Simeon. In 1 Chronicles 4:24, his name is repeated in the genealogy of the sons of Simeon, confirming his place as an ancestor of an important branch of this tribe.
H2226L.origine: The name Zerah means "to rise" or "resurrection" in Hebrew, evoking the image of the sun rising. This name is borne by several important men in the Old Testament — notably a son of Judah and Tamar, twin of Perez — which underscores its use as a prestigious name in the genealogies of Israel.
H2226L.emploi: Zerah the Simeonite is mentioned twice in the Bible: in Numbers 26:13 and 1 Chronicles 4:24. In these two texts, he appears in the official genealogical lists as the son of Simeon and father of the Zerahites. His name appears between those of Jamin and Saul, his brothers. Although few details are given about his personal life, his presence in these records shows the importance of maintaining the genealogies of the tribes of Israel after the Exodus and during the civil organization of the people.

sens: Descendant de Zérach, fils de Siméon
Membre de la famille ou du clan de Zérach
H2227.detail:
1. The Zerachites are the descendants of Zerah, a son of Simeon. Zerah lived during the time of Egypt and the wilderness, and his children formed a distinctive family or clan within the tribe of Simeon, as seen in the census of the people in Numbers 26:13.
2. This term also broadly refers to the members of the clan or family of Zerah, who was an important man and founder of a lineage. We encounter it in Numbers 26:20, where the families of Judah are listed according to their ancestors, showing that several tribes had their own families bearing the name of their ancestor.
H2227.origine: The word comes from the name 'Zerah' (זֶרַח), which literally means 'rising sun' or 'dawn.' Zerachite is formed by adding the suffix of belonging to a family or clan. This term follows the common pattern in Hebrew for designating a group of descendants: a termination is added to the name of the founding father to obtain the name of his entire lineage.
H2227.emploi: The word appears five times in the Old Testament, primarily in census lists and genealogical records. In Numbers 26:13 and 26:20, the Zerachites are mentioned during the second census, as one of the families of the tribe of Simeon and then of Judah. In Joshua 7:17, during the designation by lot (under Joshua, concerning the sin of Achan), the family of Zerah is designated. In 1 Chronicles 27:11 and 27:13, military officers belonging to the family of the Zerachites are mentioned, showing that this family held important positions in the military organization of Israel.

sens: Prêtre lévite du temps de la monarchie divisée
Père du prêtre Meraioth et ancêtre du scribe Ezra
H2228G.detail:
1. Zerachja is a priest from the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of the divided monarchy of Israel. He is the son of Uzzi and the father of Meraioth, holding an important place in the priestly lineage. He is first mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6:6, in the genealogy of the priests.

2. Zerachja is also known as the father of Elihoenai, one of the sons of Pahath-moab whose descendants returned from captivity with the scribe Ezra. He is a direct ancestor of Ezra the scribe, highlighting his importance in the history of God's people and the restoration of worship after the exile.
H2228G.origine: The name Zerachja means 'The Lord has risen' or 'The Lord has shone' in Hebrew. It is formed from Zerah ('to rise', 'to shine') and Yah ('the Lord'). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the divine name, expressing a confession of faith in God's power.
H2228G.emploi: Zerachja appears in the genealogy of the Levitical priests who served in the Temple. In 1 Chronicles 6:6, he is situated in the genealogical chain linking the high priests of the time of the monarchy. In 1 Chronicles 6:51, his name appears again in a parallel list of the descendants of Aaron. In Ezra 7:4, he is mentioned as an ancestor of the scribe Ezra in his priestly genealogy. He is an important but little-detailed figure, known mainly by his place in these genealogical lists essential for establishing priestly legitimacy after the return from exile.
H2228G.portee: Zerachja reminds us that God preserved a faithful priestly lineage even during times of political turmoil and exile. His name, which means 'The Lord has risen,' invites us to see how God continues to watch over His people and the worship due to Him, generation after generation. It is a testimony to the continuity of divine grace in the history of Israel.

sens: Prêtre israelite du temps de l'Exil et du Retour
Père d'Éljoénaï, chef d'une famille qui revint de captivité avec Esdras
H2228H.detail:
1. Zérachja is an Israelite priest who lived during the time when God's people were in exile in Babylon and began to return to the Promised Land. His name means 'the Lord has risen' — a statement of trust in God during the difficult time of exile. He appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:4, where he is identified as the father of Elihoenai.
2. Elihoenai, the son of Zérachja, was a family leader from the descendants of Pahath-moab. When Ezra organized the return of the Israelites from Babylon to Jerusalem, Elihoenai led his group: two hundred men followed him. This mention shows that Zérachja was the head of a priestly household whose children participated in the restoration of God's people.
H2228H.origine: The name Zérachja is composed of two Hebrew elements: 'Zerah' (זרח), which means 'to rise' or 'to shine' (like the sun), and 'Yah' (יה), an abbreviation of the divine name. Literally, it means 'God has risen' or 'God has risen.' It is a typical theophoric name from the time of the return from exile, expressing the confidence that after the darkness of captivity, God raises His people.
H2228H.emploi: Zérachja is mentioned only once in the entire Bible: in Ezra 8:4. He is presented as the father of Elihoenai, a family leader belonging to the descendants of Pahath-moab. His son brought two hundred men during the return from the Babylonian exile organized by Ezra around 458 BC. This single mention shows that he was a figure of some importance in his community, sufficiently respected for his patronymic to be preserved in the official register of families that participated in the return.
H2228H.portee: The mention of Zérachja reminds us that behind every act of spiritual restoration are men and women, many of whom remain in the shadows. His name — 'the Lord has risen' — expresses what every exile awaited: that God would rise and lift up His people. For the Christian reader, this story of exile and return foreshadows the salvation brought by Jesus Christ, who raises us from the captivity of sin.

sens: Faire couler l'eau en abondance, en torrent
Emporter, balayer avec force
Épandre, répandre la puissance divine
H2229.detail:
1. The word first evokes the concrete image of water pouring out in mass: the clouds pour torrents of water during a violent storm (Psalms 77:18). It is a powerful and sudden action, irresistible, like a flood or inundation.
2. By extension, the word applies to anything that is swept away with the same force. Men are swept away like a dream that fades in the morning (Psalms 90:5): the action sweeps away, removes, erases.
3. Finally, this verb is used to describe how God unleashes His power in a striking manner, spreading and pouring it out. Divine strength is not held back: it manifests freely and completely, like water flooding or wind sweeping.
H2229.origine: The verb יָרַם (zarah) expresses the idea of something that gushes, flows, or spreads abundantly and uncontrollably. It comes from a root that refers to the impetuous movement of a flow: water, but also any form of overflowing power. The Bible uses this word in contexts of spectacular divine manifestation.
H2229.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalm 77, it describes the thunder and rain pouring down during a theophany, that is, a manifestation of God in nature: the clouds pour water. In Psalm 90, it takes on a more spiritual meaning: God sweeps men away in time as a flood sweeps everything away. These two uses show the transition from the concrete sense (pouring water) to the figurative sense (removing, making disappear with force).
H2229.portee: This word reminds us that divine power manifests itself irresistibly: it does not infiltrate gradually, it floods and sweeps away. For the believer, this can mean both the impressive greatness of God in creation and the seriousness of His judgment. In the face of eternity, our human lives are as fragile as grass: they pass quickly, swept away by the flow of divine time.

sens: Heavy downpour with thunder and lightning
Storm, deluge that falls upon the earth
Torrential rain that floods and destroys
Figurative image of violence or anger
H2230.detail:
1. The word designates a heavy and sudden rain, with its noises and crashes; it is a mountain downpour that devastates everything in its path, as in Job 24:8 where it "pierces" the poor who have nowhere to take refuge.
2. It is a violent storm that strikes and destroys: in Isaiah 28:2, it is compared to a hail hurricane that is "made to fall to the ground violently."
3. The image evokes destructive force: in Isaiah 25:4, God is a refuge against the storm as well as against the heat, and in Isaiah 32:2, one seeks shelter from it as one seeks shade.
4. In a figurative sense, the rainstorm symbolizes divine anger that falls: in Isaiah 30:30, it accompanies "the fierceness of the Lord's anger" with fire and hail.
H2230.origine: The Hebrew word זֶרֶם (zerem) expresses the idea of water flowing with force and impetuosity. Its root evokes gushing, overflowing. The word belongs to the family of terms that describe violent and sudden natural phenomena. It is a very concrete word, rooted in the experience of the inhabitants of the Levant, where torrential storms are feared and devastating.
H2230.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Isaiah (5 occurrences) and in Habakkuk. It always designates a violent meteorological phenomenon. The Segond translates it as "storm" (4 times), "tempest" (2 times), or by descriptive terms like "rain" or "strike." In Isaiah, zerem first appears as a concrete threat from which the poor have no protection, then becomes an image of divine power: either God is the refuge from it, or He is the author of it in His anger. God's storm is a sign of His fearsome intervention.
H2230.portee: This word reminds us that God controls the powers of nature and that He is a sure refuge in the face of storms, both material and spiritual. For the ancient reader, it was a concrete warning: the threat is real and terrifying. But for the believer, the lesson is clear: only God offers lasting protection when everything collapses around us.

sens: Physiological flow or emission from the body
Mating or sexual relationship
Intense and degrading sexual desire
H2231.detail: 1. The word first designates a bodily flow, an emission or discharge: it is an anatomical term, neutral in itself, that is also found in other contexts of the body. 2. In Ezekiel 23:20, it speaks of the sexual activity of horses; it evokes the act of mating itself, the brute virility of the animal. 3. In this verse, the prophet compares the degrading passion of the unfaithful woman to that of animals: the "approach" becomes an image of carnal desire, of uncontrolled and base lust.
H2231.origine: The Hebrew word זִרְמָה comes from a root that speaks of flow or stream. It properly designates what flows from the body, hence its use in a context of seminal emission. The Segond chose the term "approach" to maintain the decency of French while remaining concrete: it is the act of mating that "approaches" or manifests itself.
H2231.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 23:20. It is found in an oracle of the prophet who denounces Israel's spiritual unfaithfulness under the image of a woman who prostitutes herself. Ezekiel compares her passion to that of animals to highlight the bestiality of her abandonment of God. The context is polemical and visual: the prophet wants to strike the imagination of his listeners with crude language and an animal comparison.
H2231.portee: This passage reminds the believer that unfaithfulness to God is not merely a legal or theoretical matter: it is a diversion of our desires and life forces. The harsh image invites the reader to recognize the seriousness of sin and the necessity of redirecting one's passions toward God alone. It also shows how Scripture does not hesitate to use bodily language to speak of spiritual realities.

sens: To throw seed on the ground so that it germinates and grows
To bear or contain seed; said of a plant that produces seeds
To be in a state of gestation or pregnancy
H2232.detail:
1. To sow is to intentionally throw seeds into a prepared field so that they germinate and produce a harvest. It is the fundamental act of the farmer (Deuteronomy 11:10: one "sows" his seed in the fields). This word also evokes the action of the sower as a profession, the patient effort of the tiller who prepares the ground before sowing (Isaiah 28:24).
2. A plant that bears or produces seed is capable of reproducing; God commands the earth to produce greenery "bearing" seed (Genesis 1:11), which means that each plant contains within it the capacity to perpetuate its species.
3. To become pregnant is to begin to carry a child within oneself; the text of Leviticus 12:2 uses this same word to say that a woman has become pregnant, establishing a striking parallel between the seed that germinates in the ground and the fruit that forms in the womb.
H2232.origine: The Hebrew verb זָרַע (zara) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to spread" or "to scatter" something over a surface. The noun קֶרֶס (zera), the seed or grain, is from the same root. The word captures the image of an action of dispersion: one throws grains to the wind or onto the ground, hence the idea of production and descent (the seed literally becomes the offspring). This root conveys the central biblical idea of growth and fertility.
H2232.emploi: The verb to sow appears 54 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the law books (Leviticus, Deuteronomy), prophetic narratives (Jeremiah, Isaiah), and wisdom poems (Psalms, Proverbs, Job). Its concrete and agricultural meaning dominates: one sows wheat, and the harvest depends on what has been sown (Jeremiah 12:13: "They have sown wheat, and they reap thorns"). The word also extends to the idea of consequence: one reaps what one has sown, in a moral sense (Job 4:8; Proverbs 22:8). The notion even applies to the justice and good sown by God in the hearts of the righteous (Psalms 97:11). The context of pregnancy (Leviticus 12:2) shows the use of the word to express conception.
H2232.portee: The word to sow invites the reader to meditate on the responsibility of their actions and choices: what one sows, one will reap. It is a call to cultivate one's heart and works wisely, understanding that every gesture has consequences. For the believer, sowing also evokes the work of God who plants His word in the heart and expects fruit from it, and the personal commitment to cooperate with God in the work of transforming oneself and the world.

sens: Grain intended to be sown to produce a harvest
Material that falls from the plant and spreads in the field
Descendants, all the children and future generations
Act or time of sowing
Population, settlement established somewhere
One who practices righteousness, in a figurative sense
H2233G.detail:
1. The seed is the grain entrusted to the earth to germinate and produce a harvest: the plants seen in Genesis 1:11 have within them their seed, meaning the power to reproduce.
2. The word also refers to the act of sowing or the time of sowing: in Genesis 47:24, a portion of the harvest is retained to sow the fields the following year, and Leviticus 27:16 measures the value of a field according to the amount of barley seed needed to plant it.
3. Figuratively, the seed represents descendants, all those who are born: Jeremiah 31:27 announces that God will sow Israel with a seed of men and beasts, meaning He will fill the land with inhabitants and livestock.
4. Sometimes the word refers to the act of sowing itself: in Ecclesiastes 11:6, one sows in the morning and sows in the evening, multiplying the sowing.
5. When populating a region, one casts a seed of men, just as one casts grain: this is establishing a colony or community.
6. In wisdom literature, the seed can represent the righteous themselves, those who bear justice within them and produce its fruits.
H2233G.origine: The Hebrew word זֶרַע comes from a root that essentially means "to throw" or "to spread" — the basic idea is that of grain thrown into the ground to grow. The image is very concrete and agricultural: the seed is what falls, disperses, and germinates. The same root gives the notion of descendants because to give birth is also to "throw" or "produce" a new generation, just as one produces a harvest. Thus, the seed is both the material grain and what symbolically comes from it: children, posterity.
H2233G.emploi: This word appears 38 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Pentateuch (the first five books) and among the prophets. It is used first in the concrete agricultural sense: the seed of wheat, barley, or flax sown to obtain a harvest (Genesis 1:11-12, Deuteronomy 28:38, Isaiah 5:10).
