It is also found in practical calculations of tithes and estimations of fields according to the amount of seed (Leviticus 27:16, Deuteronomy 14:22). Early on, the word extends to the sense of descendants and posterity: it is a human seed, a lineage (Jeremiah 31:27). The prophets also use it to speak of the populating of a land or the multiplication of a population. The transition from the material image to the moral image occurs naturally: there exists a seed of the righteous, those who bear justice as a future harvest.
H2233G.portee: The word seed runs throughout Scripture: it states that everything that matters — our actions, our words, our lives — is a grain thrown, whose fruits will appear tomorrow. For the believer, it reminds us that God's promise to His people resembles the work of the sower: a gift of life that develops, multiplies, and fills the earth. It is a word of hope, for it speaks of growth and a coming harvest, not immediate destruction.

sens: Semen, male seed
The seed sown in the ground
One who is born of a parent, child or descendant
The entirety of a person's descendants, their lineage
A group of people sharing the same origin or quality
H2233H.detail:
1. Posterity primarily refers to semen, the seed generated by man — this very concrete word comes from the realm of procreation (Genesis 38:9: Onan refuses to give his posterity to his brother's widow).
2. The word then evokes the seed sown in the field, the very image of what germinates and produces fruit — a natural image that the Bible uses to speak of descendants.
3. In the most common sense, posterity refers to the child who is born, the son or daughter that one begets (Genesis 4:25: Eve bears a child in place of Abel).
4. More broadly, it refers to all descendants, the chain of generations that arise from an ancestor: Abraham will have a posterity as numerous as the stars (Genesis 15:5), and God promises David that his posterity will reign after him (2 Samuel 7:12).
5. Finally, the word can designate a group or class of people who share the same nature or origin: "race" (Psalms 21:11 — the wicked, their race will be erased from the earth).
H2233H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to sow" or "to disperse." It is closely related to the idea of production and multiplication: just as the seed sown produces a harvest, posterity is what comes from a person, what prolongs and multiplies them. The family of Hebrew words covers the entire domain of seed, from semen in the strictly physiological sense to historical and spiritual lineage.
H2233H.emploi: The word appears 160 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis and in historical narratives. It is omnipresent in patriarchal promises: God promises Abraham an innumerable posterity (Genesis 13:16, 15:5, 22:17), to Isaac (Genesis 26:3-4), to Jacob (Genesis 28:14, 35:12). The word also designates immediate descendants (children) or future generations (race). The Law uses this word to speak of the descendants of priestly families (Leviticus 21-22: the defects that exclude from the priest's posterity from service). Genesis 3:15 applies the word to the future offspring of the woman who will crush the head of the serpent — a passage where posterity becomes central to the plan of salvation.
H2233H.portee: This word speaks of God's faithfulness to His promises: He offers a posterity, a lineage, a continuation of life and blessing. For the believer, it reminds us that God sees beyond the present, that He has plans that extend across generations. Genesis 3:15 even roots the hope of the Messiah in this promise of a victorious posterity: Christ Himself will be that seed who crushes the serpent.

sens: Emission of seed
Sexual relationship between a man and a woman
Carnal union of a man with another man's wife
Ritual impurity related to the emission of seed
H2233I.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the emission of male seed: it is a physiological phenomenon described in Leviticus 15:16, which causes a ritual impurity requiring washing and waiting until evening.
2. More broadly, the word designates the sexual act itself, the carnal union between a man and a woman (Leviticus 18:20 speaks of not having "commerce" with your neighbor's wife).
3. It is specifically used to designate illicit or adulterous union: it is the forbidden act, particularly with another man's wife (Numbers 5:13 mentions a man who would have "commerce" with a married woman in secret).
4. The word also refers to the ritual impurity resulting from these emissions, which defiles the one affected and requires purification (Leviticus 15:32 speaks of one who is "defiled by a pollution").
H2233I.origine: The Hebrew word זֶרַע (zéra) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to sow" or "to throw." In the Old Testament, this same word is used for "seed" in a broad sense: the seed that is sown, but also the descendants, the children (the "offspring" in English). Here, applied to the human body, it specifically designates male seed, either by image of what is "sown," or as a euphemistic term to speak of the physiological emission.
H2233I.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the Torah, concentrated mainly in Leviticus 15 (law of ritual purity) and in the laws regarding marital relations and adultery (Leviticus 18—19, Numbers 5). It first designates the natural phenomenon (Leviticus 15:16—18), which renders one temporarily impure. It is then used for the sexual act itself, particularly when it transgresses a prohibition: commerce with another man's wife (Leviticus 18:20, 19:20), hidden adultery (Numbers 5:13). In all these cases, the word remains sober and technical, proper to legal and ritual language.
H2233I.portee: This word sheds light on how the Torah views sexuality: it is not shameful in itself, but it creates a ritual impurity that requires purification, and it is framed by strict laws protecting marriage and fidelity. For the Christian reader, this vocabulary reminds us that the Bible never treats sexuality with indifference: it is sacred, linked to the heart of the marital covenant, and adultery is a serious violation.

sens: Contractual union between two parties
Mix or fusion of two distinct elements
Mutual commitment sealed by promise
H2234.detail:
1. A covenant is a contract that unites two parties in a solemn agreement. In Daniel 2:43, Nebuchadnezzar sees in a dream future kingdoms and understands that their leaders will seek to strengthen themselves through human alliances: marriages and treaties to maintain power, but without true stability.
2. The image also evokes a mixture: just as iron and clay are mixed but do not truly bond (they remain separate at heart despite their fusion), the peoples united by covenant lose their own strength without gaining true cohesion.
3. The covenant implies a mutual commitment and a promise: each party obligates themselves to the other, hence its use to describe the ties that empires seek to forge for longevity.
H2234.origine: In Aramaic (the language of the text of Daniel), זְרַע (zera) literally means "seed" or "descendant." It comes from the same root as in Hebrew, where זֶרַע (zera) primarily refers to the seed. The word has extended to anything that comes from a source, hence its meaning of "covenant" or "commitment" that "produces" a union: it is a mutual descent, a contractual offspring of the parties.
H2234.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in Aramaic, in Daniel 2:43, where it translates the intention of the kings at the end of times to mingle through human alliances. This prophetic context shows King Nebuchadnezzar interpreting the statue of clay and iron: the alliances between peoples are presented as fragile, incapable of creating true unity despite all efforts.
H2234.portee: This passage reminds us that human alliances, even well-intentioned, cannot create true cohesion without a solid common foundation. For the believer, it is an invitation to seek the covenant with God, which alone provides stability and longevity, rather than placing trust in purely human commitments.

sens: Cultivated plant grown for food
Simple and frugal plant-based food
H2235A.detail:
1. A vegetable is a plant that is cultivated in a garden or field for consumption — plants like lentils, peas, or other garden herbs. The Hebrew word evokes the idea of something that is sown and grown specifically for nourishment, as opposed to wild fruits or plants that grow without being sown.
2. By extension, vegetables refer to simple, modest, and frugal food — that of people living without luxury. In the account of Daniel 1:12, the young Hebrews refuse the king's meat and wine and ask to eat only vegetables and water, a choice that demonstrates their obedience to the law of Moses and their detachment from worldly pleasures.
H2235A.origine: The Hebrew word זֵרֹעַ comes from a root meaning "to sow": vegetables are literally what is sown and cultivated. It is a word from the family of the word זֵֽרְעֹן (zar.on), which also refers to vegetables or garden herbs. The Greek of the Old Testament often translates this word with a term denoting edible grass.
H2235A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 1:12. It describes the choice made by four young Hebrews — Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah — when they are deported to Babylon. Refusing to defile themselves with the king's food — which came from his tables and tainted their ritual purity — they request a simple diet: vegetables and water. It is in this context that the word receives its full force: vegetables are not so much a matter of taste as an act of faithfulness to God and separation from pagan customs. The unique and concentrated use of the word highlights this virtue of sobriety and obedience.
H2235A.portee: This account of Daniel and his three companions shows that remaining faithful to God may require renouncing what the world offers, including pleasures and comfort. The choice of simple vegetables speaks to the contemporary reader: it is a call to vigilance about what one allows into their body and life, and a trust that God provides for those who seek His kingdom first. God indeed blesses this choice: the young men become "ten times better in appearance" than the others (Daniel 1:15).

sens: Cultivated plant whose fruits, seeds, or green parts are eaten
Simple plant-based food, without meat or wine
H2235B.detail: 1. A vegetable is a plant that is cultivated and eaten: it is concrete, what is harvested from a garden or field. In Daniel 1:16, the young Hebrews in Babylon receive vegetables, meaning plant-based foods — probably squashes, lentils, legumes — instead of royal dishes. 2. The word also denotes a simple and austere lifestyle: eating vegetables is to refuse the luxury of the king's table. For Daniel and his three companions, it is a choice of fidelity to the Law: they eat only plants to avoid defiling themselves with the impure foods of the Babylonian palace. It is an act of piety, not merely a matter of taste.
H2235B.origine: This Hebrew word comes from the same family as the main word זֵרֹעַ (zeroua), which also means "vegetable" or "thing sown." The root evokes the idea of sowing, cultivating: it is what is sown and grown. This family of words is related to agriculture, to the food obtained from the earth through labor.
H2235B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 1:16. It is a crucial moment: the young captives from Judah refuse the Babylonian royal food and ask to eat only vegetables and water. This act of temperance becomes a test of their fidelity to God. At the end of this period, they are healthier than all the young men who eat the king's delicacies — a sign that piety and obedience to the Law are more precious than luxury. The vegetable thus symbolizes humility and respect for religious convictions.
H2235B.portee: This passage shows that eating simply is not a shameful deprivation, but an act of courage and faith. For the Christian, it invites not to seek luxury or comfort at all costs, but to place obedience to God above the pleasures of the world. It is also an encouragement to persevere in one's convictions even when far from home, in foreign territory.

sens: To pour liquid, especially blood, by throwing or pouring it around an altar or space
To throw or project a solid substance, such as ash or dust, upwards or far away
To disperse, to spread widely over a surface
To apply a substance to something or someone in a ritual manner
H2236.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to pour blood around the altar during sacrifices: this is a central act of Israelite worship. Moses pours the blood on the altar (Exodus 24:6), the priests pour the blood of the offerings around the altar (Leviticus 3:13, Leviticus 9:12). This ritual gesture purifies and consecrates.

2. The word also refers to throwing a substance upwards or far away: Moses throws furnace ash towards the sky before Pharaoh, causing boils (Exodus 9:8). The action is quick and deliberate, the object travels a distance.

3. It can express the idea of dispersing, spreading widely: King Josiah spreads the dust of the idols on the graves (2 Chronicles 34:4), covering the space with residues.

4. The word is used to ritually apply a substance to a person: the water of purification has not been poured on someone who remains unclean (Numbers 19:20). This is an act of separation or consecration.
H2236.origine: The Hebrew verb זָרַק comes from a root that expresses the idea of projecting, throwing with force. The basic image is that of a quick and dispersive action: something is thrown that scatters or spreads widely. The word belongs to the vocabulary of Israelite worship rituals, where the pouring of blood is a fundamental act of offering to God.
H2236.emploi: The verb appears 33 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the ritual books (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and in the history of the kings. It is very frequent in descriptions of sacrifices: blood is poured around the altar, sometimes sprinkled on the people. It also appears in contexts of destruction (overturning altars, grinding idols to dust) or cursing (the ash, the boils). In Ezekiel and Hosea, it takes on a prophetic dimension: God pours out the water of purification or looks with disgust at one who degrades. The fundamental meaning remains this: to pour or throw widely a substance, often in a ritual or judgment act.
H2236.portee: This word reveals the importance of blood in Israel's worship: pouring blood is not a trivial act; it is the key to reconciliation with God. For the Christian, the blood shed by Christ in the New Covenant fulfills and replaces all these ritual gestures. Understanding the weight of the word "pour" in the Old Testament helps grasp the gravity and beauty of what the Gospel proclaims: the blood shed once for all on the cross.

sens: To breathe suddenly through the nose and mouth, often several times in succession
H2237.detail: 1. Sneezing is expelling air from the lungs through an involuntary reflex — usually due to nasal irritation or to clear the airways. It is a simple and natural physical gesture. In 2 Kings 4:35, the child resurrected by Elisha "sneezed seven times, and he opened his eyes": the sneeze marks the return to life, the moment when breathing resumes normally.
H2237.origine: The Hebrew verb זָרַק means literally "to sneeze" and describes this universal bodily reflex. It is a simple verb that reproduces the sound and movement of sneezing. The word appears only once in the Old Testament, making this passage from 2 Kings particularly striking: the sneeze becomes a visible and tangible sign of the child's resurrection.
H2237.emploi: This verb appears only once in the entire Hebrew Bible, in 2 Kings 4:35. It is found in the miraculous account where the prophet Elisha resurrects the son of the Shunammite woman. After praying and lying on the body of the dead child, Elisha rises — and the child sneezes seven times before opening his eyes. The sneeze is the first physical sign of regained life, a concrete and living manifestation of the miracle.
H2237.portee: This humble detail — a simple sneeze — underscores the reality of the miracle: it is not a vision or a spectral appearance, but life authentically returning to the body. The child regains his most basic vital functions. For the reader, this sneeze makes the miracle both more wonderful and more human, showing that God acts in the ordinary and material world.

sens: The wife of Haman, the Agagite, during the time of the exile and the return of the Jews from Babylon
H2238.detail: 1. Zeres is the wife of Haman, the grand vizier of King Ahasuerus. She appears in the book of Esther at key moments of Haman's conspiracy against the Jews: first when Haman returns home and boasts of his wealth and position to his family (Esther 5:10), then when she and her friends advise him to set up a gallows to hang Mordecai (Esther 5:14), and finally when she recognizes, after Haman's humiliation, that he will not be able to do anything against Mordecai "of the race of the Jews" and that he will fall before him (Esther 6:13). She represents an influential woman, capable of advising her husband and participating in his plans.
H2238.origine: The name Zeres means "gold" in Hebrew, evoking wealth and splendor — fitting for the wife of a powerful man like Haman. It is a proper name, unrelated to other Hebrew words in the biblical text.
H2238.emploi: Zeres appears only three times in the Bible, all in the book of Esther (chapters 5 and 6). She is mentioned as Haman's wife, always in his company or that of his friends. In each appearance, she plays an active role: she hears of her husband's exploits, advises him on a cruel action, and then announces his fate. She embodies the woman who shares her husband's ambitions and calculations, likely coming from a family of some importance since she bears a significant name.

sens: A unit of length measurement equal to the distance from the open hand from thumb to little finger
Distance measured by the palm of the hand
H2239.detail:
1. The span is a measure of length based on the human body: it is the distance between the thumb and the little finger when the hand is fully opened. This measure corresponds to about half a cubit (Ezekiel 43:13 specifies that the priestly cubit was "a span longer than the ordinary cubit"). It is found in the measurements of the high priest's breastplate: "its length was a span, and its width was a span" (Exodus 39:9).
2. By extension, it is also the palm of the hand itself used as a measuring instrument. Isaiah 40:12 uses it to evoke the greatness of God: "Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and marked off the heavens with the span." It is a poetic image of divine power that holds the universe in a measure so small that it fits in the palm.
H2239.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of spreading apart, opening widely. It is a very ancient measure, based on the body: like the cubit (length of the forearm) or the closed hand, it allowed everyone to measure with what they had on them. These anthropomorphic measures — based on the body — are common in ancient Middle Eastern cultures.
H2239.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Bible (6 times translated as "span"). It is mostly found in construction and measurement texts: the high priest's breastplate was a square of a span by a span (Exodus 28:16 and 39:9); the base of the golden altar also had a span in height (Ezekiel 43:13). Goliath measured six cubits and a span (1 Samuel 17:4), making him an impressive giant. Isaiah uses it poetically and theologically to show that God measures the heavens with his span — in other words, the infinite fits in the hand of the Creator.
H2239.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible uses the human body to speak of God and his works. When Isaiah says that God measures the heavens with his span, it shows that even what seems immense to us — the heavens, the mountains — is just a handful for him. It is a source of confidence: if the universe fits in God's hand, our lives fit there too.

sens: Head of an exiled family who participated in the return from Babylon
Family of descendants of the people of Judah who returned from exile
H2240G.detail: Zatthu is a man mentioned for the first time during the return of the exiles from Babylon in the time of Zerubbabel. He is the head of a large family that returns with the exiles: according to Ezra 2:8, "the sons of Zatthu, nine hundred forty-five." He appears again in Nehemiah 7:13 with a slightly different number, "eight hundred forty-five," in a similar context of counting the returned exiles. His name also designates this family of descendants who return from exile: in Ezra 10:27, several of the sons of Zatthu who had taken foreign wives are listed and had to separate from them.
H2240G.origine: The name Zatthu means "his clarity" or "his brightness," composed of a Hebrew root evoking light or brightness. It fits within a Hebrew tradition of names that evoke divine light, like Zerubbabel or Hananiah. This name reflects the hope of the ancients for their children.
H2240G.emploi: Zatthu is one of the family heads of the exiles returning from Babylon after the destruction of the temple and the exile: the text places him at the heart of the return lists established at the time of Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:8; Nehemiah 7:13). His family is among the most significant: between 845 and 945 people. He is also mentioned in Ezra 8:5, confirming that his descendants actively participate in the reconstruction. In Ezra 10:27, several of his descendants are named in the context of measures against mixed marriages, showing that the family of Zatthu played an active role in the returned community.
H2240G.portee: Zatthu embodies the faithfulness of Jewish families who, after seventy years of captivity, return to rebuild the temple and their community life. His name and that of his family remind us that God never abandons His people: even exile does not extinguish hope. The regular presence of his descendants in community affairs shows how the people of God engage in obedience and reconstruction after judgment.

sens: Leader of the people after the Babylonian exile
H2240H.detail: 1. Zatthu is a leader of the people of Israel at the time of the return from the Babylonian exile. He is among the signers of the solemn document listed in Nehemiah 10:14, where the leaders commit to observing the Law of Moses alongside Nehemiah and the priest Ezra. His name appears in this official list of the authorities of the reconstituted people.
H2240H.origine: The name Zatthu literally means "his clarity" or "his brightness" in Hebrew (from the root zah, which evokes brilliance or luminosity). It is a typical name of the post-exilic period, reflecting the hopes and new energy of the people returning from captivity. It is likely that Zatthu is also the name of a family of exiles who returned with Zerubbabel for the reconstruction of the Temple.
H2240H.emploi: Zatthu is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:14. He appears in the solemn context where the leaders of the people, after the Babylonian exile, seal a commitment to observe the Law of the Lord. This single mention indicates that he was a prominent figure in the civil and religious hierarchy of the returned people, even though the details of his life and actions are not communicated to us.

sens: Gershonite Levite during the divided monarchy of Israel
H2241.detail: Zétham is a member of the tribe of Levi, belonging to the Gershonite clan. He appears in the genealogical records of the Levites established during the reign of King David. Son of Jehiieli and grandson of Laadan, Zétham is first mentioned in 1 Chronicles 23:8 among the descendants of Laadan who served the Lord. He is the brother of Joel. His main role was to guard the treasures of the house of the Lord, as indicated in 1 Chronicles 26:22, where he is presented alongside his brother as responsible for this important task of guarding the temple treasury.
H2241.origine: The name Zétham means "olive tree" in Hebrew, referring to the olive tree, a symbol of peace and blessing in Israeli culture. This name was likely given to express the hope that this child would be a source of blessing for his family and for the people of Israel.
H2241.emploi: Zétham is mentioned twice in the Scriptures, exclusively in the first book of Chronicles. He lived during the divided monarchy, during the reign of David who organized the temple service. He was part of the Gershonite Levites designated to serve and maintain the worship of the temple. His responsibilities included guarding the treasures of the house of the Lord, a position of trust that showed his importance in the hierarchy of Levitical service.

sens: One of the seven eunuchs serving King Ahasuerus
H2242.detail: Zéthar is one of the seven eunuchs of the royal court of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes I, Persian king of the 5th century BC). He is mentioned in Esther 1:10, where he is among the servants to whom the king, his heart merry with wine during a banquet, commands to bring Queen Vashti before him. These eunuchs had access to the inner palace and executed the direct orders of the sovereign.
H2242.origine: The name Zéthar means "star" in Old Persian. It reflects the Persian onomastics of the time of the Babylonian exile and return, a period when Persian names were common among royal court figures. The context of the book of Esther shows the Persian influence on the names and functions of the administration of the empire.
H2242.emploi: Zéthar appears only once in the entire Bible, in Esther 1:10. He is named as the seventh of the seven eunuchs who served King Ahasuerus. The text presents him simply as one of the king's trusted officers, without providing further details about his life or actions. His mention in the list of the king's servants shows his status as a high-ranking official at the Persian court.

sens: The chest of a person, particularly the hollow formed by crossed arms or the space between the two breasts
The heart or conscience, seat of emotions, secrets, or hidden thoughts
H2243.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the chest, this hollow of the body where something can be held: it is the image of intimacy and what is hidden or enclosed. In Job 31:33, Job swears that he has not hidden his transgressions "in his bosom," meaning he has not kept his faults secret within himself out of shame or deceit.

2. By extension, the "bosom" becomes the symbol of the inner person, of their heart or conscience. It is the place where one encloses what others do not see: thoughts, guilt, affections. The expression "to hold something in one's bosom" means to protect it, keep it hidden, or cherish it intimately.
H2243.origine: The word חֹב (chov) designates the hollow of the body, particularly the pectoral area. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of enclosing or containing. In Hebrew, the bosom is often used as an image of intimacy and what is hidden from others, as it is a concealed, deep part, close to the heart. This image also appears in ancient Greek and other Semitic languages.
H2243.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 31:33. Job, defending himself against the accusations of his friends, swears that he has not buried his sins within himself. The context shows that "to enclose in one's bosom" means to hide something shameful or guilty, to keep a heavy secret. It is a poetic expression that highlights the hypocrisy of a person who feigns righteousness while hiding their faults. The usage is unique but very significant, as it illustrates how biblical poets used body vocabulary to speak of the inner state of conscience.
H2243.portee: This word reminds us that God knows what we keep hidden within ourselves: our secret thoughts, our faults, our intentions. For a believer, this invites honesty before God and confession rather than inner deceit. It is also a call not to lead a double life, where one displays righteousness in public while keeping evil buried within.

sens: To withdraw, disappear from sight
To take shelter, to seek refuge
To keep hidden, conceal something or someone
To be hidden, remain concealed
To thicken, to densify (of material)
H2244.detail:
1. To withdraw, disappear from sight: the action of removing oneself from in front of someone, ceasing to be visible. Adam and Eve hide from the face of God among the trees of the garden (Genesis 3:8), and the kings flee and hide in a cave (Joshua 10:16).

2. To take shelter, to seek refuge: to find a safe place to escape danger or pursuit. Saul seeks to kill David, who must hide in a secluded place (1 Samuel 19:2), and the enemies hide like mice in the cracks and crevices (Isaiah 2:21).

3. To keep hidden, conceal something or someone: the active action of voluntarily hiding, protecting by keeping secret. Obadiah hid a hundred prophets of the Lord, fifty by fifty in a cave, and fed them (1 Kings 18:13).

4. To be hidden, remain concealed: the state of what is kept apart. Saul was hidden among the baggage when he was sought (1 Samuel 10:22).

5. To thicken, to densify: speaking of material (water, ice), to compact, to become denser and more opaque (Job 38:30).
H2244.origine: The verb חָבָא (chavà) fundamentally expresses the idea of withdrawing, moving away from the field of vision. The word is related to the notion of cave or hidden refuge: one who hides withdraws into darkness or a closed space. In biblical Hebrew, the word is used in various grammatical forms (reflexive, causative) that give the action a nuance: to hide oneself, to hide someone else, or to be hidden by an external force. This flexibility reflects concrete situations of ancient life: the fugitive who eludes, the servant who hides the fugitives, the man concealed by circumstances.
H2244.emploi: The verb חָבָא appears 33 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives and poetry. In Genesis, it evokes shame and flight before God; in the books of Samuel, it is a key verb in the narratives of flight and refuge (David fleeing from Saul, Samuel hiding Jehu). In 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, we see it during persecutions: Obadiah hides the prophets, Joash is hidden in the temple. The word also enriches itself with figurative meanings: Isaiah speaks of one who is hidden and protected by the hand of God (Isaiah 49:2); Job mentions those whom God hides from the eyes of the inhabitants of the land (Job 24:4). The usage shows that hiding is not always wrong: it can sometimes be an act of justice and mercy. The verbal forms vary depending on whether one expresses the reflexive action (to hide oneself) or causative (to hide someone else).
H2244.portee: This word reveals a major spiritual reality: shame creates separation from God, and sin drives man to hide (Genesis 3:8). But the Bible also shows that God protects His faithful by hiding them — not out of shame, but by grace. For the believer, to hide also means to preserve, protect, keep safe. It is a word of comfort: he who trusts in God does not fear, for God is his hiding place, his refuge. The term invites discernment: when we hide from the Lord out of fear or guilt, we distance ourselves; but when God hides us under the secret of His face, it is protection.

sens: To feel a strong and passionate affection
To have tenderness and attachment to someone
To cherish, to hold precious
H2245.detail:
1. The verb חָבַב expresses an intense and warm love, not cold or distant, but alive and engaged. It is the affection one has for those one truly cherishes. In Deuteronomy 33:3, Moses proclaims that God "loves" the people of Israel ardently, showing that this divine love is active and protective.
2. This word emphasizes personal attachment and tenderness: one who loves in this way holds the other close to their heart and desires their well-being. It is less an abstract feeling than a relationship of intimacy and deep affection.
H2245.origine: The root חָבַב evokes the idea of warmth, intimacy, and heart. The word arises from the image of embracing, holding close what one cherishes. In the ancient Near East, this ardent love designated passionate attachment within families and alliances, marked by fidelity and mutual devotion.
H2245.emploi: This Hebrew verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 33:3, where Moses describes the love that God has for His people. Although rare in biblical Hebrew, it expresses one of the most personal and affectionate nuances of love: not commanded or legal love, but love that springs from the heart with fervor, that of the most intimate relationships. The context shows God loving "the peoples" and holding them "in His hand," combining tenderness and protection.
H2245.portee: This word reminds the believer that God's love for His people is not distant or detached, but ardent and tender. It reveals that God truly cherishes His people, holding them close with affection. It is an invitation to recognize that we are loved, not only accepted, but passionately cherished by the One who created us.

sens: Son of Reuel, the Midianite, and father-in-law of Moses
H2246.detail: Hobab is the son of Reuel (also called Jethro), the Midianite priest who became the father-in-law of Moses after his marriage to Zipporah. He is therefore Moses' brother-in-law. In Numbers 10:29, Moses invites him to accompany the Israelites in the desert to the promised land, promising him that God will do good to Israel and that Hobab will benefit as well. Later, Judges 4:11 mentions that Heber the Kenite was descended from Hobab: this passage shows that Hobab's family had settled in Canaan and formed an alliance with Heber's clan.
H2246.origine: The name Hobab means "beloved" or "cherished," evoking affection or favor. Hobab belonged to the Midianite people, a nation of the Arabian desert that maintained ties with Israel through Moses. His presence in the biblical genealogy shows how foreign families integrated into Israel.
H2246.emploi: Hobab appears only twice in the Bible. First in Numbers 10:29, at the time of the departure from Sinai: Moses asks him to guide Israel in the desert, recognizing his skills as a desert nomad. Then in Judges 4:11, he is mentioned as an ancestor of the Kenites, a people who had settled in Canaan. These two occurrences show that Hobab accepted to follow Israel and that his descendants became rooted in the promised land.
H2246.portee: The invitation that Moses extends to Hobab illustrates how God opens His covenant to those who accept to join His people, even if they are not born Israelites. Hobab represents one who, through marriage and friendship, becomes a participant in divine promises. His story also shows that mutual trust and the integration of foreigners into the community of Israel are important biblical values.

sens: To withdraw to a safe place, out of sight
To remain hidden, to stay concealed
To escape capture or destruction
H2247.detail:
1. To withdraw to a safe place, out of sight: the verb describes the action of taking cover, finding refuge. In Joshua 2:16, the spies are instructed to hide in the mountains for three days to avoid their pursuers — it is a strategic withdrawal for safety.

2. To remain hidden, to stay concealed: this is the state of one who stays apart, invisible, out of reach. In Isaiah 26:20, the people are called to hide in their chambers until the divine anger passes — a patient and invisible waiting.

3. To escape capture or destruction: the word emphasizes the impossibility of escaping when the verb is used in the negative. In Jeremiah 49:10, God declares that Esau will not be able to hide: he will find no refuge against judgment — no retreat will save him.
H2247.origine: The Hebrew verb חָבָה (chabah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of withdrawing, of standing apart. The root evokes the movement of folding back, of withdrawing from sight. The noun חִבָּיוֹן (hibbayôn, "retreat") belongs to the same family and reinforces this notion of a place of refuge or concealment.
H2247.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the Segond, always in the sense of hiding or withdrawing. It is found in action narratives (Joshua 2:16: the spies hiding from their pursuers; 2 Kings 7:12: the Syrians hiding in the fields) and in broader prophetic texts. In Isaiah 26:20, it is a soothing exhortation before judgment. In Jeremiah 49:10, the negation of the verb ("will not be able to hide") emphasizes the inevitability of divine punishment: no retreat, no refuge is sufficient.
H2247.portee: This word shows that human refuge, even found in fleeing and hiding, depends on God's will. When Isaiah invites to hide, it is a call to trust: wait for God's salvation in cover. But when Jeremiah asserts that one cannot hide from God's judgment, it is a warning: no hiding place can shield us from divine justice. The Christian is called to seek refuge not in secret places, but in God alone.

sens: Evil action that harms or injures others
Act of malice or wickedness
Deliberate wrongdoing or injustice
H2248.detail: 1. The word primarily designates an act that causes harm, a moral or physical injury inflicted on someone else — a harmful and culpable action. In Daniel 6:22, a "crime" is mentioned against the king, suggesting a serious transgression that would offend authority. 2. More broadly, it refers to any act of malice or wickedness: a conduct deliberately contrary to justice and morality. 3. The word can also designate the harm or injustice itself, the damaging effect of the act — what is broken or damaged in relationships between people.
H2248.origine: This Aramaic word derives from a root that evokes rupture or injury (related to the Hebrew חַבּוּרָה "wound"). The initial image is that of a wound, a break in a person's integrity. The word has evolved to designate not only physical injury but also moral and legal wrong — any act that "wounds" the just order.
H2248.emploi: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Daniel 6:22, in the context of the plot against the prophet Daniel. The accusers seek to have him condemned by claiming he committed a "crime" against the king, while in reality, according to the text, Daniel did not commit any wrongdoing. The word thus fits into a narrative where human injustice is denounced in the face of the faithfulness of one who only transgresses unjust laws.
H2248.portee: This passage reminds the reader that even when accused unjustly of a crime, God sees the truth and protects those who remain faithful to Him. For the Christian, it is an assurance that false accusations do not triumph before God.

sens: River of Assyria, tributary of the Euphrates
H2249.detail: 1. The Chabor is a watercourse in Assyria, an ancient Near Eastern region located in Mesopotamia. It is a tributary of the Euphrates, meaning it flows into this great river. The name literally means "junction" or "joining," likely recalling the point where this river meets the Euphrates (1 Chronicles 5:26).
H2249.origine: The Hebrew name חָבוֹר (Chabor) comes from a root meaning "to join" or "to unite," in reference to geography: this river joins the Euphrates. It is a proper geographical name, borrowed from the actual hydrographic system of ancient Mesopotamia.
H2249.emploi: The word Chabor appears three times in the Bible, always in the context of deportation. When Assyria conquers the kingdom of Israel (around 722 B.C.), it disperses the Israelites into various regions of its empire, notably around the Chabor (2 Kings 17:6 and 18:11). The river is mentioned as one of the places where the Israelite captives are settled, alongside Chalach and the cities of the Medes. Thus, in the biblical text, the Chabor becomes a geographical symbol of exile and the dispersion of God's people.

sens: mark or lesion on the skin resulting from a blow
wound, injury, or bruise
physical damage caused by trauma
figuratively: moral or spiritual suffering
H2250.detail: 1. A bruise is primarily the mark left by a blow on the body: a swollen, bruised, discolored area. In Exodus 21:25, the law of retaliation states that the compensation for a bruise must be measured by the injury suffered: "bruise for bruise." 2. The word also designates a more serious wound or sore, open or infected. Psalm 38:6 describes the psalmist's wounds as "infected and festering, because of my folly": they are not just bruises, but lesions that suppurate. 3. In Isaiah 1:6, after a list of bruises and contusions, the text speaks of "open wounds": it is the image of skin lacerated, open, bruised from head to foot, symbolizing a state ravaged by sin. 4. Isaiah 53:5 transfers this image to the spiritual realm: "it is by his bruises that we are healed." The wounds of the suffering Servant are no longer just physical injuries, but the means of redemption: his suffering heals our guilt.
H2250.origine: The Hebrew word חַבּוּרָה comes from a root meaning to strike, to break, to mark. That is why it primarily evokes the visible impression of a blow on the flesh. The root appears in other words designating injuries or blows. The related Aramaic word חֲבוּלָא means crime or damage: it is the act that produces the bruise.
H2250.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 4:23, Lamech boasts of having killed a man for a bruise he received. Exodus 21:25 uses it in the context of the law of retaliation: a bruise must be repaired by an equivalent bruise, which shows that the law rigorously frames physical violence. The Psalms and Proverbs use it to describe real injuries (Psalm 38:6: festering wounds) or to symbolize corrective discipline (Proverbs 20:30: blows heal the wicked). Isaiah uses it twice: in 1:6 to depict the desolation of the people, and in 53:5 to announce salvation through the sufferings of the Messiah. As one progresses through these usages, the bruise shifts from the physical realm to the spiritual and redemptive realm.
H2250.portee: This word gives the reader a stark image of what suffering represents in Scripture. It is not abstract, but embodied: it hurts, it bleeds, it infects. When Isaiah 53:5 asserts that "it is by his bruises that we are healed," the reader understands that the Messiah did not suffer symbolically, but truly, and that this tangible physical suffering is the price of our forgiveness. It is a call to meditate on the cost of redemption.

sens: to strike repeatedly
to separate the grains from their husks by striking
to shake vigorously to make them fall
H2251.detail:
1. To strike something repeatedly with an object (stick, rod, flail). This is the primary meaning: one "beats" the spelt with a stick, one "beats" the wheat (Isaiah 28:27; Judges 6:11).
2. To separate the grains from the chaff by striking: this is the work of threshing. Gideon "threshed" wheat in the winepress to isolate it from its husk and preserve it (Judges 6:11). Ruth "threshed" what she had gleaned to obtain barley (Ruth 2:17).
3. To shake a tree or plant vigorously to detach the fruits. When one "shakes" the olive trees, the remaining fruits fall to the ground (Deuteronomy 24:20). The Lord will "shake" the fruits of the earth like a harvest (Isaiah 27:12).
H2251.origine: The Hebrew verb חָבַט (chavat) expresses the action of striking or beating. It is related to the idea of repeated impact, typically that of a flail or stick. The agricultural context is central: in biblical times, "beating" the harvest was an essential daily activity to separate the grain from the chaff.
H2251.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in agricultural contexts. Two usages describe the threshing of grain (Judges 6:11, Ruth 2:17, Isaiah 28:27), and two describe the shaking of fruits for harvest (Deuteronomy 24:20, Isaiah 27:12). The translation alternates between "to beat" (threshing of grain) and "to shake" (detaching of fruits), depending on the context, but the action is similar: to strike or shake to separate. The word reflects a rural world where the harvest requires direct physical labor.
H2251.portee: This word reminds the believer that the harvest requires labor: one must beat, shake, strike to obtain the fruit. Spiritually, this evokes the idea that God produces fruit in us through processes that can be difficult. It also emphasizes the value of honest manual labor, at the heart of the agricultural life that the Law protects.

sens: Leader of a priestly family during the time of exile and return
Priest whose descendants returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel
H2252.detail: Habaja is a family leader among the priests who returned from exile to Jerusalem. His descendants are mentioned in the list of priestly families that accompanied Zerubbabel during the return (Ezra 2:61). He also appears under the similar name of Hobaja in Nehemiah 7:63, where the same genealogy is noted: his sons were among those who returned from captivity in Babylon but could not prove their priestly genealogy, raising questions about their right to serve in the temple.
H2252.origine: The name Habaja literally means "the Lord has hidden" (from the Hebrew root meaning "to hide"). It is the name of an important priestly family at the return from exile. The variant Hobaja in Nehemiah is a slightly different spelling of the same name in manuscript traditions.
H2252.emploi: Habaja is mentioned only twice in Scripture, in two parallel passages: Ezra 2:61 and Nehemiah 7:63. These two references recount the same episode of the return from exile, each providing a list of priestly families. The context is the same: after the fall of Jerusalem and captivity in Babylon, during the return under Zerubbabel in the 6th century B.C., those returning are enumerated. Habaja and his descendants were part of these priests, but the transmission of their priestly genealogy had been compromised during the exile, which explains why they are specifically named in these verification lists.

sens: to dwell, to have one's seat
to be hidden or concealed
H2253.detail:
1. To dwell or have one's seat in a place: this conveys the idea of stable presence, a place where one resides. In Habakkuk 3:4, divine strength "resides" in the hand of God — it has its seat there, where it concentrates and operates.
2. To be hidden, concealed, or covered: the word also carries the idea of what is veiled or covered, not immediately apparent. Divine strength, very real, remains as hidden in the brilliant light that manifests it.
H2253.origine: The Hebrew word חֶבְיוֹן (chevyon) comes from a root related to the idea of covering, hiding, or veiling. This image of what is covered, hidden, or that remains in one place forms its fundamental meaning. The word conveys both the idea of stable presence (to dwell) and of veiled or mysterious character (to be hidden).
H2253.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Habakkuk 3:4. It is a passage where the prophet describes the theophany, that is, the majestic appearance of God. The poetic context plays on the idea that divine strength and power "reside" in the hand of God, inhabit that place of manifestation. The unique usage and rarity of the word underscore its solemn and poetic character.
H2253.portee: This word invites reflection on the fact that divine power resides and concentrates in God Himself. It is never distant or dispersed, but always present, anchored, stable — even when it seems veiled or mysterious to us. For the Christian reader, it is an assurance that the strength of God that directs history is never absent: it "resides" constantly at the source of all that is.

sens: to retain an asset as security for a debt
to demand something as collateral
to strip someone of their belongings as a sign of commitment
H2254A.detail:
1. To take as a pledge means to retain a person's property as security until a debt is repaid. In Exodus 22:26, if a creditor takes the garment of a poor person as a pledge, he must return it before nightfall, for it is his only shelter. This was a common practice in the ancient Near East to secure a loan.
2. By extension, it refers to the property itself that is demanded as security — the "pledge." In Deuteronomy 24:6, the Law prohibits taking the millstones of a miller as a pledge, for that would deprive him of his means of living, that is, "to take his life."
3. The word also evokes the act of exerting pressure or unjustly stripping someone of their belongings. In Job 22:6 and 24:3, those who take pledges from orphans and widows commit social violence: they exploit the weakest and most vulnerable.
H2254A.origine: The verb חָבַל (chàval) comes from a root that originally means "to bind" or "to tie." The pledge is what "binds" the debtor to his creditor until repayment. In Hebrew, the word pledge itself (גַּחַל or חַבְלָה) derives from this same root. The root also appears in other senses: "to destroy" or "to spoil" (as in חִבֵּל, "he has damaged"), since the pledge can damage or plunder.
H2254A.emploi: This verb appears 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the laws of Deuteronomy and the poems of Job. Exodus 22:26 and Deuteronomy 24:6 and 24:17 use it in a legal regulation context: the Law strictly regulates the practice of pledging to protect the poor and widows. In contrast, Job 22:6, 24:3, and 24:9 denounce those who take pledges illegally or abusively, particularly from orphans and widows, which constitutes a serious social injustice. Proverbs 20:16 and 27:13 mention one who "stands surety" (a closely related term), equally reckless as one who takes pledges without measure.
H2254A.portee: This word reminds the reader that divine Law protects the poor and vulnerable. God does not tolerate the exploitation of others' weakness by unjustly withholding their property or without compassion. Taking someone's garment at night leaves them exposed to the cold: that is why the Law forbids it. This invites the believer to exercise justice with mercy, especially towards those who have nothing.

sens: Cause material damage, ruin something physical
Spoil, corrupt, damage
Lose, annihilate, make disappear
Offend, violate (a law, a commandment)
Be ruined, perish (passive sense)
H2254B.detail:
1. To destroy something concrete, to reduce it to nothing. The little foxes "ravage" the vineyards in Song of Solomon 2:15: they destroy the plants and the harvest through their damage.
2. To spoil or corrupt through a negative action; to damage what was good or intact. This is the sense of evil that spoils, of sin that corrupts.
3. To completely lose something, to make it disappear. Job says, "My breath is lost" (17:1): his life is extinguishing, annihilating little by little.
4. To offend or violate, particularly in transgression of a divine law. The Israelites acknowledge, "We have offended you" (Nehemiah 1:7): we have violated your commandments and thereby harmed you.
5. To be ruined or destroyed, to perish — this is the passive form of the verb. "He who despises the word will perish" (Proverbs 13:13): he ruins himself by despising.
H2254B.origine: The verb הָבַל (hâval) comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of breaking, damaging, destroying. The word depicts the action of undoing, putting into ruin. This root expresses both the voluntary action (to destroy, to corrupt) and the passive effect (to be destroyed, to be ruined). In Aramaic, חֲבַל (chaval) carries the same meaning.
H2254B.emploi: The verb appears 11 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the writings of wisdom and the prophets. It denotes material destruction (the foxes ravaging the vineyards), but also moral or spiritual ruin — the corruption of a life, the violation of a covenant or a law. In Nehemiah 1:7, it expresses offense against God through transgression. In Proverbs 13:13 and Job 17:1, it describes loss or decline. The word can also express divine judgment that destroys (Ecclesiastes 5:5: God will destroy the work of your hands if you are a liar). It is a word of ruin and desolation.
H2254B.portee: This word reminds us of the seriousness of transgression: to offend God or despise His word are not acts without consequence — they destroy, they ruin. Whether through words (a broken vow), actions (neglecting commandments), or thoughts (contempt), one exposes their life to ruin. Conversely, respecting the word of God preserves what is good and whole.

sens: Bring a child into the world, deliver
Produce, generate (in a figurative sense)
Suffer the pains of childbirth
H2254C.detail: 1. The primary meaning is to give birth, to deliver a child. In Song of Solomon 8:5, it is said of a mother that she "gave birth" to her daughter under the apple tree: it is the biological and physical act of bringing forth. 2. The word extends to a figurative sense: to produce, generate, create something through one's efforts or thoughts. In Psalms 7:15, the psalmist describes the wicked who "conceives iniquity, and gives birth to nothingness" — his evil thoughts produce vain and destructive acts, as if evil were a creation of his heart. 3. The verb also evokes the pains and contractions of childbirth: the mother twists, contracts in the effort to give life. This image of intense labor and suffering always accompanies the word, even in the figurative sense.
H2254C.origine: The Hebrew word חָבַל (chavàl) comes from a root that expresses the idea of twisting, contracting, bending under effort. The form used here (Piel, intensive form) reinforces this notion of convulsion and labor. This root appears rarely in the Bible, but it always evokes violent effort, physical childbirth, or the generation of something through painful work.
H2254C.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Bible at the provided references. In Psalms 7:15, it describes how the wicked "gives birth" to evil — the image is that of the sinner generating iniquity as a mother gives birth to a child, which underscores the responsibility and intention behind sin. In Song of Solomon 8:5, the word denotes the actual act of childbirth: the mother has given birth to her daughter. These two uses show how biblical Hebrew employs the language of birth to express both a physical event and a spiritual or moral reality.
H2254C.portee: This word teaches that our thoughts and actions are not without consequence: the wicked "gives birth" to evil just as a mother gives birth to a child — it is a creation that belongs to him and for which he is responsible. For the believer, this reminds us that our life produces fruits, whether we are aware of it or not. The term also values motherhood and childbirth as a profound and central reality of human life, worthy of being compared to the generation of good or evil in the human heart.

sens: Cause damage, harm to someone or something
Annihilate, reduce to nothing
Make disappear, abolish a power or established order
H2255.detail:
1. To destroy means to cause harm, to injure or damage. It is a voluntary and direct act: to hurt someone, as when Daniel tells the lions that they have done him no "harm" (Daniel 6:22).
2. The word also describes the complete annihilation of an existing reality — to destroy a house, a tree, an entire building, as the king's order to "cut down the tree and destroy it" (Daniel 4:23).
3. In a broader sense, to destroy applies to kingdoms and dominions: Darius fears that someone might destroy the temple (Ezra 6:12), while the prophets affirm that the divine kingdom will never be "destroyed" and that its dominion will last forever (Daniel 2:44, Daniel 7:14).
H2255.origine: The Hebrew verb חֲבַל (chaval) denotes the action of causing damage or ruin. Its root evokes the idea of breaking, corrupting, putting out of operation. It is found in the noun חֶבֶל (chével), which denotes a cord or a tie — the underlying image being that of what binds, leads to ruin, chains to disaster.
H2255.emploi: This verb appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophets Daniel and in the account of Ezra. Ezra 6:12 uses it to express the fear that someone might destroy the temple. In Daniel's visions (2:44, 4:23, 6:26, 7:14), the word takes on prophetic resonance: it demonstrates that human kingdoms will be destroyed and abolished, while the kingdom of God itself will never be destroyed. In Daniel 6:22, the meaning nuances: "harm" refers to the injury that could have been done to Daniel. The context oscillates between material destruction and political destruction, always with the idea of cessation of existence or power.
H2255.portee: This word invites the Christian to meditate on the fragility of the powers of this world and on the unshakability of God's reign. While human empires are destined for destruction (Babylon, Persia), the eternal Kingdom of God remains indestructible. For the reader, it is a promise: God alone possesses a dominion that will never pass away, and the kingdoms that oppose His plan will be annihilated.

sens: Region or defined territory
Geographical area assigned to a tribe or people
H2256A.detail:
1. A country is a defined geographical region or territory, often a specific land area. In Joshua 19:29, the country of Aczib refers to the particular region near Aczib, a coastal city within the territory assigned to the tribe of Asher.
2. The word is also used to designate a territorial sector assigned to a group or people: it is a portion of land with recognizable borders, used to describe how God divided the promised lands among the tribes of Israel.
H2256A.origine: The Hebrew word חֶבֶל (chével) comes from a root that primarily evokes the idea of rope or cordage. From there, it took on the meaning of "region" or "territory" — perhaps because lands were delineated with ropes or because a region is a space "bound together." This shift from the concrete image (the rope) to the abstract (the region) is common in ancient languages.
H2256A.emploi: This word appears at least once in the Hebrew Bible, in Joshua 19:29, during the precise description of the borders of the territory assigned to the tribe of Asher. There it specifically designates the country of Aczib, a place on the Mediterranean coast. The term serves to mark the geographical limits of the land distribution that God commanded Joshua to allocate to the twelve tribes.
H2256A.portee: This word reminds the reader that the God of Israel is not only a spiritual God: He is a God who owns the land, who establishes borders, and who precisely assigns each people their portion. The meticulous mention of these countries in Joshua shows that God fulfills His promises concretely, giving each tribe a marked and defined earthly inheritance.

sens: Intense physical suffering, especially the contractions of childbirth
Torment, anguish, affliction of the soul
Painful labor, arduous effort
Calamity, misfortune that strikes
H2256B.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes acute physical pain, particularly the spasms and contractions felt by a woman in labor: Isaiah 26:17 describes "a pregnant woman, about to give birth, [who] writhes in the midst of her pains" — this is the main image of the word, one that recurs constantly. 2. By extension, it applies to any form of inner torment, moral distress: Jeremiah 13:21 warns that "pains will seize you, as they seize a woman in labor" — an image of spiritual agony, of punishment that grips you. 3. The word can also evoke painful effort, exhausting labor, as in Isaiah 13:8 where men "writhing like a woman in labor" are seized with "spasms and pains" in the face of terror. 4. Finally, it can designate calamity itself, the misfortune that befalls: Job 21:17 speaks of those upon whom "misery falls."
H2256B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of twisting, convulsion. The basic image is that of violent and involuntary muscle contraction — hence its preferred use for the pains of childbirth. This same root is found in other contexts of effort or struggle. It is a vivid and concrete word, rooted in common bodily experience.
H2256B.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah) and Job. It is almost always used in the plural ("pains," "sufferings") and regularly attaches to the image of the woman in labor — not to speak literally of childbirth, but as a comparison to express distress, fear, massive affliction. Jeremiah and Isaiah use it to describe divine punishment and the anguish of the people. Job employs it in contexts of misfortune and calamity. The word always carries a charge of intensity: it is not a passing discomfort, but a suffering that grips, that paralyzes.
H2256B.portee: This word reminds us that suffering is a serious biblical reality, neither denied nor minimized. The image of the woman in labor, central in several prophecies, invites the believer to see in present affliction the sign of a coming birth — a suffering that bears fruit. It also speaks of God's judgment as a formidable reality, and of the spiritual distress of the people far from their God.

sens: Fraternal bond between two groups, two peoples
H2256C.detail: 1. An union designates the bond that unites people or peoples together — the harmony, brotherhood, solidarity that keeps them together. In Zechariah 11:7, the prophet names one of his staffs "Union" to symbolize this bond; in Zechariah 11:14, breaking this staff means breaking precisely this fraternal bond between Judah and Israel.
H2256C.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of bond or connection. It is a concrete term: a staff (shepherd's rod) that bears this name does not simply designate an object, but represents a relational reality — just like the other staff named "Grace." The choice of these symbolic names shows how the ancient Israelites thought of spiritual realities through image and action rather than abstraction.
H2256C.emploi: The word appears only twice, exclusively in the prophetic vision of Zechariah 11, where the prophet acts as a poor shepherd. The two staffs symbolize two divine realities: Grace and Union. Zechariah breaks them successively to signify divine rejection and the rupture of covenants. The notion of union emphasizes the solidarity of God's people: it is the bond that should hold the tribes of Israel and Judah together — a bond that God's refusal destroys.
H2256C.portee: This text reminds us that the unity of God's people is never naturally acquired: it rests on grace and on the covenant with the Lord. When the bond with God breaks, even the fraternal union among believers collapses. For the Christian, this is a warning: the unity of the Church flows from our common attachment to Christ and depends on faithfulness to the Lord.

sens: intense and sudden physical suffering
moral or spiritual affliction
deep sorrow, grief
H2256D.detail:
1. This word primarily denotes violent and acute physical pain, like that which seizes the body — here in Micah 2:10, the pain accompanying the destruction of a house ("there will be pains, violent pains").
2. By extension, it expresses moral affliction: the inner suffering in the face of the misfortune that befalls, the sorrow of a soul in distress before God's judgment.
H2256D.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that refers to the idea of twisting, of the body's or heart's cramping under the effect of suffering. It belongs to the semantic field of raw, immediate pain, whether physical or emotional — not a chronic or bearable pain, but a harm that imposes itself violently.
H2256D.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Micah 2:10. It occurs in a passage of prophetic judgment: the people, guilty of moral defilement, will be cast out of their dwellings, and this expulsion will be accompanied by extreme pains. The context shows that the pain is linked to the consequence of God's judgment — it is not an abstract suffering, but the concrete and painful price of transgression.
H2256D.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's judgment is not a mere verbal threat, but a reality that strikes the body and soul. For the believer, it emphasizes that distance from God and disobedience have tangible and painful consequences — a lesson that invites us to take prophetic warnings seriously and to seek justice and mercy.

sens: physical object: rope, string, material link
measuring instrument: cord or chain used to delimit and measure land
extent of land: region, territory assigned or conquered
part, portion, inheritance assigned to someone
trap or bond in a figurative sense: that which holds, chains, or strangles
imminent destruction or ruin
H2256M.detail:
1. The cord is primarily a concrete object: a rope or string used to bind, suspend, or lower (Jeremiah 38:11: Ebed-Melech uses ropes to lower Jeremiah into the cistern). It is also what is placed around the neck as a sign of supplication (1 Kings 20:31: the servants put ropes on their heads).
2. The cord becomes a measuring instrument to delimit and divide lands: a cord or surveyor's chain stretched between two points (Zechariah 2:1: a man measures Jerusalem with a measuring line).
3. It then designates the territory itself, the measured and assigned region: what the cord borders becomes the cord, by extension (Deuteronomy 3:4: the region of Argob designates the conquered territory).
4. It signifies the part or inheritance assigned to a tribe or an individual (Psalms 16:6: "a delightful inheritance has fallen to me"; Joshua 19:9: the portion of the sons of Simeon).
5. In a figurative sense, the cord becomes a net that holds, a trap that suffocates: it symbolizes misfortune, servitude, or death that chains (Psalms 140:6: the proud set a trap; Job 18:10: the cords of the trap seize him).
6. Finally, it can designate imminent destruction, annihilation (Ecclesiastes 12:8 mentions the cords that break at death).
H2256M.origine: The Hebrew word חֶבֶל comes from a root that expresses the idea of binding or twisting together. Its fundamental meaning is that of a braided object: a cord. From there comes the image of the surveyor's cord that delimits land, then the territory itself, and then the inheritance derived from it. The Hebrew word חֶבֶל is also the term that evokes the work or the pain of childbirth (literally "pain of cord"), emphasizing the idea of embrace and tension. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (Septuagint), this word is rendered by σχοῖνος (schoinós, the rush, the string) or σχοῖνος (the braided reed).
H2256M.emploi: The word חֶבֶל appears 47 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical and poetic books. In the texts of land division (Deuteronomy, Joshua, Chronicles), it designates the territory assigned to a tribe or people by a surveyor's cord (Deuteronomy 3:4, Joshua 19:9, 1 Chronicles 16:18). In the Psalms and Job, it shifts to a figurative sense: the cord becomes the instrument of suffering, of the trap, or of death (Psalms 18:5-6: the cords of death have encompassed me; Job 18:10). In the prophets, it can designate a people or a region under threat (Zephaniah 2:5-7: the coast of the Philistines). The context determines whether the word remains concrete (material cord) or becomes metaphorical (territory, trap, destiny).
H2256M.portee: This word enriches the biblical understanding of inheritance and divine Providence. When the Bible speaks of the "inheritance" or "portion" that "has fallen to me," it uses the concrete image of the surveyor's cord: God measures and assigns to each their place, their land, their vocation (Psalms 16:6 thus expresses trust in the order that God establishes). Conversely, when the sinner is caught in the cords of the trap, it is because their own path binds and suffocates them. This dual image teaches that all earthly destiny proceeds from God, but also that sin forges its own chains.

sens: Harm, injury, detriment to a person or property
Wound, lesion of the body
H2257.detail:
1. The word primarily designates harm or injury caused to someone or something. In Ezra 4:22, there is fear that the "evil" may increase to the detriment of the kings — it refers to the damage that a rebellious city would cause. It is an affront, a wrong, a material or moral detriment.
2. It can also refer to a physical wound or lesion of the body. When Daniel is taken out of the lion's den (Daniel 6:23), "no injury was found on him" — not a scratch, not a mark of attack. Similarly, the three young men in the furnace (Daniel 3:25) have "no evil": they are not burned, not harmed.
H2257.origine: The Hebrew word חֲבָל (chaval) comes from a root that means "to bind" or "to tie," then "to destroy" or "to damage." The basic idea is that of a rupture or destruction. The word is used for anything that breaks, tears, wounds, or causes harm — hence its meanings of "harm" and "injury."
H2257.emploi: The word appears three times in the provided biblical texts, all in the prophetic books of the Exile (Ezra and Daniel). In Ezra 4:22, the political context: there is fear of harm to the king's interests. In Daniel 3:25 and 6:23, the context is miraculous: despite the fire or the lions, no evil reaches those who trust in God. The word never designates a moral evil or sin, but always a concrete and observable damage.
H2257.portee: These usages show that God protects those who trust Him: they will suffer no harm, no injury, even in the face of the worst dangers. The word "evil" here becomes a sign of the absence of divine protection — yet God grants it to those who trust in Him.

sens: object given as security for a debt or promise
property confiscated or held as security for payment
H2258A.detail:
1. A pledge is an object that a person gives to another to guarantee that they will repay a debt or fulfill a promise. If they do not pay, the one holding the pledge may keep or sell it. In Ezekiel 18:12, the oppressor "does not return the pledge": he has taken a possession from someone poor as security for a debt, and he refuses to return it — which shows that he does not respect justice.
2. By extension, the pledge designates the very property that has been confiscated. Ezekiel 33:15 shows repentance: the one who "returns the pledge" restores what he had unjustly withheld, thus fulfilling the law that commands the return of the poor's property.
H2258A.origine: The Hebrew word חֲבֹל (chabol) comes from a root that evokes the idea of binding, holding. A pledge is what is held, what binds the debtor to their commitment. This term specifically designates the ancient practice of the creditor who keeps a personal object of the poor as security for the repayment of their debt — a common practice in Israel, but strictly regulated by the Law to protect the weak.
H2258A.emploi: The word appears three times in the prophecies of Ezekiel, always in relation to social justice. In Ezekiel 18:12 and 18:16, the refusal to return the pledge is presented as a serious sin: the unjust man oppresses the unfortunate by not returning this withheld property. In Ezekiel 33:15, on the contrary, sincere repentance includes the restitution of the pledge — it is one of the concrete acts that proves one has renounced iniquity. Ezekiel uses this term to illustrate how one judges a person's heart: by their behavior towards the poor.
H2258A.portee: This word reminds Christians that justice towards the poor and the weak is not a secondary issue: it is a revealer of the heart. Refusing to return the poor's property is to refuse justice; restoring it is to show a transformed heart. The Law protected the poor by limiting what could be taken as a pledge — a protection that the disciple of Jesus is called to honor with generosity and justice.

sens: an object given as security for a debt
a garment or personal item entrusted as assurance for the repayment of a loan
H2258B.detail:
1. In the biblical context, a pledge is an object that a debtor gives to their creditor as a guarantee that they will repay their debt. It is a kind of security deposit: as long as the debt is unpaid, the creditor keeps the pledge. In Ezekiel 18:7, the righteous man "returns the pledge to the debtor," meaning he restores this object given as security — for example, a garment or a tool — as soon as he can or without delay, instead of keeping it unjustly.
2. Specifically, it often refers to a personal item important to the debtor, such as a garment (a coat) or a work tool. The word pledge evokes the image of a hand that grips or holds: it designates what is "held" or "seized" as collateral. Israelite law, inspired by justice and compassion, strictly regulated this usage: one could not indefinitely keep the pledge of a poor person, especially their night garment.
H2258B.origine: The Hebrew word חֲבֹלָה (chavola) comes from the same root as חֲבֹל (chavol, H2258A), which literally means "rope" or "tie" — the original image being that which binds, that which holds. The pledge is what "binds" the debtor to the creditor until repayment. This family of words always evokes an idea of taking or seizing.
H2258B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible in Ezekiel 18:7, in the description of the righteous man according to God. The passage enumerates acts of justice: not oppressing, returning pledges, not committing robbery, sharing bread and clothing with the poor. The pledge is presented as a particular case of restitution — a test of righteousness towards those who suffer from poverty. It is a legal and social term that reflects the economic realities of the people of Israel: borrowing was common among the poorest, and the law protected debtors from creditor abuses.
H2258B.portee: This word reminds Christians that justice is not abstract: it is measured by how one treats the poor and indebted. Returning a pledge is to recognize the dignity of the borrower, refusing to take advantage of their misery by withholding what belongs to them. It is a call to economic mercy, still relevant today: how do we respect those who owe us or depend on us?

sens: a man who directs a ship at sea
one who possesses the expertise and authority over the boat
an experienced sailor in charge of navigation
H2259.detail: 1. The pilot is the man responsible for directing a ship at sea: he is the chief navigator. In Tyre, the great port city, pilots were renowned for their expertise (Ezekiel 27:8). They knew the routes, the dangers, the coasts, and how to maneuver the ship according to the conditions. 2. The pilot represents one who possesses the know-how and authority to command on board. That is why in the storm threatening Jonah's ship, it is the pilot who steps forward as responsible: he approaches the sleeper and urges him to call on God (Jonah 1:6). His authority over the ship is recognized by all. 3. The word more broadly designates any experienced sailor engaged in navigation: pilots are among the important tradesmen of the ancient maritime world, alongside mariners and rowers. During the fall of Tyre, all its pilots will perish, as they represented the very expertise of the city (Ezekiel 27:27-29).
H2259.origine: The Hebrew word חֹבֵל (chobel) comes from the root חבל which primarily means "to be tied, to hold, to master." From this arises the image of the pilot: one who "holds" the ship, who controls and governs it through the art of navigation. He is a man who masters the ropes, the sails, and the direction of the vessel. The word belongs to the well-established ancient maritime vocabulary in Phoenicia, the homeland of the greatest navigators of the ancient world.
H2259.emploi: The word appears five times in the Old Testament, exclusively in the prophet Ezekiel and in the book of Jonah. Ezekiel uses it to describe the renowned pilots of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:8), then in the prophetic vision of the fall of this great city: the pilots are part of the wealth, expertise, and prestige that God will destroy (Ezekiel 27:27-29). Jonah uses it in the context of a storm (Jonah 1:6), where the pilot acts as a figure of authority and responsibility on board. In all cases, the pilot embodies the experienced and commanding sailor.
H2259.portee: The pilot reminds Christians that the conduct of life, like that of a ship, requires experience, vigilance, and sure guidance. In particular, the scene of Jonah shows that even the most competent pilot cannot master the storm: only calling on God can save us. The fall of Tyre warns that wealth, prestige, and human competence do not last against the will of God.

sens: a vertical piece of wood or metal that supports the sails of a ship
figuratively: that which dominates and rises, a high point
H2260.detail:
1. The mast is the large vertical piece planted at the center or on the deck of a ship, to which the sails are attached to catch the wind and propel the boat forward. It is the essential element of the structure of a sailing vessel. In Proverbs 23:34, the image of the mast expresses extreme instability: the drunken man is compared to someone lying on a mast swaying above the ocean, tossed about on all sides, without any stable support.
2. Figuratively, the mast symbolizes that which rises, that which dominates, that which is high — a position from which one can be thrown, where balance is fragile. Intoxication, in this passage, makes the man as unstable as one resting on such a dizzying and perilous position.
H2260.origine: The Hebrew word חִבֵּל (chib.bel) designates the mast of a ship. Its exact origin remains uncertain in ancient Hebrew, but the image is clear: it is the vertical and stable element of the ship, even though it remains exposed to the movements of the sea. The word may have an etymological link with the idea of "rope" or "attachment" (חֶבֶל, chevel, means rope in Hebrew), since the sails are fixed to the mast by rigging.
H2260.emploi: The word חִבֵּל appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 23:34. In this context, the wise Solomon uses the image of the mast to describe the pitiful state of the man who abuses wine. Lying on the top of a mast, swayed by the movements of the sea, this man embodies the ridiculousness and danger of drunkenness — total instability, a complete loss of self-control. The image is striking because it evokes both height (the top of the mast), vulnerability, and the absurdity of the situation.
H2260.portee: This image of the mast helps the reader to concretely understand the ravages of drunkenness: not an abstract intoxication, but a total loss of balance, dignity, and self-control. For those who heed biblical wisdom, it is a powerful call to reject excessive alcohol, not through dry moralism, but by seeing through the eyes of the text the absurdity and fragility that drunkenness creates.

sens: Flower of the fields, with a pleasant fragrance and delicate petals
Symbol of natural beauty and splendor in the desert
Poetic image of joy and transformation
H2261.detail:
1. The narcissus is a wildflower that grows in the meadows and arid lands of the Middle East. It is a delicate flower, with fine petals, often yellow or white. It blooms in the spring and brings color to rocky or desert spaces. In Song of Solomon 2:1, the beloved compares herself to a narcissus, emphasizing her natural and fragile beauty among the flowers of the valleys.
2. The narcissus also symbolizes the splendor that emerges from the arid desert. When the prophet Isaiah 35:1 announces that "the desert...will blossom like a narcissus," he evokes a miraculous transformation: the barren and abandoned lands suddenly cover themselves with flowers, an image of restoration and hope. It is a promise that God will bring life and beauty where desolation once reigned.
H2261.origine: The Hebrew word חֲבַצֶּלֶת refers to a wildflower from the Mediterranean regions. Some believe that the term may be related to a root meaning "to shine" or "to radiate," which fits well with the luminous aspect of this flower.
