In the Hebrew Bible, this word appears only in these two poetic passages, where it symbolizes delicate beauty or glorious transformation each time.
H2261.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in a poetic and evocative context. In the Song of Solomon, the lover expresses the simple yet radiant beauty of the beloved. In Isaiah, the messianic prophet announces the future transformation of the world: when the Lord intervenes, even the barren desert will wear the splendor of a flower. These two uses show that the narcissus embodies natural beauty and hope.
H2261.portee: For the Christian reader, the narcissus reminds us that true beauty is often humble and natural, not artificial or pretentious. It also invites us to believe in divine transformation: the desert of our arid and hopeless lives can one day green and bloom when God intervenes. These poetic images strengthen the confidence that nothing is too ravaged or lost for God to bring life and beauty back to it.

sens: Man from the time of the divided monarchy
Head of a family among the Rechabites
H2262.detail: Habazinia is a man whose name appears only once in the Bible, during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two. He is mentioned in Jeremiah 35:3 as the grandfather of Jaazania and apparently as the head of one of the families of the Rechabites, a people who observed strict life rules passed down by their ancestors (not drinking wine, not building houses, remaining nomadic).
H2262.origine: The name Habazinia means "Light of Jehovah" (from the Hebrew חֲבַצִּנְיָה). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, which was common in Israel to express divine blessing upon a person.
H2262.emploi: Habazinia appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 35:3. The prophet Jeremiah is commanded to summon the Rechabites to test them: he must verify if they will remain faithful to their ancestral vows. Habazinia is named as the ancestor and leader of the lineage of Jaazania, establishing his foundational role in this branch of the Rechabites.

sens: To hold someone in one's arms
To hold something close to oneself
To remove or surround
To cross one's arms, to remain inactive
H2263.detail:
1. To embrace someone means to hold them close in a sign of affection, joy, or welcome. Laban "embraced" Jacob when he first saw him (Genesis 29:13), and Israel "embraced" the sons of Joseph tenderly (Genesis 48:10).
2. The word can also refer to holding something firmly, surrounding it, or clasping it — as when one "embraces" a rock by holding it close (Job 24:8), or when one "embraces" someone's breast (Proverbs 5:20).
3. By extension, to embrace can mean "to surround" or "to hold together," as in the expression "crossing one's hands" (Ecclesiastes 4:5), where the arms remain still against each other.
4. Figuratively, "crossing one's arms" or "embracing inactivity" expresses idleness and refusal to act: "The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh" (Ecclesiastes 4:5).
H2263.origine: The Hebrew verb חָבַק (chavaq) paints the primary image of two arms enclosing something or someone. It comes from an ancient root whose fundamental meaning is "to surround" or "to embrace." The word evokes the natural movement of an embrace — the arms closing in towards each other. This image of bodily gesture extends to the figurative sense: just as crossed arms bind and immobilize, inactivity "enfolds" a person in their inertia.
H2263.emploi: The verb appears about a dozen times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poetry and in the narratives of the Old Testament. In its simple state, "to embrace" expresses physical affection and welcome: Laban embraces Jacob, Israel embraces the children of Joseph. The word can also describe the action of holding an object firmly — the rocks that the poor hold against themselves as refuge (Job 24:8), or a woman held in one's arms (Proverbs 5:20, Song of Solomon 2:6 and 8:3). An important nuance appears in the passages that speak of "crossing one's hands" (Ecclesiastes 4:5): here, the gesture of crossing the arms symbolizes culpable idleness and abandonment of all effort. The verb thus paints both tenderness and inactivity.
H2263.portee: For the believer, the word reminds us that God shows affection and closeness to His people — He does not remain distant, but "embraces" in a sense those He loves. Conversely, learning that the fool "crosses his hands" invites reflection on one's own choices: are we active in faith, or do we allow inactivity to dominate us? Love for one's neighbor requires open arms, not crossed arms.

sens: Action of folding and joining the hands one over the other
Attitude of inaction and laziness, in which one crosses their hands to do nothing
H2264.detail:
1. To cross one's hands means to fold and intertwine them by placing one over the other, a natural gesture of rest or relaxation. This is the literal and physical meaning of the word: to join one's hands in a way that embraces them.

2. Figuratively, crossing one's hands becomes a symbol of laziness and inactivity. One who "crosses their hands to sleep" (Proverbs 6:10 and 24:33) is a person who yields to fatigue and slackness, who refuses effort and obedience. It is a gesture of abandonment: crossed hands do not work, do not grasp anything, do not build anything.
H2264.origine: The Hebrew word chibbouq comes from a root meaning "to fold" or "to embrace." It describes a simple physical movement — joining one's hands — that has become a moral image: one who crosses their hands abandons action and sinks into laziness. This image of sterile rest, repeated twice in Proverbs, emphasizes how the gesture has become proverbial in Hebrew to express inertia.
H2264.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Proverbs, and in the same verses (6:10 and 24:33). In these two passages, it describes the gesture of one who "crosses their hands to sleep," that is, who yields to laziness and refuses to get up to work. The context is a wise warning: a little sleep, a little rest, and behold, one crosses their hands — and poverty comes like a thief. The word is thus used exclusively to describe the attitude of the lazy, a symbol of one who does not resist slackness.
H2264.portee: Crossing one's hands is the biblical image of spiritual and material laziness. For the believer, this gesture reminds us that accepting inactivity is to accept misery and ruin. The Bible calls us to vigilance and effort, not to abandon our hands to sterile rest. This word challenges the reader: do you refuse to "cross your hands"? do you accept to rise and act according to God's wisdom?

sens: Prophet of Israel who lived during the time of the divided monarchy
Author of the prophetic book that bears his name
H2265.detail: 1. Habakkuk is a prophet of Israel mentioned for the first time in Habakkuk 1:1, where he receives a divine revelation. His name means "embrace" or "clutch," evoking the idea of holding firmly. It is believed that he lived around the 12th or 13th year of King Josiah's reign, during a troubled time in the history of the kingdom of Judah. 2. Habakkuk is also the author of the prophetic book that bears his name in the Bible. In Habakkuk 3:1, we read his prayer addressed to God, composed in the mode of lamentations, where the prophet expresses his questions and complaints in light of the events of his time. His message focuses on the themes of divine justice and faith in God despite the troubling appearances of the world.
H2265.origine: The name Habakkuk comes from a Hebrew root that means "to embrace," "to clasp," or "to hold firmly." This name evokes an image of strength and stability, a firm grasp. Although few details are given about the prophet himself in the Old Testament, his name and the content of his book allow us to understand his role as a divine messenger.
H2265.emploi: Habakkuk appears twice in the Segond in chapters 1 and 3 of the book that bears his name. In Habakkuk 1:1, the oracle or divine revelation is addressed directly to him, marking the beginning of his prophetic mission. In Habakkuk 3:1, we see Habakkuk presenting a prayer or lament to God, which shows that his role as a prophet includes not only the transmission of divine words but also intercession and the expression of Israel's complaints before the Lord. Habakkuk thus stands out as a prophet who questions God in the face of the mysteries of His justice.

sens: To link together, unite two or more things into one
To assemble, gather into a common group
To form an alliance, associate with someone
To accumulate, pile up (words or things)
H2266.detail:
1. To join two elements to make a whole: this means to physically link, to assemble. In the Tabernacle tent, one must "join" the curtains together to form the roof (Exodus 26:9); the boards and the clasps must also be "joined" so that the tent "forms a whole" (Exodus 36:18).
2. To assemble, gather people or things around a common goal. When several kings "gathered" against Abraham in the valley of Siddim (Genesis 14:3), they joined together to act collectively, with a common intention.
3. To form an alliance, to associate with someone for a concerted action. Jehoshaphat "allied" himself with King Ahaziah of Israel (2 Chronicles 20:35), which means to forge a political and military pact with him.
4. To accumulate, pile up words or elements that add to one another. Job says: "I would overwhelm you with words" (Job 16:4), meaning he would pile up, accumulate words against his friends.
H2266.origine: The verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of binding, assembling, bringing closer. Its basic image is that of a link, a knot that unites. The Hebrew word chabar appears in various forms: the simple form expresses the action of joining two things, while other forms reinforce this idea or turn it toward association, alliance. This root well translates the transition from a mechanical action (binding two curtains) to a political or moral action (contracting an alliance).
H2266.emploi: The verb chabar is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in the description of the Tabernacle (Exodus 26, 36, 39) where it is necessary to "join" the curtains and the boards. It is also found to describe the assembly of people who come together in coalition (Genesis 14:3), the formation of political alliances (2 Chronicles 20:35-37), and even, more rarely, to evoke the accumulation of words (Job 16:4). The context determines whether the link is material or political, mechanical or moral. In the Psalms and in Ezekiel, it sometimes expresses the idea of being united or being in close relationship.
H2266.portee: This word reminds the believer that God unites His people by strong bonds, just as the curtains of the Tabernacle were "joined" to form a single dwelling. It also invites vigilance: the alliances we "join" must not lead us away from faithfulness to God, as shown by the warning addressed to Jehoshaphat. Finally, it shows that no accumulation of words, no human coalition can endure if it ignores the Lord.

sens: Word or magical formula intended to produce a supernatural effect
Practice of magic and spells
One who practices magic, the magician
H2267.detail:
1. A word or magical act intended to exert a supernatural power: it is a formula, often secret, that is pronounced to cast a spell or invoke a hidden power. In Isaiah 47:12, Babylon is urged to "stand fast in your enchantments": these are the magical acts on which it relies for protection or dominance.
2. The entirety of magical practice, spells and rituals to which one dedicates oneself: this refers to an activity, a profession of magician. Isaiah 47:9 mentions "the multitude of your enchantments," listing all the spells and incantations that a person accumulates and practices.
3. The person themselves who practices these arts: an enchanter or magician. In Deuteronomy 18:11 and Psalms 58:6, the "enchanter" is one who consults spirits, speaks to the dead, or promises to read the future through magical formulas.
H2267.origine: The Hebrew word חֶבֶר (chever) is related to the idea of association and companionship: an enchanter is one who "associates" with spirits or occult powers. The root expresses the link, the connection — but here it is a perverse connection, a pact with the invisible world of magic. In the Bible, this word stands in direct opposition to trust in God alone.
H2267.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a context of condemnation or warning. In Deuteronomy 18:11, it designates one of the magical practices forbidden to Israel, listed among those of the spirit consultant or necromancer. Psalms 58:6 invokes God's judgment against the "most skillful magician" (literally "one who binds enchantments"), an image of charm rendered harmless. Isaiah 47:9-12 develops the picture: Babylon, the great power, places its trust in its countless enchantments, but the Lord declares them vain. The meaning oscillates between the magical formula itself and the practitioner, but always with the same biblical judgment: enchantment is a human attempt to control the supernatural outside of God.
H2267.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that any search for supernatural power outside of God — whether through magic, divination, or occultism — is vain and forbidden. The Bible does not say that enchantment has no effect, but that its effect is never protective or salvific: it is seduction and deceit. True power belongs to God alone; whoever seeks elsewhere abandons their trust in Him.

sens: Son of Asher, ancestor of the Hebrews
Descendant of Asher during the Exodus and conquest
H2268G.detail: Heber is a proper name that designates a character in the genealogy of Israel. He is the son of Beriah and grandson of Asher, one of the twelve sons of Jacob (Genesis 46:17). From him descended the family of the Hebrews, mentioned in the census of the desert (Numbers 26:45). His own sons — Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and Shua — are listed in the genealogies of the tribe of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:31-32). Thus, he represents a link in the genealogical line of Israel, preserved in the records of the people.
H2268G.origine: The name Heber (חֶ֫בֶר) literally means "comrade" or "companion" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of being bound or associated with others. It is a theophoric name that appears in several Israelite genealogies, although it is borne by several distinct characters in Scripture (notably the Kenite husband of Jael).
H2268G.emploi: Heber appears four times in the Bible, all in the official genealogies of Asher. He is first presented in Genesis 46:17 as one of the sons of Beriah during Jacob's migration to Egypt. About forty years later, in Numbers 26:45, we find the "family of the Hebrews" descended from him, which shows that Heber's line had developed and multiplied during the stay in Egypt and the beginning of the desert. The two passages in 1 Chronicles 7:31-32 confirm this genealogical role and detail his own descendants. Heber only appears in these genealogical lists; no events or specific actions are attributed to him, indicating that the Bible mentions him mainly to establish the line of succession and the structure of families within the tribe of Asher.

sens: Kenite man, husband of Jael, living during the time of the Judges
Head of a family who established his clan near Kadesh in Canaan
H2268H.detail: Heber is a Kenite man (member of the Kenite people) who lived during the time of the Judges, before the monarchy in Israel. His name means "companion" or "ally." He had separated from the rest of the Kenites and pitched his tent near the oak of Zaanannim, near Kadesh (Judges 4:11). Heber is best known as the husband of Jael, the woman who killed the general Sisera by driving a tent peg through his temple while he slept (Judges 4:21). At that time, there was a peace alliance between Heber and Jabin, king of Hazor, which explains why Sisera sought refuge in his tent (Judges 4:17). The poet who composed the Song of Deborah praises Jael for her act of courage and explicitly mentions that she is "the wife of Heber the Kenite" (Judges 5:24).
H2268H.origine: The name Heber comes from a Hebrew root meaning "companion" or "associate," evoking the idea of bond and alliance. The Kenites were a nomadic people who maintained relations with Israel and with the Canaanites; they often forged diplomatic alliances. Heber embodies this intermediary position: he separated from his own to establish an independent clan, which earned him peace with both powers of the time.
H2268H.emploi: Heber appears only four times in the Bible, all in the account of Judges 4-5, which tells of Israel's victory over Jabin and his general Sisera. He is first presented as a Kenite who established his camp independently of his people (Judges 4:11). We learn that there was peace between his house and the king of Hazor, which makes his role in the story ambiguous: his tent becomes a refuge for the enemy of Israel, but it is there that the turning point of the battle takes place (Judges 4:17). Jael, his wife, kills Sisera there, leading to the definitive victory. Although Heber is a key figure in the narrative, he remains in the background: we know nothing of his opinion on what his wife does, and the text mentions him mainly to establish the context of peace that allowed Sisera to seek refuge with him.
H2268H.portee: Heber reminds us that God uses ordinary circumstances and even complex human alliances to accomplish His purposes. His tent becomes the stage for Israel's deliverance, not through a dazzling warrior act, but through a courageous woman in the intimacy of the home. His story invites the reader to see how God remains active, even among those who are not of Israel, and how divine justice is fulfilled in unexpected ways.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Old Testament
H2268I.detail: Heber is a man of the tribe of Judah who appears only in 1 Chronicles 4:18. He is the son of Mered and Jehudijah, and the father of Soco. His name means "companion" or "comrade" in ancient Hebrew, evoking the idea of association or bond between people.
H2268I.origine: The Hebrew name Heber (חֶבֶר) literally means "companion" or "associate," derived from a root that expresses union or bond between people. This name appears several times in the Old Testament to designate different individuals, including a Kenite who married Jael and killed Sisera, and a grandson of Asher. The same Hebrew root underlies the biblical concept of community bond and association.
H2268I.emploi: Heber is mentioned only once in the genealogical lists of 1 Chronicles 4:18, where he is included in the descendants of Mered and his Egyptian wife Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh. He is presented there as the father of Soco. This unique reference provides little information about his life or role; he is simply recognized as an important link in the genealogical chain of the Judean families during the divided kingdom.

sens: Benjamite during the divided monarchy
Son of Elpahal
H2268J.detail: 1. Heber is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two (after the death of Solomon). The text places him in a specific genealogy of Benjaminite families.
H2268J.origine: The name Heber means "companion" or "comrade" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of association or solidarity. It is a name carrying a positive connotation of social bond. Several different characters bear this name in the Old Testament: a famous Kenite (husband of Jael, who killed the general Sisera), a grandson of Asher, a father of Soco, and several other Benjamites and Gadites.
H2268J.emploi: This Heber is mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 8:17, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. He is identified as the son of Elpahal and the brother of about ten other men (Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Ishmerai, Izlia, Jobab, and others). This unique reference suggests that, although he is part of the recognized ancestors of the tribe of Benjamin, the details of his personal life are not reported.

sens: one who shares life, fate, or work with another person
one who forms a friendship or alliance with someone
one who secretly acts with others for a common, often evil, purpose
H2269.detail:
1. A companion is primarily one with whom you live or work together. In the book of Daniel, Daniel's three companions — Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah — are his fellow exiles and trainees at the court of Babylon. They share the same fate and dangers (Daniel 2:17-18).
2. The word also refers to one with whom a friendship or alliance has been formed. It is a bond of trust and solidarity between two people who esteem each other.
3. In the sense of "ambush" in Hosea 6:9, the word describes a band that acts together in the shadows: priests who form a united group to do evil — a meaning that retains the idea of "associates" or "companions," but for a criminal enterprise.
H2269.origine: The Aramaic word חֲבַר comes from the same root as the Hebrew word חָבֵר (cha.ver), both expressing the idea of "binding together" or "assembling." The root evokes the image of one who is bound to oneself, who is joined. The fundamental meaning is that of an association or a bond created between people.
H2269.emploi: This word appears six times in the Aramaic Bible, mainly in the book of Daniel. It primarily refers to Daniel's three Hebrew companions in Babylonian exile: Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, presented as his peers, his comrades in captivity and faithfulness to God (Daniel 2:13, 2:17, 2:18). Once in Hosea 6:9, it takes on the meaning of a band acting in ambush, a united group secretly committing evil — the priests forming a criminal league. The context of Proverbs shows that "companion" can also refer to one with whom one shares fate or dwelling.
H2269.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of community in faith. Daniel's three companions illustrate the strength of brotherly bonds in the face of trial: it is together that they implore God and together that they are delivered. But Hosea also warns that those who "associate" with evil bear collective responsibility. A Christian must choose companions wisely.

sens: A person united to another, associated with them in a common activity or state
A faithful friend, one who shares the same convictions or beliefs
One who accompanies someone, who is by their side in daily life
H2270.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to one who is linked or united to another. In Judges 20:11, the men of Israel gather "united as one man": they form a single block, each being the companion of all the others. It conveys the idea of connection, belonging to the same group.

2. A companion is also a true friend, someone with whom one shares values. The psalmist says in 119:63: "I am a friend of all those who fear you" — he recognizes as companions all those who share his fear of God and obedience to His Word.

3. In practical life, a companion is one who is present and helpful. In Ecclesiastes 4:10, when a man falls, "his companion lifts him up" — it is the comrade, the colleague at work or on a journey, the one who is there and can lend a hand when needed.
H2270.origine: The Hebrew word חָבֵר comes from a root meaning "to unite" or "to join." It belongs to the same family as the verb "to assemble" or "to bind." The initial image is that of ropes or ties that connect things together: a companion is someone to whom you are attached, united. The word can also function as an adjective to describe what is "united" or "associated."
H2270.emploi: The word appears about a dozen times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes. It refers to workmates (Ecclesiastes 4:10, the companions of shepherds), faithful friends in faith (Psalms 119:63), or associates in a common cause, whether good or bad (Proverbs 28:24, being the companion of a destroyer). The term also applies to those who share a status or privilege: in Psalms 45:8, the king has his "colleagues" or companions of anointing. Each time, the companion is someone with whom one is linked by a concrete relationship and a common identity.
H2270.portee: This word reminds the believer that faith is never lived in solitude. Being a companion of those who fear God (Psalms 119:63) is to recognize that one belongs to a community, a spiritual family. The companion is also one on whom one can rely: he lifts up the one who falls (Ecclesiastes 4:10). This invites every Christian to be reliable and helpful, and to surround themselves with true companions, those who share their convictions.

sens: to engage in commerce or commercial exchanges
to practice a trade as a merchant or intermediary
to share the profits of a business with others
H2271.detail:
1. To trade means to engage in commerce or merchant exchanges. The word evokes the image of merchants who buy, sell, or negotiate goods. In Job 40:25, it questions whether fishermen can trade on the leviathan (a mythical and symbolic creature): the text asks if they can sell or exchange such a creature.
2. The word also refers to one who practices a trade as an associate or merchant, engaged in transactions. It is one who actively deals in commercial affairs and trade.
3. Finally, to trade can mean to share among merchants or partners the profits of a sale or transaction. The passage in Job 40:25 asks whether fishermen share among themselves the profits of their catch.
H2271.origine: The Hebrew word chabbār comes from a root (חבר) that fundamentally means "to join" or "to associate." It expresses the idea of binding together, of uniting. From this arises the meaning of "associate" or "partner," then that of "merchant" who associates with others to engage in trade. The word thus designates one who is linked to another by a commercial affair.
H2271.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 40:25, where God addresses Job regarding the leviathan. The question posed is rhetorical: can fishermen really trade on such a powerful and elusive creature as the leviathan? This unique usage underscores human impotence in the face of God's great creatures. The commercial context — trade, sale, sharing profits — ironically contrasts with the impossibility of subduing this monstrous being.
H2271.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate the ineffectiveness of human wisdom and trading power in the face of the greatness of divine creation. By evoking commerce and exchange, it reminds us that human affairs, even legitimate ones, remain fragile and limited before what only God can master. It is an invitation to humility.

sens: Visible mark or stain on the skin of an animal
Figurative defect or blemish
H2272.detail:
1. The word refers to a natural visible mark on the skin, particularly the spots of a leopard. In Jeremiah 13:23, the prophet asks: "Can a leopard change its spots?" — an image of the indelible nature of something. The spots of the leopard are innate and permanent.
2. By extension, this word is used figuratively to evoke a moral stain or deep flaw, something that cannot be erased by mere willpower. The same rhetorical question about the leopard's spots means: similarly, you who are accustomed to evil, can you really change?
H2272.origine: The Hebrew word חֲבַרְבֻּרָה is related to roots that express the idea of mark or stripe. It literally refers to what adorns or marks a surface — here, the visible spots that characterize the animal. The leopard is indeed known for these natural and inseparable marks of its appearance.
H2272.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 13:23. The prophet Jeremiah uses it in a striking comparison addressed to the people of Judah: if the leopard cannot remove its spots nor the Ethiopian change the color of his skin, how can this people, long accustomed to evil, truly convert? It is an image of human impossibility, and implicitly of the necessity of divine intervention to truly change.
H2272.portee: This image of the leopard and its permanent spots challenges the Christian: it reminds us that a habit of sin is deeply rooted in us, and that we cannot heal from it by purely natural effort. It reveals our absolute need for God's grace to be transformed. It is a call to humility before our incapacity, and an openness to the Holy Spirit who alone can renew us.

sens: companion, associate, one who accompanies someone in the same condition
H2273.detail: 1. The word refers to a companion, someone of equal status whom one associates with or shares a situation. In Aramaic (the language of the later passages of Daniel), it is the equivalent of the more common Hebrew term "companion." Daniel 7:20 uses it to describe the horns of the apocalyptic beast: one of them stands out from the "others" by its appearance and power, highlighting that they are of the same type, simply with notable differences.
H2273.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same Semitic universe as the Hebrew חָבֵר (chaver, "companion"). The root expresses the idea of being united, associated, forming a whole with others. The two forms (Hebrew and Aramaic) reflect how the Semitic languages spoken in Israel enriched themselves with borrowings and regional variants. The basic idea is one of equality and closeness: one is the companion of one with whom one shares something.
H2273.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:20, a passage from the prophetic book written in Aramaic. It is used in the plural ("others") to qualify the horns of the monstrous beast in Daniel's vision, contrasting the one that rises with arrogance to its peers. This unique usage in an apocalyptic context shows that the term retains its simple and direct meaning: what is "other" shares the same basic nature, while being distinguished by certain characteristics.

sens: group of people united for a common purpose
band, company of people who associate with each other
set of people living together or acting in concert
H2274.detail:
1. A society is a group of people who come together around a common purpose or activity. In Job 34:8, this word refers to those who "do evil" — a company bound by the same actions, the same moral direction.
2. The word also evokes the idea of closeness and brotherhood: one walks "in society" with someone, one is paired with them. It is the image of people going together, sharing the path.
H2274.origine: The Hebrew word חֶבְרָה comes from a root that means "to be a friend" or "to be a companion." It is from the same family as חָבֵר (haver), which denotes a friend or companion. The word expresses the idea of bonds that unite people together, a group bound by a form of camaraderie or communion.
H2274.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 34:8. In this context, Job is accused by Elihu of keeping company with those who do evil and walking alongside the wicked. It is a reproach: by associating with these people, Job would share their guilt or promote their actions. The word emphasizes here the moral danger of association.
H2274.portee: This verse reminds believers that our companions, friendships, and associations profoundly influence us. The society we frequent shapes our choices and actions. It is a biblical warning about the formative power of the moral environment in which we live.

sens: Important city in southern Judah, about 30 km south of Jerusalem
H2275A.detail: 1. Hebron is a major city in the hill country of Judah, ancient and well-fortified. It is associated with Abraham, who built an altar there near the oaks of Mamre (Genesis 13:18), and it is where Sarah died and was buried (Genesis 23:2, 23:19). David reigned there for seven years before conquering Jerusalem and transferring his capital there (2 Samuel 2:1-3; 1 Kings 2:11). The city is also a city of refuge and a Levitical center (Joshua 20:7; Joshua 21:11). Its strategic importance makes it one of the strongholds of the kingdom of Judah (2 Chronicles 11:10).
H2275A.origine: The name means "association" in Hebrew, perhaps reflecting its role as a gathering place and community life. Kirjath-Arba, the ancient name of the city, means "city of Arba" (Joshua 21:11): Arba was an ancestor of the Anakim, the giants of the region. The city is very ancient, occupied long before the time of Abraham.
H2275A.emploi: Hebron appears 57 times in the Bible, mostly in the historical books (Genesis, Joshua, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles). It is first a place of life for Abraham and his family (Genesis 13, 23, 35), then it becomes a major military objective during Joshua's conquest of Canaan (Joshua 10:36-39). After Saul's death, it is there that David is anointed king over Judah, and then over all Israel (2 Samuel 2:3-4; 2 Samuel 5:1-3). It retains its importance as an administrative and religious center in the monarchy, and as a place of refuge for those accused of involuntary manslaughter (Joshua 20:7).
H2275A.portee: Hebron tells the story of God's faithfulness to Abraham and his descendants. It is the cradle of David's dynasty, through which God established the messianic promise. For the believer, this city symbolizes how God leads His people from one stage to another, from the patriarchs to the king of the covenant, and reminds us that our lives are not limited to a single place or moment, but are part of God's plan.

sens: Son of Kehath, himself son of Levi, ancestor of the Hebronite Levites
Leader or representative of the Hebronite Levites during the organization of worship
H2275B.detail:
1. Hebron is a man from the tribe of Levi, one of the four sons of Kehath (who is the son of Levi). He lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. He appears in the sacred genealogies of Israel, listed alongside his brothers Amram, Jitschar, and Uziel (Exodus 6:18). He is the father of four sons: Jerijah, Amarjah, Jahaziel, and Jekamém, and his descendants form the family of the Hebronites within the tribe of Levi.
2. The Hebronites play a specific role in the organization of the sanctuary service. At the time when David organizes worship in Jerusalem, we see Eliel, a leader of the sons of Hebron, appearing with eighty of his brothers to participate in this organization (1 Chronicles 15:9). They are thus servants of the temple, responsible for certain liturgical tasks.
H2275B.origine: The name Hebron means "association" in Hebrew. It carries a meaning that evokes the idea of joining or gathering, which is fitting for a man whose descendants form an established and organized family in the worship of God. His descendants are called Hebronites (a derived form), and this nomenclature clearly identifies them within the Levitical genealogies. The word expresses family unity and gathering around a sacred function.
H2275B.emploi: Hebron appears only seven times in the Bible, always in genealogical texts or in the organization of worship. He is first mentioned in the lists of the sons of Kehath at the time of the Exodus (Exodus 6:18, Numbers 3:19, 1 Chronicles 6:2 and 6:18), where he is simply listed with his three brothers. Later, his descendants, the Hebronites, play an active role in the temple service: in 1 Chronicles 15:9, one of their leaders accompanies David. These usages emphasize that Hebron is primarily important for his offspring and the office that his family fulfills in the worship of Israel.

sens: Valley where the flocks of Israel grazed
Region of Canaan inhabited by the descendants of Abraham
H2275H.detail:
1. The word literally means "association" or "union," and refers to a fertile valley in Canaan where the patriarchs led their flocks to graze. It is there that Israel sends Joseph to find his brothers and check on the state of the livestock (Genesis 37:14).
2. Hebron later becomes a major location in the history of Israel, linked to the lives of the patriarchs and God's covenant with Abraham.
H2275H.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew root evoking association or communion. Hebron was a valley in Canaan, a region that God had promised to Abraham and his descendants. This name has been borne by several important places in biblical history.
H2275H.emploi: The word appears in the account of Joseph in Genesis 37:14, where Israel (Jacob) sends his son Joseph from the valley of Hebron to find his brothers who were tending the flocks. This valley was a major pastoral center for Abraham's family. Hebron will remain a significant place in the Old Testament, associated with the patriarchs and the life of God's people in Canaan.
H2275H.portee: Hebron reminds the reader of God's faithfulness to His promises made to the patriarchs and the reality of His divine presence in the places where His people dwelled. It is also the setting where the story of Joseph unfolds, a story of trust and divine providence.

sens: Descendant of Caleb, son of Mareshah and father of four sons
Man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H2275I.detail:
1. Hebron is a man from the tribe of Judah, son of Mareshah and father of four children: Koré, Thappuach, Rékem, and Schéma (1 Chronicles 2:43). He is a descendant of Caleb, one of the great figures in the history of Israel, who explored the promised land before the conquest.
2. He is mentioned during the time of the divided monarchy, several centuries after Moses and Joshua. His name, which means "association" in Hebrew, recalls the idea of connection and community within his family and his people.
H2275I.origine: The name Hebron literally means "association" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of union and bond. This same name has a much older history in the Bible: it first designated a direct descendant of Kohath and grandson of Levi (the ancestors of the Levitical priests), and later it was borne by this man from Caleb. It is a family name that has been passed down through generations.
H2275I.emploi: Hebron appears twice in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, in chapter 2. He is first presented in 1 Chronicles 2:42 as the son of Mareshah and brother of Jerachmeel, and then in 1 Chronicles 2:43 where his four sons are listed. These genealogical mentions show the importance given to the lineages of Caleb and the continuity of his descendants among the tribes of Judah. The genealogies in the book of Chronicles serve to establish family ties and inheritance rights of the tribes of Israel.

sens: Descendants of the Levite Hebron, grandson of Levi
Family of priests and Levites responsible for the service of the Temple
H2276.detail:
1. The Hebronites are the descendants of the Levite Hebron, son of Kehath and grandson of Levi. Hebron is first mentioned in the Exodus during the counting of the Levitical families (Numbers 3:27).
2. They form a distinct Levitical family, responsible for priestly tasks in the service of the Tabernacle and later the Temple. During the time of King David, the Hebronites oversee the administration of Israel and monitor the religious and civil affairs of the kingdom (1 Chronicles 26:30-31).
H2276.origine: The name comes from Hebron (חֶבְרוֹן), the eponymous ancestor of this Levitical clan. Hebron was the son of Kehath, himself the son of Levi, and had four sons: Jerijah, Amarjah, Jahaziel, and Jekameam. The term designates both the founding individual and all his descendants who form a family house within the Levitical priesthood.
H2276.emploi: This name appears five times in the Bible, always to designate the group or family of the Hebronites in the context of the Levites. It is found in both counts of the Levitical families (Numbers 3:27 and 26:58), and then in the texts of Chronicles that describe the organization of the Temple service under David. The Hebronites appear as a powerful family: in 1 Chronicles 26:30, there are 1,700 valiant men among them, tasked with overseeing the affairs of the Lord and the royal service.
H2276.portee: The Hebronites remind us that God organizes His people into families and lineages, each having a place and a specific responsibility in worship. This model shows how divine service is not an individual burden, but a family vocation passed down from generation to generation within the people of God.

sens: Member of the clan descended from Heber, son of Beria of the tribe of Asher
H2277.detail: 1. The Hebrites are the descendants of the patriarch Heber, who lived during the time of the Exodus and the desert. Heber was the son of Beria and a member of the tribe of Asher (Numbers 26:45). This name designates a family group or clan, similar to many collective names in Israel — just as we speak of the Benjaminites or the Judeans.
H2277.origine: The word Hebrite comes from Heber (חֶ֫בֶר, "Heber" in French), a man from the tribe of Asher. In Hebrew, a clan name is formed by adding a suffix to the patronymic: Heber becomes Hebrite, which literally means "those of Heber" or "the family of Heber." This usage is common in the Bible to designate groups descended from an ancestor: just as the Judeans descend from Judah, the Hebrites descend from Heber.
H2277.emploi: The Hebrites appear only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:45, during the counting of the Israelites after the forty years in the desert. Moses counts the families of the tribe of Asher, and Heber is listed as one of the sons of Beria, along with his brother Malkiel. The text enumerates the clans descended from these two men: the family of the Hebrites and that of the Malkielites. This unique usage shows the importance of this genealogy for the administrative and religious organization of Israel, particularly the distribution of land at the conquest of Canaan.

sens: Woman united to a man in marriage
Wife considered as a partner and ally
H2278.detail:
1. The word designates the woman of a man in the bond of marriage, emphasizing sharing and alliance rather than simple domination. In Malachi 2:14, the Lord calls the wife of your youth your "companion," the one with whom you have made a covenant, highlighting that she is your equal in this pact, not merely a possession.
2. By extension, the word emphasizes the dimension of communion: the companion is one who accompanies you, who is bound to you by a solemn promise. Therefore, rejecting her or being unfaithful constitutes a betrayal of this mutual commitment.
H2278.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be bound" or "to be joined." It belongs to the family of Hebrew words that express covenant, pact, and close association between two beings. Its meaning is based on the idea of a union contracted and sealed.
H2278.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Malachi 2:14. It is found in a prophetic oracle where the Lord reproaches the men of Israel for their unfaithfulness to their wives. The context is that of divorce and renunciation of covenant: the men were breaking with the wife of their youth, forgetting that she was their companion, their ally in the marriage covenant. This rare word underscores the importance that God attaches to the mutual commitment of marriage.
H2278.portee: This term reminds believers that marriage is not a relationship of unilateral submission, but a covenant where each is the equal and companion of the other before God. It invites one to see his wife not as a servant, but as one who shares life and commitment. It is a word of tenderness and respect that should shape the way one views the marital bond.

sens: Set of pieces joined together
Group of fabric panels of the tabernacle connected by loops
H2279.detail:
1. The word first designates an assembly: several elements brought together into a coherent whole. In the context of the tabernacle, it refers to panels of fabric that are joined together using blue loops. In Exodus 26:4, Moses commands: "You shall make loops of blue on the edge of the curtain of the first assembly" — we see that each assembly is composed of several curtains sewn together to form a large piece of fabric.
2. More specifically, the word designates one of the two main groups of panels that constitute the curtain of the tabernacle. According to Exodus 26:10, "fifty loops shall be made on the edge of the curtain of the first assembly, and fifty loops on the edge of the curtain of the second assembly." The two assemblies face each other and are connected by these loops, thus creating a complete and functional barrier for the holy dwelling.
H2279.origine: The word comes from the root חבר (ḥ-b-r), which means "to join" or "to bind together." This root evokes the action of gathering several disparate elements to make a unit. The word חֹבֶרֶת is a noun that receives this image: it is literally "that which is joined," the united thing. The same root is found in other biblical words expressing union or communion.
H2279.emploi: The word appears only three times in biblical Hebrew, and always in passages that describe the construction of the tabernacle (Exodus 26 and 36). It specifically designates the two large sections of the main curtain — each composed of five panels of fine linen, connected to each other by seams or loops. The usage is strictly architectural and technical: the word serves to clarify how the different fabric panels assemble to form a coherent and functional whole. It is a very precise construction term, with no figurative use in the Bible.
H2279.portee: This word reminds us that the tabernacle, God's dwelling among His people, is built with order and integrity. Each element — each panel, each loop — has its place and role in the whole. For the Christian reader, this evokes how the different members of the Church, in their diversity, are joined together to form one body. The assembly of the tabernacle reflects divine wisdom in which nothing is left to chance.

sens: to place a saddle on a pack animal
to attach, tie something around something
to bandage a wound, wrap a dressing
to hold upright, strengthen
to govern, direct
H2280.detail:
1. To saddle an animal means to put a saddle on its back to prepare it for travel or work (Genesis 22:3: Abraham saddles his donkey before departing). This is the basic image: securely attaching a saddle to the animal so that it can be ridden or loaded.
2. The verb expands to the idea of attaching, tying, fixing anything: putting a strap, a belt, a bandage. It is the action of tightening, surrounding to keep together or in place.
3. To bandage a wound means to wrap it with a band, to cover it to protect and heal (Isaiah 30:26: the Lord "will bandage" the wounds of His people, He will heal them). This is an act of care and restoration.
4. To strengthen means to make stable, solid, upright: one can bandage a wound so that it heals, bandage a man's arm so that it holds strong (Ezekiel 30:21: Pharaoh's arm was not "bound" to be strengthened).
5. Figuratively, to govern or reign means to "bandage" justice, that is, to direct it firmly, to maintain it in place (Job 34:17: would an enemy of justice "reign"?).
6. The general idea is one of obligation, constraint: to bandage is to tighten the ties, impose a limit or structure.
H2280.origine: The root ח-ב-ש (ch-v-sh) evokes the concrete gesture of binding, attaching, tying. It gives rise to other verbs of the same family in Hebrew that all revolve around this idea of encirclement and maintenance. The primary image is that of the hand that ties, that tightens the bonds to keep together. It is a very concrete word, drawn from daily life: bandaging wounds, saddling animals, binding prisoners are universal and eternal gestures.
H2280.emploi: This verb appears about thirty times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in narratives and wisdom poetry. Three-quarters of the usages refer to saddling donkeys and mules (Genesis 22:3, 1 Kings 13:23, 2 Samuel 16:1): this is the everyday context of the Near East, where saddling a pack animal is a very ordinary action. About a quarter of the usages employ the verb in the sense of bandaging or dressing a wound, a sore (Isaiah 30:26, Ezekiel 30:21, Psalms 147:3): this is the medical image of care. One or two passages use it figuratively to govern or direct (Job 34:17). The word does not carry a moral nuance, but it always conveys the idea of maintenance, firmness, structure.
H2280.portee: This word reminds the reader of two things. First, it shows that the Bible is grounded in the concrete, material world: it does not shy away from speaking of saddles and wounds. Secondly, when the Bible speaks of divine care (God bandages the wounds of His people), it adopts the language of humble and simple gestures, of the physician who tenderly wraps a wound. It is a God who heals as one repairs: with care, link by link.

sens: Flat and thin bread baked on a heated surface
Unleavened or slightly leavened cake
Offering for cultic use in the tabernacle
H2281.detail: 1. It is a very flat bread, baked directly on a heated plate or stone, unleavened or with very little leaven. The image is that of a thin and crispy cake, quite different from ordinary leavened bread that is baked in an oven (1 Chronicles 9:31 speaks of the cakes that the Levites prepared). 2. This type of bread was a simple, quick-to-prepare cake, often used for ritual offerings at the tabernacle or temple. It is made from fine flour, without elaborate flavor, intended for worship and the daily sustenance of the priests and attendants. 3. In Israelite worship, these cakes-plates were part of the grain offerings presented to God: it was a consecrated food, carefully prepared according to purity rules, as seen with Matthithia, who was responsible for it at the temple.
H2281.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to cover" or "to wrap," as the dough is spread thinly and covered by the heat of the plate. It literally designates a cake of this type, distinct from ordinary leavened bread. It is a specialized term for one of the breads used in Israelite worship, with no exact equivalent in our modern kitchens.
H2281.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 9:31, where it refers to the cakes-plates prepared by Matthithia, son of Shallum, one of the Levites in charge of the service of the tabernacle. His role was to prepare these cakes baked on the plate, which were included in the offerings and the worship service. The context shows that it was a precise and respected task assigned to a Levite of great importance.
H2281.portee: This word reminds us that the worship rendered to God in Israel was a daily worship: even simple and humble breads, baked on a plate, could be consecrated to God and become offerings. It is an invitation to sanctify the ordinary gestures of our lives.

sens: Religious celebration instituted by the law, with sacrifices and gathering of the people
Solemn assembly of believers gathered to honor God
Joy and feast accompanying the celebration
Offering or sacrifice presented on the occasion of a feast
Act of worship or honor towards God
H2282.detail:
1. A feast is an official religious celebration prescribed by the law of Moses, where the people of Israel gather to honor the Lord. Several feasts mark the religious year: Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles. Exodus 10:9 shows Moses declaring: "it is a feast for us in honor of the Lord," emphasizing the sacred nature of the event.
2. The feast involves an assembly: the multitude gathers in one place, often the temple. Deuteronomy 16:14 invites all members of the community — children, servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, widows — to "rejoice at this feast."
3. The feast is marked by joy, rejoicing, and feasting. It is a time of collective merriment where everyone celebrates together, with children and the elderly participating (Exodus 10:9).
4. The feast includes animal sacrifices offered to God according to precise rules: Exodus 34:25 mentions "the sacrifice of the feast" and its ritual provisions.
5. Broadly speaking, the feast becomes an act of honor and worship towards God: it is the heart of legitimate worship.
H2282.origine: The Hebrew word חַג comes from a root that evokes the idea of "dancing" or "moving in a circle," hence the meaning of a processional march or a celebration accompanied by movements. The same family produces words related to dance and festive rhythm. In the Old Testament, the word primarily designates the three major institutional pilgrimages (Passover, Weeks, Tabernacles) where Israel flocked to the temple in Jerusalem.
H2282.emploi: The word appears 55 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Pentateuch and historical books. Exodus and Deuteronomy establish the three major annual pilgrimages (Exodus 23:15-16, Deuteronomy 16:10-16). Leviticus 23 details the ritual rules for each feast. The kings of Judah and post-exilic restorers (Solomon, Nehemiah) celebrate the feasts solemnly: 2 Chronicles 7:8 reports that Solomon "celebrated the feast at that time for seven days." The prophets (Amos, Hosea) criticize impious feasts, without repentance, showing that the feast is pleasing to God only if it comes from a sincere heart.
H2282.portee: The feast teaches that the worship of God is a communal, joyful, and orderly act. It reveals that the encounter with the Lord is not dark or austere, but festive, bringing together children and widows in shared joy. It also shows that true joy comes from obedience to God and communal sharing, not from pride or injustice. For the Christian believer, the feast reminds us that faith is lived together and invites us to celebration, even in the midst of moral discipline.

sens: Intense and sudden fear that paralyzes
Deep disturbance that causes one to stagger
Consternation in the face of danger or threat
H2283.detail:
1. Terror is an extreme fear that seizes the soul and body when confronted with something terrifying or unexpected. It is that emotion that removes the ability to act or think. In Isaiah 19:17, the land of Judah becomes an object of terror for Egypt — meaning that its mere mention provokes insurmountable fear in those who hear it.
2. The word also evokes the idea of staggering, losing one's footing, as terror shakes the one who experiences it. Egypt, upon learning what the Lord has decided against it, finds itself in a state of dizziness and paralysis.
3. It is the consternation that overwhelms when one realizes that a formidable power has risen against them: it is not just fear, but the feeling of being crushed by a superior will against which one cannot defend themselves.
H2283.origine: The Hebrew word חָגָּא (chagga) expresses the idea of swirling, staggering under the impact of a violent emotion — hence the sense of terror that disturbs and causes one to lose balance. The root evokes the movement of one who is seized by panic and does not know where to turn. This word appears only once in the Bible, underscoring its particular emotional weight.
H2283.emploi: The word חָגָּא is used only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 19:17. It designates the terror that the people of Egypt will feel upon learning that the Lord of hosts has made a decision against them. In this context, it is the political and religious terror of the people in the face of a superior power — that of the living God whose will imposes itself on all human empires.
H2283.portee: This word reminds us that the fear of God and His power is a reality that reaches even the greatest peoples of the world. It invites us to meditate on the gravity of divine judgment: when the Lord decides something, no one can escape it, and this is a reason to serve Him with respect rather than fear Him as an enemy. For the believer, this terror of the unbelievers contrasts with the assurance that faith provides in the One who controls history.

sens: Flying insect with long legs that jumps and feeds on plants
Tiny creature compared to a giant or a powerful person
Plague sent by God to devastate crops
Symbol of human fragility in the face of divine immensity
H2284.detail:
1. The grasshopper is a well-known insect to the Hebrews: it has powerful hind legs that allow it to jump, wings for flying, and it devours the plants where it lands. Leviticus (11:22) mentions it among the clean insects that could be legally eaten.

2. When the explorers sent to Canaan compare themselves to grasshoppers (Numbers 13:33), they express their smallness in the face of the giants of the land: just as this insect is tiny compared to a man, they feel insignificant before Anak and his descendants. It is an image of humiliation and fear.

3. The grasshopper also becomes a plague. In 2 Chronicles 7:13, God promises to command the grasshoppers to consume the land as punishment: they come in swarms and annihilate the harvests, leaving famine in their wake.

4. In Ecclesiastes 12:7 and Isaiah 40:22, the grasshopper symbolizes extreme fragility: in the face of the coming age (Ecclesiastes), even what seemed heavy becomes burdensome; in the face of God who reigns over all the earth (Isaiah), the inhabitants of the world are but grasshoppers, infinitely small.
H2284.origine: The Hebrew word חָגָב (chagav) designates this insect found abundantly in the Middle East. It belongs to the family of arthropods that jump and fly. The term connotes both physical smallness and, by extension, insignificance or vulnerability. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this word was translated by equivalent terms designating the same insect.
H2284.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, in very varied contexts. In Leviticus, it is a permitted food for consumption. In Numbers, the explorers invoke it to express their helplessness. In 2 Chronicles, it becomes an instrument of divine judgment. In Ecclesiastes and Isaiah, it changes meaning: it is no longer a material plague, but a metaphor for human smallness. This progression from the concrete to the figurative shows how a simple animal word can carry an entire theology: from daily reality (the insect that is eaten) to the symbol of human nothingness before God.
H2284.portee: The grasshopper teaches us two spiritual lessons. First, it reminds us that our perception of ourselves can be misleading: in the face of obstacles, we see ourselves as grasshoppers, while God has given us the strength to overcome them. Secondly, it humbles our pride: even the greatest human achievements, viewed from the divine perspective, are fragile and fleeting like this insect. It invites us to find our strength not in ourselves, but in the one who is infinitely greater.

sens: Leader of a family of exiles returned from captivity
H2285.detail: Hagab is the name of a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return of the Judeans from captivity in Babylon. His name means "grasshopper" in Hebrew, but he is a man, the leader of a family whose descendants participated in the return under Zerubbabel after the decree of Cyrus. In Ezra 2:46, the families that returned are listed: "the sons of Hagab" appear in this official list, alongside other families of the same exiled origin.
H2285.origine: The name Hagab comes from the Hebrew חָגָב (chagav), which literally means "grasshopper." It was a common name in ancient Israel, where insects and animals provided simple and memorable personal names. Why this name? Perhaps it designated a quality of liveliness or agility, or simply recalled an event or circumstance at birth. Like many biblical proper names, the original meaning was no longer at the heart of the person's identity.
H2285.emploi: Hagab is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 2:46, within a long register of families who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem. This register was drawn up to establish who had the right to reside in the land and participate in the reconstruction of the Temple. Among the 42,360 repatriates, Hagab was the father or ancestor of one of these recognized families. The list is administrative and genealogical: it tells nothing of his personal life, but attests that his descendants had retained their identity and place within the people of God upon their return from exile.

sens: Leader of a family among the exiles returned with Zerubbabel
H2286A.detail: Lebana is a man whose name appears in the list of families that returned from exile in Babylon under the leadership of Zerubbabel, around 538 B.C. He is mentioned as the ancestor of a temple family, probably servants of the worship. His name is also found written as "Hagaba" in other biblical lists.
H2286A.origine: The name means "locust" in Hebrew, which suggests an ancient origin for the family nickname, although it is unusual for a personal name. Lebana and Hagaba are two forms of the same name, probably variants according to ancient transcriptions.
H2286A.emploi: Lebana appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 7:48, in the context of the return of the exiles. He is cited among the families of temple servants who returned from captivity with Zerubbabel. This official list records the different families and their importance in the restoration of the Jewish community.

sens: Man during the time of exile and return to Jerusalem
Leader of a family whose descendants returned with Zerubbabel
H2286B.detail:
1. Lebana is a man mentioned in the list of families that returned from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel, the leader of the return expedition. His name appears among the heads of families of temple servants (Ezra 2:45).
2. His descendants, called "the sons of Lebana," formed a well-established family in Jerusalem after the return from exile. This family was probably tasked with specific duties in the service of the rebuilt temple.
H2286B.origine: The name Lebana means "locust" in Hebrew. This type of animal name was common in antiquity, often given to express a quality or characteristic. The same man is also called Hagaba in Nehemiah 7:48, a variant of the same name, which shows that Hebrew names could have multiple forms depending on the contexts.
H2286B.emploi: Lebana is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 2:45, at the time of the return of the Babylonian exiles around 538 B.C. He appears in the official list of families of temple servants who participated in this great return organized by Zerubbabel. This same character is also cited in Nehemiah 7:48 under the name of Hagaba, confirming that it is the same man and his descendants in the records of the people returned from captivity.

sens: Hold a religious feast in honor of God
Fulfill a pilgrimage to God's sanctuary
Rejoice in dancing and feasting
To stagger or sway (figuratively or in the sense of losing balance)
H2287.detail:
1. Celebrating a religious feast means gathering the people to honor God through rites and festivities. This is what Moses asks Pharaoh: to let Israel go "so that they may celebrate a feast in the wilderness" in honor of the Lord (Exodus 5:1). The three major feasts — Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles — were celebrated each year according to the law.
2. Celebrating often involves a pilgrimage: setting out and presenting oneself before God at the place He has chosen. Deuteronomy 16:15 commands to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles for seven days "at the place the Lord your God will choose."
3. The celebration is marked by joy, dance, and shouts of gladness. Psalm 42:5 speaks of a "multitude in celebration" advancing toward the house of God "with shouts of joy and thanksgiving."
4. By extension, the word can describe a movement of swaying or dizziness: distressed sailors "staggered and swayed like a drunken man" (Psalms 107:27, where the same verb expresses this instability).
H2287.origine: The verb חָגַג comes from the root חג, which evokes the circular movement of one going on pilgrimage, or the dance during feasts. The root is related to the idea of turning around, circulating — as one does when going to a holy place or dancing. The word is specifically linked to religious pilgrimages and the feasts of Israel.
H2287.emploi: This verb appears 14 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the law books (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and in the Psalms and prophets. Its main meaning is religious: to celebrate the three major annual feasts of Israel. Exodus 23:14 states clearly: "Three times a year you shall celebrate feasts to me." Leviticus 23:41 and Deuteronomy 16:15 emphasize the joyful and lasting nature of these celebrations. In the Psalms (42:5, 107:27), the word expands: it denotes both festive joy and, metaphorically, instability. The prophets Nahum and Zechariah use it to urge Judah to celebrate the Lord's feasts.
H2287.portee: Understanding this word illuminates the central place of the feast in the faith of Israel. These religious celebrations were not mere distractions, but acts of worship and submission to God, occasions to remember His work and rejoice in His presence. For the Christian, this reminds us that authentic joy arises from communion with God and recognition of His action in our lives.

sens: Cavity, natural indentation in rock or stone
Refuge, secluded and protected place where one can hide
Steep and difficult-to-access place, natural fortress stronghold
H2288.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the cracks and cavities naturally carved in stone or rock: empty spaces, hollows. In the Song of Solomon (2:14), the beloved is invited to show herself from "the clefts of the rock" where she hides, like a bird nestled in a rocky crevice.
2. These cavities form natural refuges, safe places where one can retreat and hide from sight or danger. The hollow offers protection and intimacy.
3. By extension, the word evokes rocky heights, steep and difficult-to-access places that the powerful choose as impregnable strongholds — like Edom, which "dwells in the cleft of the rocks" (Jeremiah 49:16 and Obadiah 1:3), thinking itself safe from any threat in its natural fortress.
H2288.origine: The Hebrew word חֲגָוִים (chavguim) comes from a root expressing the idea of digging or splitting. It also appears in similar forms denoting empty spaces or interstices. It is the classic image of pierced rock, of the trodden cliff — the natural habitat of birds and wild beasts.
H2288.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the plural, and always in connection with rocks. Two occurrences (Jeremiah 49:16 and Obadiah 1:3) speak of Edom in nearly identical parallel terms: Edom boasts of dwelling in "the cleft of the rocks," thinking that its geographical inaccessibility will protect it from divine judgment — which will prove false. One occurrence (Song of Solomon 2:14) uses the word lyrically: the beloved is compared to a dove safely nestled "in the clefts of the rock."
H2288.portee: This word reminds us that the hollow of the rock can be both a refuge and an illusion. For Edom, trust in natural fortresses becomes pride and spiritual blindness: no earthly citadel escapes God's judgment. In contrast, in the Song, the hollow of the rock symbolizes a place of true intimacy and safety — the place where love finds its hidden and protected space. The Christian discovers that the true fortress is not built of stone.

sens: Wearing a belt around the waist
State of one who is dressed and equipped for action
Preparation for battle or travel
H2289.detail:
1. The word describes wearing a belt around the waist, which tightens the clothing. In Ezekiel 23:15, horsemen are described as "girded with belts" at the waist, showing how a belt cinches the garment and gives a controlled silhouette.
2. Being girded means being dressed and prepared to act, to move. A girded person is ready, equipped, adjusted in their attire.
3. Figuratively, this verb evokes preparation for effort, struggle, or travel: one girds oneself as one prepares mentally and materially for what is to come.
H2289.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to gird, to surround." It evokes the action of wrapping something around the body. It is a concrete word that paints the image of a belt that envelops and holds.
H2289.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 23:15, where the prophet describes Babylonian horsemen as young and strong men, "girded with belts" at the waist. In this context, the belt is a detail of the warrior's costume and Eastern prestige: it shows equipped men, imposing and warrior-like in appearance. The word emphasizes the virile and military aspect of these horsemen who impress with their appearance.
H2289.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, the belt is not just a simple accessory: it symbolizes preparation, strength, and self-control. Those who are girded are ready to act. It is an image that Jesus will take up when speaking of girding the loins of one's mind (1 Peter 1:13) to live a vigilant and active life.

sens: Strip of fabric or leather tied around the waist to hold clothing
Object of value or status, worn as a badge of dignity
Symbol of belonging or connection between people
H2290A.detail:
1. The belt is a strip that one ties around the waist to keep clothing in place and for convenience. It is a practical accessory of Eastern attire, often richly adorned. In 1 Samuel 18:4, Jonathan gives David his belt along with his robe, sword, and bow: it is a belt that represents something personal and precious.
2. As a badge of status or power, the belt carries particular significance: the one who wears it enjoys a certain authority or dignity. It can be ornate and signify a function or rank. In 2 Samuel 20:8, Joab wears a belt with his sword: it is part of his warrior equipment and his status as a commander.
3. When one gives their belt to someone else, it is a gesture of deep friendship, transfer of authority, or establishment of a covenant. It is an act filled with emotion and meaning, showing intimacy and trust between two people.
H2290A.origine: The Hebrew word חֲגוֹר (cha.gor) comes from the root חגר (cha.gar), which means "to gird, to bind, to prepare." This root evokes the action of girding one's loins before acting, preparing for effort or battle. The word is closely related to the idea of personal preparation and readiness.
H2290A.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the books of Samuel. In 1 Samuel 18:4, Jonathan removes his belt and gives it to David as a sign of covenant and brotherly friendship. In 2 Samuel 20:8, Joab wears a belt over his tunic with a sword at his side, emphasizing his warrior status and role as a military leader. In these two contexts, the belt is not just a useful garment: it is a significant personal object, carrying social and relational meaning.
H2290A.portee: The belt reminds us that simple gestures can be laden with deep meaning in relationships. When Jonathan gives his belt to David, he binds their friendship through this exchange of personal items; this invites us to reflect on what we share and how we seal our covenants. It is also an image of preparation: to gird oneself is to prepare to act, which resonates with the biblical call to be spiritually ready.

sens: garment or object tied around the waist
object of value, symbol of status or wealth
military equipment, armor
external sign of dignity or respectability
H2290B.detail:
1. The belt in the literal sense is a garment tied around the waist to hold clothing and cover nakedness. This is the first meaning encountered in the Bible: in Genesis 3:7, Adam and Eve, having become aware of their nakedness after sin, make themselves belts of fig leaves to cover themselves. It is a basic need of the human body in society.
2. In the ancient world, the belt was also an object of value that could be offered as a prize or reward. Joab promises to the one who kills Absalom not only ten shekels of silver but also a belt (2 Samuel 18:11), showing that the belt was worth something and marked a certain prestige.
3. The belt is military equipment, inseparable from armor and warrior gear. In 1 Kings 2:5, Joab's belt bears the mark of blood shed in battle: it is stained by his crimes. In 2 Kings 3:21, it is said that all the Moabites "of age to bear arms" rise to fight: the belt or armor is the equipment of the warrior.
4. The belt also symbolizes dignity, respectability, and social order. In Isaiah 3:24, in contrast to beauty and order, the proud woman of Jerusalem will have "a rope instead of a belt": the replacement of the beautiful belt by a coarse rope is a sign of humiliation and dishonor. In the virtuous woman of Proverbs 31:24, the belt she makes and sells is the fruit of her honest work.
H2290B.origine: The Hebrew word חֲגוֹרָה (hagorah) comes from the root חגר (hagar) which means "to gird, to surround." This root expresses the action of wrapping something around oneself, particularly around the waist. The word is thus formed on the concrete image of the very action of girding oneself. Related words denote the action of preparing, of girding oneself for action or battle, which explains why the belt is military equipment.
H2290B.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in historical narratives and wisdom literature. In Genesis 3:7, it is the basic garment covering nakedness. In 2 Samuel 18:11 and 1 Kings 2:5, it is an object of value or equipment worn in battle. In 2 Kings 3:21, "to bear arms" (literally "the belts") refers to military equipment. In the three occurrences in Proverbs 31:24 and Isaiah 3:24, the belt represents both a product of labor (what one makes and sells) and a symbol of social status and dignity. The meaning thus varies from the concrete (garment) to the symbolic (mark of wealth, honor, or function).
H2290B.portee: The belt in Scripture reminds us that the body needs clothing and covering: it is a sign of our condition as creatures made to live with dignity and order. It also evokes that human dignity is not in external ornamentation, but in the heart: in Isaiah 3:24, God strips Jerusalem of its fine belts to show her that no garment saves her if her heart is proud. For the Christian, the belt reminds us that we must "gird ourselves" with truth and prepare for righteous action (see Ephesians 6:14: the belt of truth).

sens: man of the tribe of Gad, son of Gad
descendant of Haggi, member of the clan of the Haggites
H2291.detail:
1. Haggi is the name of a man belonging to the tribe of Gad. He is presented as the second son of Gad in the list of Gad's children who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:16). He has several brothers: Ziphion, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
2. The name Haggi also becomes the name of the family clan descended from this man. The descendants of Haggi are called "Haggites" and form a recognized family within the tribe of Gad. When Moses conducts the census of the people in the wilderness, the Bible mentions "the family of the Haggites" as one of the branches of the tribe of Gad (Numbers 26:15).
H2291.origine: The name Haggi means "festive" or "one who celebrates," derived from the idea of feast or rejoicing. It is a typical personal name in biblical tradition, given to one of Gad's sons at the time of Jacob's settlement in Egypt.
H2291.emploi: Haggi appears twice in the Bible. First in Genesis 46:16, he is named among the seven sons of Gad who go down to Egypt during the famine in Joseph's time. Then, in Numbers 26:15, during the census conducted by Moses in the wilderness after the exodus from Egypt, the clan of the Haggites is mentioned as one of the families descended from Gad. These two occurrences show how a personal ancestor becomes the name of a recognized family lineage in the tribal structure of Israel.

sens: Prophet who ministered after the Babylonian exile
Messenger of the Lord tasked with urging the people to rebuild the temple
H2292A.detail:
1. Haggai is a prophet who spoke to the people of Judah after their return from the Babylonian exile, during the reign of King Darius. His name means "festive" or "celebratory," evoking joy. He is the first of the minor prophets to prophesy after the captivity (Haggai 1:1).

2. The Lord addresses the people through him to urge them to rebuild the Lord's temple, which they had neglected. Haggai acts as a messenger of the Lord, delivering His messages and commands with authority: "Haggai, the messenger of the Lord, spoke to the people, according to the command of the Lord: I am with you, says the Lord" (Haggai 1:13).
H2292A.origine: The name Haggai comes from a Hebrew root meaning "feast" or "celebration." This name expresses joy and solemnity. Haggai is the tenth of the twelve minor prophets and the first to prophesy after the Babylonian captivity. His ministry takes place around 520 BC, a few years after the return of the exiles under the leadership of Zerubbabel.
H2292A.emploi: Haggai appears nine times in the book that bears his name. He is presented as the prophet through whom the Lord addresses Governor Zerubbabel and High Priest Joshua (Haggai 1:1). His messages cover several specific dates: the first day of the sixth month, then the seventh month and the ninth month of the second year of King Darius. Haggai conveys words of encouragement and exhortation. The people hear his voice and recognize that he speaks according to the mission the Lord has entrusted to him (Haggai 1:12). His prophecies aim to revive the reconstruction of the temple, which had been abandoned.
H2292A.portee: Haggai shows that God never abandons His people, even after exile and the destruction of the temple. His ministry invites believers to prioritize what honors God, rather than being solely concerned with their own homes. Through Haggai, the Lord reminds that He is present with His people and accompanies them in restoring their worship. The courage that God instills through this prophet encourages every believer in times of difficulty.

sens: Jewish prophet during the exile and return
One who encouraged the rebuilding of the temple after the Babylonian captivity
H2292B.detail:
1. Haggai is a prophet who lived at the time when the Jews were returning from captivity in Babylon. He is first mentioned in Ezra 5:1, where he is presented alongside Zechariah as a prophet speaking on behalf of the God of Israel.
2. His main role was to encourage the Jewish elders to rebuild the temple: in Ezra 6:14, it is noted that the construction of the temple was done "according to the prophecies of Haggai." He is the first prophet to have spoken after the Babylonian captivity, making him an important figure in the return to Jerusalem.
H2292B.origine: The name Haggai means "festive" or "one who is of the feast" in Hebrew (חַגַּי), perhaps evoking a joyful character or a word of celebration. It is a simple and direct name borne by this prophet of the return. The book that bears his name in the Old Testament records his prophecies.
H2292B.emploi: Haggai appears twice in the provided biblical references, always in the book of Ezra. In Ezra 5:1, he is presented as a prophet alongside Zechariah, speaking to the Jews returned to Judah and Jerusalem. In Ezra 6:14, his prophecies are mentioned as having guided the rebuilding of the temple, alongside those of Zechariah. These two passages show that Haggai played a central role in encouraging the people to resume the temple work after the end of the exile.
H2292B.portee: Haggai embodies the importance of prophetic word to restore the faith and obedience of a distressed people. His ministry during the return from exile reminds us that God never ceases to speak to His people, even in the darkest moments. For the Christian reader, he symbolizes how God raises up prophets to call His people to serve Him faithfully and restore the worship that is due to Him.

sens: Levite from the tribe of Merari during the divided monarchy
H2293.detail: Haggiah is a man of the tribe of Levi, belonging to the Merarite branch (one of the three Levitical families).
