He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:30, where he appears in the genealogy of the Levites responsible for temple service. He is the son of Shimea and the father of Asaiah, placing him in the time of the divided monarchy (after the separation of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah).
H2293.origine: His name means "feast of God" or "festival of Jehovah" in Hebrew (chag = feast, God = Jehovah). It is a typical theophoric name from ancient Israel, where parents gave their children names that recalled God's actions or religious celebrations.
H2293.emploi: Haggiah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:30. This verse is part of a long genealogical list of the Levites during the divided monarchy, enumerating their descendants and their functions at the temple. His unique mention underscores the importance of Levitical genealogies in tracing the legitimacy of worship and divine service across generations.

sens: A woman of the united monarchy, wife of King David
Mother of Prince Adonijah
H2294.detail: Haggith is one of the wives of King David. She appears in the accounts of the royal succession at the time when King David is aged. Her son Adonijah, an ambitious prince, seeks to seize the throne: "Adonijah, the son of Haggith, exalted himself, saying: I will be king!" (1 Kings 1:5). Although she is the mother of a claimant to the throne, no personal act is attributed to her in the Bible; she appears in the royal genealogies as a link in the Davidic lineage.
H2294.origine: The name Haggith means "festive" or "she who celebrates." It comes from a Hebrew root denoting feast or celebration. This name evokes an atmosphere of joy and rejoicing, although its bearer in the biblical narrative is the mother of a son who seeks to disrupt the succession order established by God.
H2294.emploi: Haggith is mentioned five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the context of the final events of David's reign and the royal succession (2 Samuel 3:4; 1 Kings 1:5, 1:11; 2:13; 1 Chronicles 3:2). She primarily appears as the mother of Adonijah when he attempts to usurp the kingship. The prophet Nathan reminds Bathsheba: "Have you not heard that Adonijah, the son of Haggith, has become king?" (1 Kings 1:11), emphasizing the filial connection. She never directly intervenes in the action; it is her maternal status that places her at the heart of the dynastic issues.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Manasseh during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness journey
H2295.detail: Hogla is one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, a man from the tribe of Manasseh, a descendant of Joseph. Her name means "partridge" in Hebrew. She first appears in the census of the people in the wilderness (Numbers 26:33), always mentioned alongside her four sisters: Mahlah, Noah, Milcah, and Tirzah. Along with her sisters, Hogla plays an important role in biblical history: she petitions Moses to obtain her deceased father's inheritance, who died without sons (Numbers 27:1-5), which results in a new law allowing daughters to inherit when there are no sons. She then marries a cousin of her father and retains the family inheritance within her tribe (Numbers 36:11). She is also mentioned in the book of Joshua during the division of the land (Joshua 17:3).
H2295.origine: The name Hogla, which means "partridge," likely comes from a Hebrew root evoking this bird. It is a characteristic feminine proper name from the patriarchal and wilderness period. The five daughters of Zelophehad form an important group in the genealogy of Manasseh and become notable figures in the Old Testament through their request for equal inheritance rights.
H2295.emploi: Hogla is mentioned four times in the Bible, always closely linked with her sisters. She first appears in the census of Numbers 26:33, then in the decisive scene where she and her sisters ask Moses for the right to inherit from their father (Numbers 27:1). The text mentions her again when she marries according to the conditions set by the new law (Numbers 36:11), and finally in the division of the land after the conquest (Joshua 17:3). In each mention, she is always named among her four sisters, never isolated, which emphasizes the unity of this sibling group and the collective importance of their act.
H2295.portee: The story of Hogla and her sisters teaches Christians that God cares about justice for the weak and marginalized. These women, without a father or brothers, should have lost all rights to inheritance according to custom; instead, they changed the law through their courage and faith. Their example shows that God's will can correct injustices and that humble petition before God can obtain grace and equity. It is a sign of the dignity that God grants to each person, including those whom human structures threaten to forget.

sens: To tie a belt or band around the waist or loins
To put on a garment, to don or to wear
To equip oneself for battle or travel
To cover oneself with a garment of mourning or penitence
To inhabit or envelop (speaking of a quality or strength)
H2296.detail:
1. To gird is primarily to fasten a belt around one's waist. In Exodus 12:11, the Israelites must eat the Passover "with their loins girded," ready to depart quickly on a journey. It is the image of someone rolling up their garments and preparing for action.

2. The word also refers to the action of putting on a garment, particularly priestly or ceremonial clothing. In Leviticus 8:7, the high priest is "girded" with his ephod (liturgical garment), which means to dress him completely. It is to put something on oneself to be clothed with it.

3. To gird can mean to equip oneself with weapons or battle attire. In Judges 18:11, the six hundred men of Dan depart "armed" with their weapons, expressing the idea of preparing for battle by arming oneself.

4. In times of mourning or repentance, girding oneself with sackcloth (a coarse fabric) is a gesture of lamentation. In 2 Samuel 3:31, the people are asked to "gird themselves with sackcloth" to mourn Abner; in Jeremiah 4:8, God calls His children to "cover themselves with sackcloth" as a sign of affliction.

5. The verb is also used figuratively to express a quality or strength that one is clothed with. In Psalms 76:11, the Lord "girds" Himself with His wrath, as if anger envelops His person and presence.
H2296.origine: The word חָגַר (hagar) comes from an ancient Semitic root expressing the idea of tightening, surrounding, or fastening. The basic image is that of a band or cord that wraps around the body. The root is common to the Semitic languages of the Levant (Arabic hajara). It concretely evokes the act of girding one's loins with a belt, a daily act in antiquity that becomes a symbolic act of preparation, dignity, or affliction.
H2296.emploi: The verb appears 41 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in historical and prophetic narratives. In contexts of preparation for travel or battle, girding expresses urgency and vigilance (Exodus 12:11, Deuteronomy 1:41, Judges 18:11, 1 Samuel 25:13). In priestly or liturgical contexts, girding describes the official vesting of the priest (Leviticus 8:7-13, 16:4). In passages of lamentation and repentance, the verb takes the form of "girding oneself with sackcloth," marking humiliation and repentance (2 Samuel 3:31, Jeremiah 4:8, Ezekiel 7:18). It is also used poetically or prophetically to describe a quality or power enveloping a person: God who girds Himself with wrath (Psalms 76:11, Isaiah 22:12), a king who girds himself with strength (Psalms 45:4). The meaning varies slightly depending on the context: practical and daily action, formal religious gesture, or symbolic language of affliction and power.
H2296.portee: This word reminds Christians that the preparation of heart and body to obey God is important. Approaching Him or committing to serve Him requires a vigilant and composed mindset, like that of Israel eating the Passover "with their loins girded." The act of girding oneself with sackcloth also speaks to the believer of sincere repentance: it is not just an internal matter, but something that visibly manifests in the humility of heart. Finally, the image of God girding Himself with His strength or wrath invites recognition of His majesty and power, which cannot be dressed or undressed at will.

sens: The cardinal number 1
Alone, unique, without another
Identical, the same
First in a series
Once, a single occasion
H2297.detail:
1. The word denotes the number one, that is, the simplest unit, what counts as 1 (Ezekiel 33:30: "one says to another").
2. It can mean "alone" or "unique": that which exists without sharing, without being accompanied by another.
3. It also expresses identity or similarity: "the same," that which has not changed, that which remains identical to itself.
4. It can mark the first rank or the first position in a succession.
5. It indicates a single time, a unique occurrence (the idea of "once" rather than multiple times repeated).
H2297.origine: The Hebrew word חַד (chad) belongs to the family of simple numbers in ancient Semitic. Its Aramaic equivalent חַד (chad) appears in the Aramaic texts of the Bible. The word expresses the most elementary idea: that which is one, indivisible, whole. It is the foundation upon which all other numbers are built.
H2297.emploi: This word appears once in the provided usages: in Ezekiel 33:30, where it is used to mark plurality by nuance ("one says to another"). Although rare in classical biblical Hebrew, חַד is common in biblical Aramaic to denote the number one, often in narrative or vision contexts. Its use nuances the idea of unity: not simply "one," but "one among others" or "one single moment." It is a technical word for counting, classifying, and distinguishing elements in a series.
H2297.portee: This word reminds the reader of the value of unity and singularity. In the Christian faith, it emphasizes that each believer counts as one before God, and that even a single prayer, a single act of faith carries weight. It also invites recognition of the uniqueness of God and His action: what is unique cannot be replaced.

sens: Who comes first in a series, starting a succession
Who is found alone or gathered with others at the same time or place
H2298.detail:
1. The word designates what occurs first in time or order. In "the first year of Cyrus" (Ezra 5:13), it marks the beginning of a period, like a starting date. It is the commencement of a sequence of years, the starting point of a reign.
2. It can also mean "at the same time" or "together," when several things are gathered in a single moment or act. In Daniel 2:35, the iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold are broken "together," meaning all at once, at the same instant.
H2298.origine: This Hebrew word is very ancient and fundamental in Semitic languages. It designates the number one and unity, from which the idea of "first" (the one who is one before others) and "together" (gathered in a single moment) naturally arises. The root evokes uniqueness and beginning.
H2298.emploi: This word appears 14 times in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which are in Aramaic (northwestern dialect). It is mainly used for dates — "the first year" of a king — and for the chronology of narratives. It is also found in the sense of "following" for the order of presentation of a text (Ezra 4:8: "the following letter"). Sometimes it marks simultaneity, as in Daniel 2:35 where several metals fall at the same time.
H2298.portee: This word reminds us of the biblical importance of order and beginning. When Scripture emphasizes "the first year" of a king, it marks how God orders history in time. It is an invitation to recognize that God controls the beginnings and seasons of our lives.

sens: That cuts sharply and effectively
That pierces or wounds, in a literal or figurative sense
That is sharp, pointed, honed
H2299.detail:
1. Tranchant primarily describes the weapon or tool that cuts well: a razor (Ezekiel 5:1), an arrow (Isaiah 49:2), or a sword (Proverbs 5:4) that strikes with precision and force. It is the image of the edge of a blade biting into the material.

2. The word then applies to what pierces or wounds the soul, such as a perverse tongue (Psalms 57:5) or the bitterness of an unfaithful woman (Proverbs 5:4): it no longer targets just physical cutting, but moral pain, the blow that reaches the heart.

3. Tranchant finally characterizes everything that is sharpened, pointed, and honed, ready to act with effectiveness and clarity.
H2299.origine: The Hebrew word חַד (chad) comes from a root that evokes the idea of pointing, piercing, becoming sharp. It is found in neighboring Semitic languages with the same meaning. The basic image is that of something being refined, becoming pointed and dangerous, like a sharpened blade or the tip of a sword. It is a very concrete word, linked to the daily life of fighters and craftsmen.
H2299.emploi: The word חַד appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe objects or words that pierce, wound, or cut. In the Psalms (57:5), it qualifies the tongue of the psalmist's enemies, metaphorically dangerous like a weapon. In Proverbs (5:4), it paints the bitterness of seduction as something painful and sharp. In Isaiah (49:2), it applies to the word of the Lord, compared to a sharp sword: it indicates its strength and effectiveness. In Ezekiel (5:1), it is a razor, a tool in the literal sense. The biblical usage thus unites the concrete (weapons, tools) and the figurative (words, feelings).
H2299.portee: This word reminds the believer that the word of God has an active power: it will not flatter, it penetrates defenses and reaches the heart (Isaiah 49:2). It also warns of the danger of wicked or seductive words, which wound like a blade. Recognizing the sharpness of the Word is to be prepared to be transformed by it, for good or for judgment.

sens: To become aged, to reach an advanced age
To be in old age, to have gray hair or lose strength
To show signs of aging
H2204.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is simply the process of aging: passing time and becoming old. This is what happens to Isaac in Genesis 27:1 — "Isaac was getting old, and his eyes were dim" — or to Samuel in 1 Samuel 8:1 — "When Samuel became old." It is the universal experience of the body advancing in time.
2. The word also denotes the established state of old age, the condition of one who is now aged. Sarah is old in Genesis 18:12 — she laughs at the idea of having a child now that she can no longer bear children. Joshua says of himself in Joshua 23:2: "I am old, I am advanced in age," to signify that he can no longer lead battles.
3. Sometimes the word carries the idea of showing one's age, of giving visible signs of old age. Barzillai in 2 Samuel 19:32 is not just old — he is described as "very old, being eighty years old," which highlights how his age is seen and felt in the fatigue of the journey.
H2204.origine: The Hebrew root za.qen expresses the idea of time accumulating on a person and aging them. In Hebrew, the same word can be an adjective ("old," "aged") or a verb ("to grow old"). The Hebrew word is also the origin of the term "zaquin," which means "ancient" — one who has age and therefore experience. The central idea is that of time: the longer one lives, the older one becomes.
H2204.emploi: This verb appears 26 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the narratives of Genesis and the Historical Books. It is used to describe aging patriarchs — Abraham, Isaac, Joshua — at moments of transition where their age becomes an issue for the transmission of authority or the fulfillment of divine promises. The word often emphasizes the weight of age: not only are Sarah and Isaac old, but their bodies bear the marks (dim eyes, fatigue from the journey). The verb also appears in Proverbs 22:6 ("Train up a child in the way he should go; when he is old, he will not depart from it"), where it underscores the persistence of habits formed in youth. The context shows that aging, in the Bible, is also moving from strength to a form of weakness, or to the wisdom of experience.
H2204.portee: To grow old, in the Bible, is not a shame but a reality that God governs. The patriarchs grow old but God still acts — Sarah becomes pregnant despite her age, Isaac blesses his sons before dying. For the believer, this word reminds us that age changes our role but does not distance us from God. It also invites us to receive instruction from those who are advanced in age, as Proverbs 23:22 says.

sens: Person of advanced age, having lived long
Man vested with authority and responsibility in a community
Advisor or judge to a leader or institution
H2205G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who has reached an advanced age, who has gray hair and the wisdom that comes with experience. This is the simplest and most natural meaning of the word.
2. It then applies to those who, due to their seniority or recognition among the people, hold authority: the elders form a council or assembly that governs and judges. In Israel, they are summoned by Moses (Exodus 3:16) and testify to important transactions, such as during the redemption of Boaz (Ruth 4:9).
3. In parallel with other leaders or magistrates, the elder represents wisdom and guidance within a society — one who is listened to and respected. Isaiah 9:14 associates him with the head of a people, in contrast to those who mislead.
H2205G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "beard" or what is "ancient." The image is clear: one who has a long white beard is old, and this seniority confers authority and credibility. This is why the same word comes to mean not only "old man" but also "one who governs," "counselor," or "judge": in ancient societies, age and experience are the foundations of power.
H2205G.emploi: The word appears 123 times in the Old Testament, particularly in the Pentateuch and the historical books. It regularly designates the elders of Israel or of a people, summoned for public affairs: they judge an unintentional homicide (Deuteronomy 21:2-6), testify to a contract or marital infidelity (Deuteronomy 22:15-18; Ruth 4:9), and advise the leader. Moses gathers them at Mount Sinai (Exodus 24:1, 9) and later, seventy elders receive the Spirit (Numbers 11:24-25). The term can also simply apply to elderly people (Genesis 50:7), but its political usage dominates: the elders are the guardians of order and law in a community.
H2205G.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize the value of experience and wisdom accumulated over the years. It shows that God entrusts authority and judgment to those who have matured and who know life. For the Christian, it is a call to respect the experience of those who have gone before and not to despise age, even in a modern culture that often values youth. It is also a model of exercising power: the elders of Israel do not rule in solitude, but in assembly, for the good of the people.

H2205H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates an elderly person, marked by the weight of years. Abraham and Sarah are described as "old," advanced in age, unable to conceive children (Genesis 18:11). It is the physical state: the body worn by time.

2. Beyond age, the old man is one who has seen and experienced many things. He carries within him the knowledge of past generations and the wisdom acquired. Job, "old and full of days" (Job 42:17), embodies this fullness.

3. On a social and political level, the old man is a man of authority. The "elders" surrounding King Rehoboam are his advisors: they served his father, Solomon, and their experience makes them worthy of guiding (2 Chronicles 10:6). It is a charge, a leadership role.
H2205H.origine: The Hebrew root means "to have a long beard" or "to be bearded," a characteristic trait of the mature man. The old man bears the visible mark of his age. The word is also used for "elder" in the sense of one who precedes, who has the experience of the past.
H2205H.emploi: The word appears 49 times in the Hebrew Bible. It primarily designates the old man in the literal sense: Abraham, Sarah, Job. But very often it takes on an institutional and political meaning. The elders form a council, a class of sages who govern or advise: around Solomon (1 Kings 12:6), in the cities (Jeremiah 6:11). The Law itself commands to rise before gray hair and honor the old man (Leviticus 19:32), a sacred recognition of his status. The word can also simply designate a person of all ages, as a category: children and old men perish together at judgment (Isaiah 65:20). In Joel's vision, the Spirit will be poured out on all, young and old (Joel 2:28).
H2205H.portee: The old man reminds the Christian that the length of days is a divine gift to be honored. The Bible invites the young to respect the experience and wisdom of age (Leviticus 19:32) — which speaks even today, in a culture often eager for youth. Conversely, the old receive a promise: in the new world, no one will perish in the prime of life; all will fulfill their days (Isaiah 65:20). It is a consolation and an exhortation to look towards eternity.
